41252.q: Which UN body can decide on embargoes that are binding on all member states?
41252.e: Only the UN Security Council can decide on sanctions that all UN members must follow. The General Assembly can only make recommendations.
41252.m: Binding UN embargoes are decided by the Security Council.

41253.q: Against which country did the UN Security Council impose a binding arms embargo in 1977 because of racial segregation?
41253.e: At that time South Africa had apartheid, a policy of racial segregation. In 1977 the Security Council responded with a binding arms embargo.
41253.m: Because of apartheid, there was an arms embargo against South Africa from 1977.

41254.q: After which event did the UN impose a comprehensive embargo against Iraq in 1990?
41254.e: Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990. Switzerland adopted this embargo at the time, even though it was not yet a UN member.
41254.m: After the attack on Kuwait in 1990, the UN imposed an embargo on Iraq.

41255.q: What is the Swiss law called that allows the Federal Council to implement international sanctions?
41255.e: With the Embargo Act, the Federal Council can adopt sanctions of the UN and of important trading partners such as the EU. It has been in force since 2003.
41255.m: The Embargo Act allows the Federal Council to implement sanctions.

41258.q: Which federal body is responsible for implementing economic sanctions in Switzerland?
a: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs SECO
The Federal Office of Public Health
The Federal Office for the Environment
41258.e: SECO implements the sanctions and checks that they are followed. Companies and banks must, for example, report frozen assets to it.

41259.q: From which international messaging system for payments were many Russian banks excluded in 2022?
41259.e: Banks around the world exchange messages for transfers via SWIFT. Without access, payments abroad become very difficult for the banks affected.
41259.m: Many Russian banks were excluded from SWIFT.

41260.q: Why did many countries want to buy less oil from Russia from 2022?
a: So that Russia has less money for the war
Because Russian oil is too thin
Because Russia has no more oil
41260.e: Selling oil brings Russia a lot of money. Sanctions such as a price cap were meant to reduce this income.
41260.m: Sanctions are meant to take away Russia’s income for the war.

41261.q: What are goods called that can be used for both civilian and military purposes and therefore may not be delivered to Russia?
41261.e: Dual-use goods have a double purpose, for example certain electronics or machine tools. Exporting them to Russia is banned so that they do not end up in weapons.
41261.m: Dual-use goods can be used for civilian and military purposes.

41262.q: What are very rich and influential Russian businesspeople called, some of whose assets were frozen?
41262.e: Oligarchs are very rich people with great influence on the economy and politics. Many of them are on sanctions lists, and their accounts and yachts were frozen.
41262.m: Rich Russian businesspeople with a lot of power are called oligarchs.

41263.q: Which principle of Swiss foreign policy was particularly debated when Switzerland adopted the Russia sanctions in 2022?
41263.e: Switzerland is a neutral state. The Federal Council argued that economic sanctions are compatible with the law of neutrality, which was politically controversial.
41263.m: The sanctions against Russia also raised the question of Swiss neutrality.

41264.e: Banking secrecy forbids banks from passing on information about their customers to third parties. So it protects financial privacy.
41264.m: Banking secrecy protects bank customers’ data.

41265.q: In which law is Swiss banking secrecy set out?
41265.e: The Banking Act of 1934 makes breaking banking secrecy a criminal offence. But the duty of confidentiality existed even before that.
41265.m: Banking secrecy is in the Banking Act.

41266.q: What do bank employees in Switzerland face if they break banking secrecy?
a: Nothing, if the customer lives abroad
Just a talk with the boss
41266.e: Anyone who breaks banking secrecy can be punished with a fine or a prison sentence. This is set out in the Banking Act.
41266.m: Breaking banking secrecy is a criminal offence.

41267.q: What is the procedure called by which Switzerland reports account data of foreign customers to their home countries?
41267.e: Since 2017 Swiss banks have collected data for the automatic exchange of information, and in 2018 it was exchanged for the first time. This way tax authorities in other countries find out about their citizens’ accounts in Switzerland.
41267.m: The automatic exchange of information has loosened banking secrecy for foreigners.

41268.q: Which big Swiss bank handed over customer data to the US authorities in 2009?
41268.e: UBS had helped US customers hide money from the tax authorities. In 2009, under pressure from the USA, customer data was handed over, which badly shook banking secrecy.
41268.m: The UBS case in 2009 shook banking secrecy.

41269.q: Because of a US law, whose accounts must Swiss banks report to the US tax authorities?
41269.e: Because of the US law FATCA, Swiss banks too must report accounts of US persons to the US tax authorities.
41269.m: Swiss banks report US citizens’ accounts to the USA.

41270.q: Which organisation based in Paris strongly pushed for the exchange of tax data between states?
41270.e: The OECD developed the international standard for the automatic exchange of account data. In 2009 Switzerland was even briefly on an OECD “grey list”.
41270.m: The OECD pushed for more exchange of tax data.

41271.q: For people living in Switzerland, towards which authorities does banking secrecy still largely apply?
a: Towards the police in criminal cases
41271.e: Swiss tax authorities usually cannot demand account data directly from the bank for residents of Switzerland. In criminal proceedings, however, banks must provide information.
41271.m: At home, banking secrecy still protects against the tax authorities.

41272.q: What does the abbreviation OPEC stand for?
a: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
Order for Prices and Energy Costs
41272.e: The members of OPEC are states that produce and sell a lot of crude oil.
41272.m: OPEC is the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.

41273.q: Which part of the world do many OPEC members come from?
41273.e: Many OPEC countries, such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran and Kuwait, are in the Middle East. There are very large oil reserves there. OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960.
41273.m: Many OPEC countries are in the Middle East.

41274.q: In which city does OPEC have its headquarters today?
41274.e: OPEC has had its headquarters in Vienna, the capital of Austria, since 1965. The oil ministers meet there regularly.

41275.q: In which Swiss city was OPEC based before it moved in 1965?
41275.e: OPEC was based in Geneva from 1961 to 1965. Because Switzerland did not give it diplomatic status at the time, it moved to Austria.
41275.m: OPEC was at home in Geneva at first.

41276.q: Which African country is a member of OPEC?
41276.e: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971 and is one of Africa’s biggest oil producers. South Africa, Kenya and Morocco produce hardly any oil.
41276.m: Nigeria is an African OPEC member.

a: OPEC together with other oil states such as Russia
An oil field in the sea
A type of oil with especially high energy
41277.e: Since 2016 the OPEC countries have coordinated with other producing countries, such as Russia, Kazakhstan and Mexico. Together they control a large share of oil production.
41277.m: OPEC+ includes OPEC and other oil states.

41278.q: How many litres of oil fit into a barrel, the unit in which the oil price is given?
41278.e: A barrel is a unit of measurement for oil and is about 159 litres. Oil prices are usually given in US dollars per barrel.
41278.m: A barrel of oil holds about 159 litres.

41279.q: What did Switzerland introduce during the oil crisis in autumn 1973 to save petrol?
41279.e: When the Arab oil states delivered less oil in 1973, the price rose sharply. In November and December 1973 Switzerland ordered three car-free Sundays.
41279.m: During the 1973 oil crisis, Switzerland had car-free Sundays.

41280.q: What usually happens to the oil price when OPEC decides to produce less oil?
41280.e: When less oil comes onto the market but demand stays the same, oil becomes scarcer. That is why the price usually rises.
41280.m: Less oil production usually makes the oil price rise.

a: All the steps from the raw material to the finished product for the customer
A chain used to secure lorries
A row of shops belonging to one company
41281.e: A supply chain includes extracting raw materials, manufacturing, transport and sale. Companies from many countries are often involved.
41281.m: A supply chain goes from the raw material to the customer.

41282.q: Which important canal for world trade links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea?
41282.e: Many ships travelling between Asia and Europe pass through the Suez Canal in Egypt. When the ship “Ever Given” blocked it for six days in 2021, deliveries around the world were delayed.
41282.m: The Suez Canal is an important route for supply chains.

41283.q: What are the large standardised metal boxes called in which goods are carried on ships?
41283.e: Containers have standard sizes. That makes it easy to move them from a ship onto a train or lorry.
41283.m: Goods travel on ships in standardised containers.

41284.q: What is it called when a factory has parts delivered exactly when they are needed?
41284.e: With just-in-time, a factory hardly needs a warehouse. But if a delivery fails, production quickly comes to a standstill.
41284.m: Just-in-time means delivery at exactly the right time.

41285.q: Which components were missing worldwide in 2021 and 2022 and badly slowed down car production?
41285.e: During the coronavirus pandemic, computer chips (semiconductors) became scarce. Many car factories had to stop production for a time.
41285.m: Missing computer chips slowed down the car industry in 2021.

41286.q: On which river can cargo ships travel from the North Sea to Switzerland?
41286.e: The Rhine is navigable for large cargo ships as far as Basel. Containers and heating oil, for example, come into the country through the Swiss Rhine ports.
41286.m: Switzerland is linked to the sea by the Rhine.

41287.q: Why did the Responsible Business Initiative, which wanted to make companies liable for their supply chains, fail in 2020?
a: It did not get a majority of the cantons
It did not get a majority of the people
41287.e: On 29 November 2020 the initiative won a narrow majority of the votes. But it was rejected by the majority of cantons and so it failed.
41287.m: The Responsible Business Initiative failed in 2020 because of the majority of cantons.

41288.q: Which Swiss city is an especially important trading centre for oil?
41288.e: Several of the world’s biggest oil trading companies have their headquarters in Geneva. The city is one of the most important commodity trading centres in the world.
41288.m: Geneva is a centre of the world oil trade.

41289.q: In which canton do many commodity companies have their headquarters, including Glencore in Baar?
41289.e: The canton of Zug is a popular location for companies because of low taxes. The commodity group Glencore has its headquarters in Baar.
41289.m: The canton of Zug is an important location for commodity companies.

a: Goods are bought and sold without coming to Switzerland
Goods are carried through Switzerland by train
Customs duties are paid on goods at the border
Goods are sold only in Switzerland
41290.e: In merchanting, a Swiss company buys copper in Chile, for example, and sells it to China. Switzerland never sees the goods.
41290.m: In merchanting, the goods never cross the Swiss border.

41291.q: Which raw material is processed in large refineries in Ticino?
41291.e: Several of the world’s biggest gold refineries are in Ticino. There gold is cast into bars that are traded around the world.
41291.m: In Ticino a lot of gold is made into bars.

41292.q: Why have many commodity companies settled in Switzerland?
a: Because of low taxes and political stability
Because of its own ore mines
41292.e: Switzerland itself has hardly any raw materials. But companies value low taxes, stability, a strong financial centre and the central location in Europe.
41292.m: Switzerland is a trading centre for raw materials, even though it has hardly any itself.

41293.q: Besides Geneva and Zug, in which Ticino city are there also many commodity trading companies?
41293.e: Lugano is Switzerland’s third important commodity trading centre. Companies there deal mainly in metals and agricultural goods.
41293.m: Lugano is a commodity trading centre in Ticino.

41294.q: Which of these raw materials is an agricultural commodity?
41294.e: Agricultural commodities come from farming, for example coffee, wheat or sugar. Copper and aluminium are metals, and crude oil is an energy commodity.
41294.m: Coffee is a raw material from farming.

41295.q: What are raw materials traded on the exchange called in English?
41295.e: Commodities are uniform raw materials such as oil, wheat or copper that are traded in large quantities. Securities, on the other hand, are financial papers such as shares.
41295.m: In trade, raw materials are called commodities.

41296.q: Which president is a famous guest bedroom in the White House named after?
41296.e: The Lincoln Bedroom served Abraham Lincoln as his office. There he signed the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
41296.m: The Lincoln Bedroom is named after Abraham Lincoln.

41297.q: What is the room called in the White House where the president discusses crises with the military and intelligence services?
41297.e: The Situation Room is in the basement of the West Wing. In a crisis, all the important information comes together there.
41297.m: The president discusses crises in the Situation Room.

41298.q: What is the famous office of the US president in the White House called?
41298.e: The Oval Office has an oval shape and is in the West Wing of the White House. The president receives guests and signs laws there.
41298.m: The president of the USA works in the Oval Office.

41299.q: What is the garden next to the Oval Office called, where celebrations and press events often take place?
41299.e: The Rose Garden is right next to the Oval Office. It was laid out in 1913 and is used for receptions and speeches.
41299.m: The White House garden is called the Rose Garden.

41300.q: What often takes place in the East Room, the largest room in the White House?
41300.e: The East Room is the largest room in the main building of the White House. Receptions, concerts and press conferences take place there.
41300.m: Receptions and concerts take place in the East Room.

41301.q: What is the address of the White House?
41301.e: The White House is at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW in Washington, D.C. The street connects it with the Capitol.
41301.m: The White House is at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.

41302.q: Why is the White House called that?
a: Because it is always covered in snow
Because the first president was called White
41302.e: The outside of the building is painted white. Since 1901 it has officially been called the “White House”.
41302.m: The White House gets its name from its white colour.

41303.q: Roughly how old is the White House?
41303.e: Building began in 1792, and the first president moved in in 1800. So the White House is over 200 years old.
41303.m: The White House is over 200 years old.

41304.q: What was the famous desk in the Oval Office made from?
a: The wood of an old ship
41304.e: The Resolute Desk was made from the timbers of the British ship HMS Resolute. Queen Victoria gave it to the US president in 1880.
41304.m: The desk in the Oval Office is made from the wood of a ship.

a: The lower house of the Russian parliament
41305.e: The State Duma is the lower chamber of the Federal Assembly, the Russian parliament. It debates and passes laws.
41305.m: The State Duma is the lower house of the Russian parliament.

41306.q: Who elects the members of the Russian State Duma?
41306.e: The 450 members of the State Duma are elected by the people: half through party lists, the other half directly in constituencies.
41306.m: The members of the State Duma are elected by the people.

41307.q: In which city does the State Duma meet?
41307.e: The State Duma is based in the Russian capital Moscow, in a building on Okhotny Ryad street near the Kremlin.
41307.m: The State Duma meets in Moscow.

41308.q: What is the upper chamber of the Russian parliament called, alongside the State Duma?
41308.e: The Russian parliament is called the Federal Assembly and has two chambers. Besides the State Duma there is the Federation Council, which represents the regions.
41308.m: The Federation Council is the second chamber of the Russian parliament.

41309.q: Under which ruler did the first Russian Duma meet in 1906?
41309.e: After the revolution of 1905, Tsar Nicholas II had to allow a parliament. The first Duma met in 1906 but had little power.
41309.m: The first Russian Duma existed in 1906 under Tsar Nicholas II.

41310.q: What is the most important task of the Russian State Duma?
a: It runs the Russian national bank
41310.e: The State Duma is part of the parliament. Like every parliament, it passes laws. It is elected for five years.

41311.q: Which state existed before today’s State Duma in place of Russia?
41311.e: The Soviet Union broke up in 1991. With the new Russian constitution of 1993, today’s State Duma was created as Russia’s parliament.
41311.m: Today’s State Duma replaced the parliament of the Soviet Union.

41312.q: What role does the State Duma play in choosing the Russian head of government?
a: It elects him without a proposal
It has no say in it
It draws lots among all its members
41312.e: The Russian president proposes the prime minister. The State Duma must approve this proposal.
41312.m: The State Duma must approve the proposed prime minister.

a: The lower house of the Indian parliament
41313.e: The Lok Sabha is the chamber of the Indian parliament that is directly elected by the people. Its name means “House of the People”.
41313.m: The Lok Sabha is the lower house of the Indian parliament.

41314.q: What does the name “Lok Sabha” mean in English?
41314.e: “Lok” means people and “Sabha” means assembly or house. The Lok Sabha is elected directly by the people.

41315.q: How many chambers does the Indian parliament have, similar to the Swiss parliament?
41315.e: The Indian parliament has the Lok Sabha as the people’s chamber and the Rajya Sabha as the chamber of the states. Switzerland also has two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States.
41315.m: Like the Swiss one, the Indian parliament has two chambers.

41316.q: Why is the election to the Lok Sabha considered the biggest election in the world?
a: India has the most people entitled to vote
41316.e: India is the country with the most inhabitants and a democracy. In 2024 almost a billion people were entitled to vote.
41316.m: The election in India is the biggest election in the world.

41317.q: From what age can you vote for the Lok Sabha in India?
41317.e: In India, as in Switzerland, you can vote from the age of 18. But to be elected to the Lok Sabha yourself, you must be at least 25.
41317.m: In India you can vote from 18.

41318.q: For how many years is the Lok Sabha normally elected?
41318.e: The Lok Sabha is elected for five years unless it is dissolved earlier. The last election took place in 2024.
41318.m: The Lok Sabha is re-elected every five years.

41319.q: Roughly how many weeks did the 2024 Lok Sabha election last, because voting took place in several phases?
41319.e: The 2024 election took place in seven phases from 19 April to 1 June. Because of the huge number of voters, India votes in stages.
41319.m: India’s 2024 parliamentary election lasted about six weeks.

41320.q: In which city does the Lok Sabha meet?
41320.e: The Indian parliament is based in the capital, New Delhi. Since 2023 it has met in a new parliament building.
41320.m: The Lok Sabha meets in New Delhi.

41321.q: Which countries mainly belong to the Commonwealth of Nations?
a: Former territories of the British Empire
All the island states in the world
41321.e: Most members of the Commonwealth used to be British colonies or territories. Today they work together voluntarily as equal states.
41321.m: The Commonwealth is mainly an association of former British territories.

41322.q: Which language links most Commonwealth countries?
41322.e: Because most members used to belong to the British Empire, English is widely spoken there. It is the shared working language of the Commonwealth.
41322.m: English is the shared language of the Commonwealth.

41323.q: Who is the Head of the Commonwealth of Nations (as of 2026)?
41323.e: The Head of the Commonwealth is the British monarch, today King Charles III. The role is mainly symbolic.
41323.m: Charles III is the Head of the Commonwealth.

41324.q: Which sporting event takes place every four years for the Commonwealth countries?
41324.e: The Commonwealth Games are a big multi-sport event for the member countries. Like the Olympic Games, they take place every four years.
41324.m: The Commonwealth Games take place every four years.

41325.q: In which city is the Secretariat of the Commonwealth of Nations?
41325.e: The Commonwealth Secretariat is based at Marlborough House in London. It organises the cooperation between the members.
41325.m: The Commonwealth Secretariat is in London.

41326.q: Which of these countries used to be a British colony and belongs to the Commonwealth today?
41326.e: Australia was a British colony and is a member of the Commonwealth today. Brazil was Portuguese, and Mexico and Argentina were Spanish.
41326.m: Australia used to be a British colony.

41327.q: Which big country in Asia belongs to the Commonwealth?
41327.e: India was a British colony until 1947. As a republic it stayed in the Commonwealth and is now its most populous member.
41327.m: India is the biggest country in the Commonwealth.

41328.q: Which of these countries is a member of the Commonwealth?
41328.e: Canada is a member of the Commonwealth. Ireland left in 1949, and Egypt and the USA are not members.
41328.m: Canada belongs to the Commonwealth of Nations.

41329.q: Which city hosted the Commonwealth Games in 2026?
41329.e: The 2026 Commonwealth Games took place in Glasgow in Scotland. Glasgow had already been the host city in 2014.
41329.m: Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games in 2026.

41330.q: In which city is Buckingham Palace, the palace of King Charles III?
41330.e: Buckingham Palace in London is the official residence and workplace of the British king. The famous Changing of the Guard also takes place there.
41330.m: Buckingham Palace in London is the British king’s palace.

41331.q: What role does King Charles III have in the Church of England?
41331.e: The British monarch is the “Supreme Governor” of the Church of England. Its spiritual leader is the Archbishop of Canterbury.
41331.m: The British king is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England.

41332.q: In which church was Charles III crowned in May 2023?
41332.e: The coronation took place on 6 May 2023 in Westminster Abbey in London. English and British monarchs have been crowned there since 1066.
41332.m: Charles III was crowned in Westminster Abbey.

41333.q: What is the speech called in which the king reads out the government’s plans at the opening of Parliament?
41333.e: In the King’s Speech, the king reads out which laws the government is planning. But the text is written by the government.
41333.m: In the King’s Speech, the king presents the government’s plans.

41334.q: Who is the heir to the throne of King Charles III (as of 2026)?
41334.e: The heir to the throne is Charles’s elder son William, who holds the title Prince of Wales. After him comes his son George.
41334.m: Prince William is the heir to the throne of Charles III.

41335.q: Which title did Charles hold as heir to the throne for longer than anyone before him?
41335.e: Charles was Prince of Wales from 1958 to 2022, more than 60 years. No other heir to the throne held this title for so long.
41335.m: Charles was Prince of Wales for longer than anyone before him.

41336.q: Charles III is not only King of the United Kingdom. In which of these countries is he also head of state?
41336.e: Charles III is also King of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and other countries. The USA, France and India are republics with their own presidents.
41336.m: Charles III is also King of Canada and Australia.

41337.q: Which cause has Charles III especially supported for decades?
41337.e: Charles was warning about environmental problems as early as the 1970s. He promotes organic farming and climate protection.
41337.m: King Charles III is strongly committed to protecting the environment.

41338.q: What form of state does Japan have?
41338.e: Japan has an emperor as head of state, but politics is done by the elected parliament and the government. This is called a parliamentary monarchy.
41338.m: Japan is a monarchy with an elected parliament.

41339.q: What role does the Japanese emperor have according to the 1947 constitution?
a: He is the symbol of the state
41339.e: The 1947 constitution calls the emperor “the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people”. He has no political power.
41339.m: The Japanese emperor is a symbol of the state without political power.

41340.q: What begins in Japan when a new emperor comes to the throne?
a: A new era with its own name
41340.e: With each emperor a new era begins in Japan. Since Naruhito became emperor in 2019, it has been called Reiwa.
41340.m: In Japan a new era begins with each emperor.

41341.q: In which city does the Japanese parliament meet?
41341.e: Japan’s parliament, called the Kokkai in Japanese, is based in the capital, Tokyo.
41341.m: The Japanese parliament meets in Tokyo.

41342.q: How many chambers does the Japanese parliament have?
41342.e: The Japanese parliament consists of the House of Representatives (Shugiin) and the House of Councillors (Sangiin). So, as in Switzerland, there are two chambers.
41342.m: The Japanese parliament has two chambers.

41343.q: Who chooses the prime minister in Japan?
41343.e: In Japan, parliament decides on the prime minister. The emperor then only formally appoints them.
41343.m: In Japan, parliament chooses the prime minister.

41344.q: What was new at the head of Japan’s government in October 2025?
a: For the first time a woman leads the government
The emperor took over the government
41344.e: In October 2025 parliament elected Sanae Takaichi as prime minister. She is the first woman in this office.
41344.m: Since 2025 Japan has had a female prime minister for the first time.

41346.q: Why did Naruhito’s father Akihito step down from the throne in 2019?
41346.e: Akihito was 85 years old and feared he could no longer carry out his duties because of age and health. A special law was needed for him to step down.
41346.m: Emperor Akihito stepped down in 2019 because of his age.

41347.q: In which city does the Arab League have its headquarters?
41347.e: The Arab League is based in Cairo, the capital of Egypt. The headquarters are on Tahrir Square.
41347.m: The Arab League is based in Cairo.

41348.q: In which year was the Arab League founded?
41348.e: The Arab League was founded in March 1945, even before the UN. It is one of the oldest associations of states in the world.
41348.m: The Arab League was founded in 1945.

41349.q: How many members does the Arab League have?
41349.e: The Arab League has 22 members in North Africa and Western Asia. Palestine is one of them.

41350.q: Which language links the members of the Arab League and is its official language?
41350.e: Arabic is spoken in all the member states. It is the official language of the Arab League.
41350.m: The official language of the Arab League is Arabic.

41351.q: Which of these countries is a member of the Arab League?
41351.e: Egypt is a founding member of the Arab League; the League even has its seat in Cairo. Iran and Turkey are not Arab countries.
41351.m: Egypt belongs to the Arab League.

41352.q: Which state was suspended from the Arab League in 2011 and readmitted in 2023?
41352.e: Syria was suspended in 2011 because of the violence against demonstrators. In May 2023 it was allowed to take part again.
41352.m: Syria was excluded from the Arab League from 2011 to 2023.

41353.q: In which regions of the world are most Arab League countries?
a: In North Africa and the Middle East
41353.e: The members are mainly in North Africa, such as Morocco and Egypt, and in the Middle East, such as Saudi Arabia and Syria.
41353.m: The Arab League includes countries in North Africa and the Middle East.

41354.q: Which member of the Arab League is in North Africa on the Atlantic?
41354.e: Morocco is in north-west Africa on the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Jordan, Iraq and Oman are in Western Asia.
41354.m: Morocco is an Arab country on the Atlantic.

41355.q: What is the aim of the African Union?
41355.e: In the African Union, the countries of Africa work together for peace, development and trade. It is similar to the EU in Europe.
41355.m: The African Union links the countries of Africa.

41356.q: What colour is the background of the African Union flag?
41356.e: The African Union flag shows a map of Africa in a white sun on a green background. Golden stars are arranged around it.
41356.m: The African Union flag has a green background.

41357.q: What is the African Continental Free Trade Area, agreed in 2018, meant to achieve?
a: The same taxes for all citizens
41357.e: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is meant to reduce customs duties between the states of Africa. This should help trade on the continent grow.
41357.m: The African free trade area is meant to strengthen trade in Africa.

41358.q: What is the African Union body called that deals with conflicts and wars?
41358.e: The Peace and Security Council can decide on peace missions and impose sanctions. It is made up of 15 member states.
41358.m: The African Union’s Peace and Security Council deals with conflicts.

41359.q: Which organisation is for Africa roughly what the EU is for Europe?
41359.e: The African Union brings together all the countries of Africa. Like the EU, it wants to strengthen cooperation between its members.
41359.m: The African Union is Africa’s association of states.

41360.q: Which important group of major economic powers has the African Union been a member of since 2023?
41360.e: At the summit in New Delhi in 2023, the African Union became a permanent member of the G20. Before that, the EU was the only group of states in it.
41360.m: The African Union has been a member of the G20 since 2023.

41361.q: What does the abbreviation AU stand for?
41361.e: AU stands for African Union, the association of the states of Africa.

41362.q: In which country is Addis Ababa, the seat of the African Union?
41362.e: Addis Ababa is the capital of Ethiopia. The headquarters of the African Union are there.
41362.m: The African Union has its seat in Ethiopia.

41363.q: Where does the Organization of American States (OAS) have its seat?
41363.e: The headquarters of the OAS are in Washington, D.C., near the White House.
41363.m: The OAS has its seat in Washington, D.C.

41364.q: Which of these countries is a member of the Organization of American States?
41364.e: Only states from the Americas are members of the OAS. Brazil is in South America. Spain, Portugal and the United Kingdom are in Europe.
41364.m: Brazil is a member of the OAS.

41365.q: Which states can be members of the Organization of American States?
a: All countries with an Atlantic coast
41365.e: The OAS brings together independent states in North, Central and South America and the Caribbean. These include Canada, the USA and Brazil, for example.
41365.m: The OAS is an association of the states of the Americas.

41366.q: How many official languages does the Organization of American States have?
41366.e: The official languages of the OAS are Spanish, English, Portuguese and French. These are the most important languages of the member states.
41366.m: The OAS has four official languages.

41367.q: Which state was excluded from taking part in the Organization of American States in 1962?
41367.e: After the communist revolution, Cuba was excluded from the OAS in 1962. The exclusion was lifted in 2009, but Cuba did not return.
41367.m: Cuba was excluded from the OAS in 1962.

41368.q: What is the OAS body called that monitors respect for human rights in the Americas?
41368.e: The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights examines complaints about human rights violations. It is based in Washington, D.C.
41368.m: The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights protects human rights in the Americas.

41369.q: Which language is spoken in most OAS member states?
41369.e: Spanish is spoken in most countries of Central and South America. English, Portuguese and French are also official languages of the OAS.
41369.m: Spanish is spoken in most OAS countries.

41370.q: Which big country in the north of the Americas is a member of the OAS besides the USA?
41370.e: Canada has been a member of the OAS since 1990. Russia, Iceland and Norway are not in the Americas.
41370.m: Canada is a member of the OAS.

41371.q: How many states belong to the Gulf Cooperation Council?
41371.e: The members are Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Oman. All of them are on the Arabian Peninsula.
41371.m: The Gulf Cooperation Council has six members.

41372.q: In which city does the Gulf Cooperation Council have its seat?
41372.e: The General Secretariat of the Gulf Cooperation Council is in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
41372.m: The Gulf Cooperation Council has its seat in Riyadh.

41373.q: Where are all the member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council?
41373.e: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Oman are all on the Arabian Peninsula. The council was founded in 1981.
41373.m: The members of the Gulf Cooperation Council are on the Arabian Peninsula.

41374.q: Which of these countries is NOT a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council?
41374.e: Iraq does lie on the Persian Gulf but does not belong to the Gulf Cooperation Council. Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain are members.
41374.m: Iraq does not belong to the Gulf Cooperation Council.

41375.q: What form of state do all the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council have?
41375.e: All six members are ruled by kings, emirs or a sultan. So they are all monarchies.
41375.m: All the Gulf states in the Cooperation Council are monarchies.

41376.q: With which member did Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Bahrain break off relations in 2017?
41376.e: From 2017 to 2021 Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Egypt blockaded Qatar. The dispute was settled with the Al-Ula Declaration in January 2021.
41376.m: Qatar was blockaded by its neighbours from 2017 to 2021.

41377.q: Which raw material has made the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council especially rich?
41377.e: There are huge oil and natural gas reserves beneath the Gulf states. Selling them brought great wealth.
41377.m: The Gulf states became rich mainly through oil.

41378.q: On which body of water, which gives the council its name, are most members of the Gulf Cooperation Council?
41378.e: The Gulf Cooperation Council is named after the Persian Gulf. Almost all members have a coast there.
41378.m: The Gulf Cooperation Council is named after the Persian Gulf.

41379.q: On which continent are most members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
41379.e: The organisation includes China, India, Pakistan, Iran and states of Central Asia, among others. It was founded in Shanghai in 2001.
41379.m: Most members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation are in Asia.

41380.q: Which two big states are among the founders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
41380.e: China and Russia were among the six founding states in 2001. India and Pakistan joined only later.
41380.m: China and Russia are founding members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

41381.q: In which city is the Secretariat of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
41381.e: Although the organisation is named after Shanghai, its secretariat is in Beijing. Its anti-terrorism office is in Tashkent.
41381.m: The Secretariat of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is in Beijing.

41382.q: Which two South Asian states became members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2017?
41382.e: India and Pakistan were admitted as full members in 2017. This made the organisation grow from six to eight members.
41382.m: India and Pakistan have been members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation since 2017.

41383.q: Which country became a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2023?
41383.e: Iran was admitted as the ninth member in July 2023. Turkey and Mongolia are not full members.
41383.m: Iran has been a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation since 2023.

41384.q: In which country is the city of Shanghai, after which the organisation is named?
41384.e: Shanghai is one of the biggest cities in China. The organisation was founded there in 2001.
41384.m: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is named after a city in China.

41385.q: What are the two official languages of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
41385.e: The official languages are Chinese and Russian, the languages of the two biggest founding states. The documents are written in them.
41385.m: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has Chinese and Russian as official languages.

41386.q: In which region are four of the six founding states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
41386.e: Besides China and Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan founded the organisation. These four countries are in Central Asia.
41386.m: Four founding states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation are in Central Asia.

41388.q: What is the capital of Liechtenstein?
41388.e: Vaduz is the capital and seat of the government and parliament. Vaduz Castle, home of the princely family, towers above the town.
41388.m: Vaduz is the capital of Liechtenstein.

41390.q: What is the official language of Liechtenstein?
41390.e: In Liechtenstein German is the only official language. In everyday life people speak an Alemannic dialect, similar to eastern Switzerland.

41391.e: Liechtenstein’s parliament is called the Landtag. Its members are elected by the people every four years.
41391.m: Liechtenstein’s parliament is called the Landtag.

41392.q: With which country did Liechtenstein conclude a customs treaty in 1923?
41392.e: Since the customs treaty of 1923, Liechtenstein and Switzerland have formed a shared customs area. That is why there are no customs checks between the two countries.
41392.m: Liechtenstein and Switzerland have been linked by a customs treaty since 1923.

41393.q: Which river forms the border between Liechtenstein and Switzerland?
41393.e: The Rhine flows along the west of Liechtenstein and separates it from the canton of St Gallen. Several bridges connect the two countries.
41393.m: The Rhine separates Liechtenstein from Switzerland.

41394.q: In which year did women in Liechtenstein get the right to vote and stand for election at national level?
41394.e: Liechtenstein introduced women’s suffrage at national level only in 1984, after a referendum. It was one of the last countries in Europe.
41394.m: Women in Liechtenstein have been able to vote since 1984.

41395.q: What is special about Liechtenstein’s location?
41395.e: Liechtenstein has no access to the sea and is surrounded only by countries without access to the sea. Apart from it, this is true only of Uzbekistan worldwide.
41395.m: Liechtenstein is a doubly landlocked country.

41396.q: On which day did the full-scale Russian attack on Ukraine begin?
41396.e: In the early hours of 24 February 2022, Russian troops attacked Ukraine from the north, east and south. This began the biggest war in Europe since 1945.
41396.m: The full-scale Russian attack on Ukraine began on 24 February 2022.

41397.q: Who is the president of Ukraine, which has been defending itself against the Russian attack since 2022 (as of 2026)?
41397.e: Volodymyr Zelensky was elected president in 2019. He stayed in Kyiv after the war began and leads the country in the war.
41397.m: Volodymyr Zelensky leads Ukraine in the war against Russia.

41398.q: Which peninsula had Russia already annexed in 2014, long before the full-scale attack?
41398.e: In March 2014 Russia occupied the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and annexed it in breach of international law. Most states do not recognise this.
41398.m: Crimea was annexed by Russia in 2014.

41399.q: Who are called civilians in a war?
a: People who do not fight as soldiers
41399.e: Civilians are people who do not take part in the fighting. Under international law they must not be attacked.
41399.m: Civilians do not fight and must be protected in war.

41400.q: Which sea does Ukraine border in the south?
41400.e: Ukraine has a long coast on the Black Sea in the south. Important ports such as Odesa are there.
41400.m: Ukraine lies on the Black Sea.

41402.q: How did Switzerland react to the Russian attack at the end of February 2022?
a: It closed its borders to all Russians
41402.e: On 28 February 2022 the Federal Council decided to adopt the European Union’s sanctions against Russia. This caused a stir internationally, because Switzerland is neutral.
41402.m: In 2022 Switzerland adopted the EU sanctions against Russia.

41403.q: Which country, together with the UN, brokered the 2022 agreement on grain exports from Ukrainian Black Sea ports?
41403.e: The agreement was signed in Istanbul in July 2022. It allowed grain ships to sail despite the war, until Russia pulled out in 2023.
41403.m: Turkey and the UN brokered the grain deal in 2022.

41404.q: Which organisation adopted a plan in 1947 to divide Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state?
41404.e: The General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the partition plan in November 1947. The Arab side rejected it.
41404.m: In 1947 the UN wanted to divide Palestine into two states.

41405.q: What is the 1967 war called in which Israel occupied the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, among other areas?
41405.e: The war lasted from 5 to 10 June 1967. Israel also captured the Sinai Peninsula, the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem.
41405.m: In the Six-Day War of 1967, Israel occupied large areas.

41406.q: What do Palestinians call the flight and expulsion of about 700,000 people in the 1948 war?
41406.e: The Arabic word Nakba means “catastrophe”. Many descendants of the refugees of that time still live in camps today.
41406.m: Palestinians call the expulsion of 1948 the Nakba.

41407.q: What is the Palestinian uprising called that began in 1987?
41407.e: In Arabic, intifada means “shaking off”. The uprising was directed against the Israeli occupation in Gaza and the West Bank.

41408.q: Which organisation carried out a major terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023?
41408.e: Hamas fighters broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip, killed about 1,200 people and took hostages. A long war in the Gaza Strip followed.

41409.q: Apart from Israel, which country does the Gaza Strip border?
41409.e: The Gaza Strip lies on the Mediterranean. In the south, at Rafah, it borders Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.
41409.m: The Gaza Strip borders Israel and Egypt.

41410.q: Which city do both Israelis and Palestinians claim as their capital?
41410.e: Jerusalem has holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, such as the Western Wall and the Dome of the Rock. The status of the city is one of the most difficult points of dispute.
41410.m: Jerusalem is equally important to Israelis and Palestinians.

41411.q: In which country is Camp David, where an important peace agreement was reached in 1978?
41411.e: Camp David is in Maryland, not far from Washington. The accords between Egypt and Israel were negotiated there in 1978.
41411.m: Camp David is in the USA.

41412.q: Which US president brokered the Camp David Accords?
41412.e: Jimmy Carter invited the two leaders to talks in the USA. He mediated personally during the tough twelve-day negotiations.
41412.m: Jimmy Carter was the mediator at Camp David.

41413.q: Which two countries made peace in 1979 following the Camp David Accords?
41413.e: The peace treaty was signed in Washington in March 1979. The two countries had fought several wars against each other before.
41413.m: Egypt and Israel made peace in 1979.

41414.q: Which prize did the Egyptian and Israeli leaders receive in 1978 for making peace?
41414.e: Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Menachem Begin of Israel jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978.
41414.m: The Camp David peace earned the Nobel Peace Prize.

41415.q: Why was the 1979 peace between Egypt and Israel so special?
a: The countries had fought several wars against each other before
The countries had always been friends
The countries had never had contact before
The countries are far apart on different continents
41415.e: Egypt and Israel had fought several wars against each other. The peace treaty was the first between Israel and an Arab state.
41415.m: In 1979 Egypt was the first Arab country to make peace with Israel.

41416.q: Which territory did Israel give back as a result of the peace with Egypt?
41416.e: Israel had captured the peninsula in 1967. It had withdrawn completely by 1982.
41416.m: Israel gave the Sinai Peninsula back to Egypt.

a: A country retreat of the US president
41417.e: Camp David lies in the mountains of Maryland, not far from Washington. Presidents often receive guests there for confidential talks.
41417.m: Camp David is the American president’s country retreat.

41418.q: In which country did the secret preliminary talks for the Oslo Accords take place?
41418.e: From January 1993 Norwegian diplomats organised secret meetings between Israelis and Palestinians. That is why the accords bear the name of the Norwegian capital.
41418.m: The talks for the Oslo Accords took place secretly in Norway.

41419.q: Who shook hands in front of the White House in 1993 after the Oslo Accords were signed?
41419.e: On 13 September 1993 the Israeli prime minister and the PLO leader shook hands in Washington. US President Bill Clinton stood between them.
41419.m: Rabin and Arafat sealed the Oslo Accords with a handshake in 1993.

41420.q: What did Israel and the PLO recognise for the first time in the Oslo process?
41420.e: In letters in September 1993, the PLO recognised Israel’s right to exist. Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinians.
41420.m: In the Oslo process, Israel and the PLO recognised each other.

41421.q: Which institution was created by the Oslo Accords?
41421.e: The Palestinian Authority was meant to govern parts of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank itself. Today it is based in Ramallah.
41421.m: The Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority.

41422.q: Who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 together with Rabin and Arafat?
41422.e: Shimon Peres was Israel’s foreign minister at the time and an important supporter of the negotiations. The three shared the prize.
41422.m: Shimon Peres received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 with Rabin and Arafat.

41423.q: What happened to the Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995?
a: He became president of the UN
41423.e: On 4 November 1995 an Israeli extremist shot Rabin after a peace rally in Tel Aviv. The murder was a heavy blow to the peace process.
41423.m: Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by an opponent of the peace process.

41424.q: Which areas were the Palestinians to partly govern themselves under the Oslo Accords?
a: The West Bank and the Gaza Strip
The Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights
41424.e: The Palestinian Authority was to govern parts of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. For this, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C in 1995.
41424.m: After Oslo, Palestinians govern parts of the West Bank and Gaza themselves.

41425.q: On which holiday was the 1998 Northern Ireland peace agreement signed?
41425.e: The agreement was signed on 10 April 1998, the Friday before Easter. That is why it is called the Good Friday Agreement.
41425.m: The Good Friday Agreement was signed on Good Friday in 1998.

41426.q: In which part of the United Kingdom was there a bloody conflict for decades that was calmed by the Good Friday Agreement in 1998?
41426.e: In Northern Ireland, two groups in particular argued about whether the area should belong to the United Kingdom or to Ireland. This period is known as “The Troubles”.
41426.m: The Good Friday Agreement brought peace to Northern Ireland in 1998.

41427.q: Which group in the Northern Ireland conflict mainly wanted Northern Ireland to belong to the United Kingdom?
41427.e: Unionists were mostly Protestant and wanted to keep the union with Great Britain. The other side was mostly Catholic and wanted a united Ireland.
41427.m: The unionists wanted Northern Ireland to stay with the United Kingdom.

41428.q: Which British Prime Minister signed the Good Friday Agreement?
41428.e: Tony Blair had been Prime Minister since 1997. He signed it together with the Irish head of government, Bertie Ahern.
41428.m: Tony Blair signed the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

41429.q: Which country did the mediator who chaired the negotiations for the Good Friday Agreement come from?
41429.e: The former US senator George Mitchell chaired the talks. At the end he set a deadline that led to the breakthrough.
41429.m: A mediator from the USA helped with the Good Friday Agreement.

41430.q: How was the Good Friday Agreement confirmed in May 1998?
a: By referendums in both parts of Ireland
41430.e: The people of Northern Ireland and of the Republic of Ireland voted on the same day. In both parts there was a clear majority in favour.
41430.m: The Good Friday Agreement was confirmed by referendums.

41431.q: How has Northern Ireland been governed since the Good Friday Agreement?
a: By a government of both communities
41431.e: The agreement provides for power-sharing. Unionists and nationalists must sit together in the regional government.
41431.m: In Northern Ireland, both communities share the government.

41432.q: Which famous prize did two politicians from Northern Ireland receive in 1998 for their work for peace?
41432.e: John Hume and David Trimble came from opposing sides. Even so, they worked together for peace and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1998.
41432.m: Peace in Northern Ireland earned the Nobel Peace Prize in 1998.

41433.q: Which two republics were the first to declare their independence from Yugoslavia in June 1991?
41433.e: Both republics declared independence on 25 June 1991. Shortly afterwards fighting began with the Yugoslav army.
41433.m: Slovenia and Croatia were the first to leave Yugoslavia in 1991.

41434.q: Roughly how long did the war in Slovenia last in 1991?
41434.e: The short war is called the Ten-Day War. After it, the Yugoslav army withdrew from Slovenia.
41434.m: The war in Slovenia lasted only ten days.

41435.q: Which capital was besieged for almost four years, from 1992 to 1996?
41435.e: The siege lasted about 1,400 days, longer than any other siege of a capital in the 20th century. Snipers and shells threatened people’s daily lives.
41435.m: Sarajevo was besieged for almost four years during the Bosnian War.

41436.q: Where were more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys murdered in July 1995?
41436.e: Bosnian Serb troops murdered the victims after capturing the town. International courts classified the crime as genocide.
41436.m: The Srebrenica massacre of 1995 is considered genocide.

41437.q: Who was president of Serbia during most of the Yugoslav wars?
41437.e: Slobodan Milošević was later handed over to the war crimes tribunal. He died in custody in 2006 before the end of his trial.
41437.m: Slobodan Milošević was Serbia’s ruler during the Yugoslav wars.

41438.q: Which Swiss woman was chief prosecutor of the Yugoslavia tribunal from 1999 to 2007?
41438.e: The lawyer from Ticino charged Slobodan Milošević, among others, in The Hague. Before that she had been Attorney General of Switzerland.
41438.m: Carla Del Ponte was chief prosecutor for war crimes in the former Yugoslavia.

41439.q: In which city was the war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia based?
41439.e: The UN set up the tribunal in 1993. It worked in the Netherlands until 2017.
41439.m: The Yugoslavia tribunal sat in The Hague.

41440.q: Which famous old bridge was destroyed in the Bosnian War in 1993?
41440.e: The Ottoman stone bridge from the 16th century was destroyed by shelling. It was rebuilt in 2004.
41440.m: The old bridge of Mostar was destroyed in 1993 and later rebuilt.

41441.q: Which war did the Dayton Agreement end in 1995?
41441.e: From 1992 to 1995 a bloody war raged in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Dayton Agreement brought peace.
41441.m: The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War in 1995.

41442.q: In which country is Dayton, where the agreement was negotiated in 1995?
41442.e: The negotiations took place at an air force base near Dayton in the state of Ohio. The treaty was then signed in Paris.
41442.m: The Dayton Agreement was negotiated in the USA.

41443.q: From which former state did Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Serbia emerge?
41443.e: From 1991 Yugoslavia broke up into several states. This led to wars, which the Dayton Agreement ended in Bosnia.
41443.m: Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia used to belong to Yugoslavia.

41444.q: Which three ethnic groups mainly live in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
41444.e: The Dayton Agreement tries to share power between Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs. That is why, for example, each group has one member in the state presidency.
41444.m: Bosnia is home mainly to Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs.

41445.q: How many members does the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina have under the Dayton Agreement?
41445.e: One member each represents the Bosniaks, the Croats and the Serbs. The chair rotates regularly.
41445.m: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a three-member presidency.

41447.q: On which date did Kosovo declare its independence from Serbia?
41447.e: The parliament in Pristina proclaimed independence on that day. Many people celebrated in the streets.
41447.m: Kosovo declared its independence on 17 February 2008.

41448.q: What is the capital of Kosovo?
41448.e: Pristina is the largest city and the political centre of the country. The parliament and government sit there.
41448.m: The capital of Kosovo is Pristina.

41449.q: Which ethnic group makes up the large majority of Kosovo’s population?
41449.e: More than 90 per cent of the population are Kosovo Albanians. Serbs live mainly in the north.
41449.m: Most people in Kosovo are Albanians.

41450.q: Which country still does not recognise Kosovo’s independence today (as of 2026)?
41450.e: Serbia still regards Kosovo as one of its provinces. Some other states, such as Spain or Russia, also do not recognise Kosovo.
41450.m: Serbia does not recognise Kosovo’s independence.

41451.q: What is the Swiss Army contingent called that has been deployed in Kosovo since 1999?
41451.e: Swisscoy is part of the international peacekeeping force KFOR. It is the Swiss Army’s largest mission abroad.
41451.m: Swisscoy helps keep the peace in Kosovo.

41452.e: In 2008 Switzerland was one of the first countries to recognise Kosovo as an independent state. Many people in Switzerland have roots in Kosovo.

41453.q: Which alliance bombed targets in Serbia in 1999 to end the Kosovo War?
41453.e: The air strikes lasted from March to June 1999. Afterwards Serbian troops withdrew from Kosovo.
41453.m: NATO intervened in the Kosovo War in 1999.

41454.q: Which currency is used in Kosovo?
41454.e: Kosovo introduced the euro without being a member of the eurozone. Before that the Deutschmark was used.
41454.m: In Kosovo you pay with the euro.

41455.q: Against which population group was the genocide in Rwanda mainly directed?
41455.e: Extremist Hutu murdered mainly Tutsi, but also moderate Hutu. Estimates range from 800,000 to a million dead.
41455.m: The genocide in Rwanda was directed mainly against the Tutsi.

41456.q: Which event set off the genocide in Rwanda on 6 April 1994?
a: The shooting down of the president’s plane
41456.e: President Juvénal Habyarimana’s plane was shot down as it approached Kigali to land. The killings began that same night.
41456.m: The shooting down of the president’s plane set off the genocide.

41457.q: Which medium particularly stirred up people to kill in Rwanda?
41457.e: The station RTLM spread hatred against the Tutsi and called for violence. It insultingly called the Tutsi “cockroaches”.
41457.m: A radio station called for genocide in Rwanda.

41458.q: Roughly how long did the genocide in Rwanda last in 1994?
41458.e: The genocide began in April 1994 and ended in July 1994. In these roughly 100 days, hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
41458.m: The genocide in Rwanda lasted about 100 days.

41459.q: What is the capital of Rwanda?
41459.e: Kigali is in the centre of the country. A large memorial there commemorates the victims of the genocide.
41459.m: The capital of Rwanda is Kigali.

41460.q: What is Rwanda often called because of its landscape?
41460.e: Rwanda is very hilly and lies mostly more than 1,000 metres high. In French the nickname is “pays des mille collines”.
41460.m: Rwanda is the land of a thousand hills.

41461.q: What happened to many of those responsible after the genocide in Rwanda?
41461.e: The UN set up a special criminal tribunal for Rwanda. In addition, village courts in Rwanda itself judged many perpetrators.
41461.m: Many of those responsible for the genocide in Rwanda were put on trial.

41462.q: Which war did the Panmunjom armistice end?
41462.e: The war had begun in 1950 when North Korea invaded South Korea. Troops of the UN and China intervened.
41462.m: The Panmunjom armistice stopped the Korean War.

41463.q: In which year was the Panmunjom armistice signed?
41463.e: The agreement was signed on 27 July 1953. Since then the guns at the front have largely been silent.
41463.m: The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice.

41464.q: Why are North and South Korea legally still at war?
41464.e: A peace treaty was never signed. The 1953 armistice still applies today.
41464.m: There is only an armistice between North and South Korea.

41465.q: What is the border strip called that has separated North and South Korea since 1953?
41465.e: The strip is about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. It is one of the most heavily guarded border areas in the world.
41465.m: The Demilitarised Zone separates North and South Korea.

41466.q: Which two neutral states have had officers on the supervisory commission in Korea since 1953?
41466.e: The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission checks that the armistice is kept. Originally Poland and Czechoslovakia were also members.
41466.m: Swiss officers have been monitoring the armistice in Korea since 1953.

41467.q: Which country did not sign the Panmunjom armistice?
41467.e: It was signed by the US-led UN Command, North Korea and China. South Korea’s president wanted to keep fighting and refused.
41467.m: South Korea did not sign the 1953 armistice.

41468.q: Who met in the border village of Panmunjom in April 2018?
a: The leaders of North and South Korea
The Pope and the US president
The coaches of two football teams
The kings of Sweden and Norway
41468.e: South Korean President Moon Jae-in and North Korea’s ruler Kim Jong-un met right at the border. Kim briefly stepped onto South Korean soil.
41468.m: In 2018 the leaders of both Koreas met in Panmunjom.

41469.q: From which country did Cyprus become independent in 1960?
41469.e: Cyprus had been under British administration since 1878 and later became a crown colony. After independence, the United Kingdom kept two military bases.
41469.m: Cyprus became independent from the United Kingdom in 1960.

41470.q: Which country occupied the north of Cyprus in 1974?
41470.e: It was triggered by a coup by Greek nationalist officers who wanted to unite Cyprus with Greece. The troops have remained in the north to this day.
41470.m: Turkey occupied the north of Cyprus in 1974.

41471.q: How many states recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (as of 2026)?
41471.e: The north declared itself a separate state in 1983. Internationally the area is still considered part of the Republic of Cyprus.
41471.m: Only Turkey recognises Northern Cyprus as a state.

41472.q: Which capital is divided by the Cyprus conflict?
41472.e: The UN buffer zone runs right through the city. Since 2003 there have been crossing points between the two parts.

41473.q: Who monitors the buffer zone between the north and south of Cyprus?
41473.e: The UN mission UNFICYP has been on the island since 1964 and is one of the UN’s oldest peacekeeping missions. The buffer zone has existed since 1974 and is also called the Green Line.
41473.m: UN peacekeepers guard the buffer zone on Cyprus.

41474.q: Which two large ethnic groups live on Cyprus?
41474.e: Mainly Greek Cypriots live in the south, mainly Turkish Cypriots in the north. The island has been divided since 1974.
41474.m: Greek and Turkish Cypriots live on Cyprus.

41475.q: Since when has Cyprus been a member of the European Union?
41475.e: Cyprus joined on 1 May 2004, together with nine other countries. In the north, however, EU law is suspended.
41475.m: Cyprus has been in the EU since 2004.

41476.q: Why do peace talks, for example about Cyprus, often take place in Switzerland?
a: Because Switzerland is neutral and offers good offices
Because it never rains in Switzerland
41476.e: Switzerland is neutral and often invites parties to a conflict for talks. In 2017, for example, there were negotiations about Cyprus in Crans-Montana.
41476.m: Neutral Switzerland often hosts peace talks.

41477.q: With whom did the government of Colombia conclude a peace agreement in 2016?
a: With a rebel group in its own country
41477.e: In Colombia the rebel group FARC had been fighting the state since the 1960s. In 2016 the government and the FARC made peace, and the fighters laid down their weapons.
41477.m: Colombia made peace with the rebel group FARC in 2016.

41478.q: Which famous prize did the president of Colombia receive in 2016 for the peace with the FARC?
41478.e: President Juan Manuel Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016. He was honoured for his efforts to end the long civil war in Colombia.
41478.m: Colombia’s president received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016.

41479.q: Colombia and the FARC negotiated for years in Havana. In which country is Havana?
41479.e: Havana is the capital of Cuba, an island in the Caribbean. The peace talks took place there from 2012 to 2016.
41479.m: The peace talks for Colombia took place in Havana in Cuba.

41480.q: What was the result of the referendum on the first peace agreement in Colombia in October 2016?
41480.e: About 50.2 per cent voted against the agreement. It was then revised and approved by parliament in November.
41480.m: The Colombian people narrowly rejected the first peace agreement.

41481.q: What did the FARC become after the peace agreement?
41481.e: The former fighters founded a party and received guaranteed seats in parliament for a few years. Today the party is called Comunes.
41481.m: After the peace, the FARC became a party.

41482.q: What was the pen made from that was used to sign the peace agreement in Colombia in 2016?
41482.e: The pen was made from a cartridge case and bore the words “Bullets wrote our past, education our future”. It was meant to show the path from violence to peace.
41482.m: The peace agreement was symbolically signed with a pen made from a bullet.

41483.q: Roughly how long did the armed conflict between the Colombian state and the FARC last?
41483.e: The FARC was founded in 1964. By 2016 the conflict had cost more than 200,000 lives and displaced millions of people.
41483.m: The conflict with the FARC lasted more than half a century.

41484.q: Was there peace everywhere in Colombia after the 2016 agreement with the FARC?
a: No, other armed groups kept fighting
Yes, all fighting stopped at once
Yes, Colombia even abolished its army
No, the FARC immediately started a new war
41484.e: The FARC laid down its weapons and became a party. But other groups such as the ELN did not take part in the agreement and kept fighting.
41484.m: After 2016, other groups such as the ELN kept fighting in Colombia.

41485.q: Which two countries have been arguing over the Kashmir region since 1947?
41485.e: Since the partition of British India in 1947, India and Pakistan have both claimed Kashmir. They have fought several wars over it.
41485.m: India and Pakistan have been arguing over Kashmir since 1947.

41486.q: Which event of 1947 is at the beginning of the Kashmir conflict?
41486.e: When British rule ended, India and Pakistan were created. The princely states had to join one of the two.
41486.m: The Kashmir conflict began with the partition of British India in 1947.

41487.q: In which mountain range is the Kashmir region?
41487.e: Kashmir lies in the north of India and Pakistan in the Himalayas and the Karakoram. There are very high mountains and large glaciers there.
41487.m: Kashmir lies high in the Himalayas.

41488.q: Which religion do most people in Kashmir follow?
41488.e: Most people living in Kashmir are Muslims. Pakistan is a mainly Muslim country, India mainly Hindu. This is also one reason for the dispute.
41488.m: Most people in Kashmir are Muslims.

41489.q: Which third country also controls part of the Kashmir region?
41489.e: China administers, among others, the area of Aksai Chin in the east. India also claims this area.
41489.m: Besides India and Pakistan, China also controls part of Kashmir.

41490.q: What is Kashmir, which India and Pakistan are arguing over?
a: A mountain region in South Asia
An island in the Indian Ocean
A port city by the sea
41490.e: Kashmir is a mountain region in the north of India and Pakistan. A small part is also controlled by China.
41490.m: Kashmir is a mountain region in South Asia.

41491.q: Which animal does the fine cashmere wool, named after the region, come from?
41491.e: The cashmere goat has very fine, soft hairs under its coat. Expensive cashmere wool is made from them.
41491.m: Cashmere wool comes from the cashmere goat.

41492.q: Why is the Kashmir conflict considered especially dangerous?
a: It affects the whole of Europe
It is fought only at sea
It is the newest conflict in the world
41492.e: India and Pakistan have both tested nuclear weapons, Pakistan most recently in 1998. So every escalation causes worry around the world.
41492.m: In the Kashmir conflict, two nuclear powers face each other.

41493.q: What is considered the highest battlefield in the world in the Kashmir conflict?
a: A glacier high in the mountains
41493.e: On the Siachen Glacier, Indian and Pakistani soldiers face each other at over 5,000 metres. More soldiers have died there from cold and avalanches than from fighting.
41493.m: The highest battlefield in the world is a glacier in Kashmir.

41495.q: What is the person called who heads an embassy?
41495.e: The ambassador is the highest representative of a country in the host country. He or she heads the embassy.
41495.m: An ambassador heads their country’s embassy.

41496.q: What must the host country do before a new ambassador may start work?
a: It must give them a house
It must have them elected by the people
41496.e: An ambassador may only work if the host country agrees. This approval is called accreditation.
41496.m: An ambassador needs the host country’s approval.

41497.q: What does a consulate help Swiss people abroad with, for example?
a: When they have lost their passport
41497.e: A consulate looks after its own citizens abroad. For example, it issues new identity documents or helps in emergencies.
41497.m: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad.

a: A person who represents their country abroad
A person with a school diploma
41498.e: Diplomats look after relations between countries. They negotiate, provide information and represent their country’s interests.

41499.q: What special protection do ambassadors have in the host country?
a: They may vote in elections there
41499.e: Diplomats enjoy immunity. The host country may not arrest them, but it can expel them.
41499.m: Diplomats are protected from arrest in the host country.

41500.q: In which Swiss city do most foreign embassies have their seat?
41500.e: Embassies are usually in the capital, where the government sits. In Switzerland that is Bern.
41500.m: The embassies in Switzerland are in Bern.

41501.q: Who sends a nuncio as ambassador to other countries?
41501.e: The Pope heads the Holy See, which has ambassadors like a state. They are called nuncios, and one works in Bern.
41501.m: The Pope’s ambassador is called a nuncio.

41502.q: What is a country’s mission in the capital of another country called?
41502.e: Diplomats work in an embassy. They represent their country and also help their own citizens abroad. The rules for this are in the Vienna Convention.
41502.m: An embassy represents a country abroad.

41503.q: What does it mean when a host country declares a diplomat “persona non grata”?
a: They are unwelcome and must leave
They are made a guest of honour
41503.e: Under Article 9 of the Convention, a host country can declare a diplomat unwelcome at any time and without giving reasons. The sending state must then recall them.
41503.m: A persona non grata is an unwelcome diplomat who must leave the country.

41504.q: What may the authorities of the host country not do without the consent of the head of mission?
a: List the embassy in the phone book
41504.e: The premises of an embassy are inviolable (Article 22). Police and other authorities may only enter them with the ambassador’s permission and must also protect them.
41504.m: An embassy’s premises are off limits to the host country’s authorities.

41505.q: May customs open an embassy’s official consignment?
41505.e: Official consignments of embassies, the so-called diplomatic bag, are protected. The host country’s authorities may neither open nor hold them back.
41505.m: An embassy’s official post must not be opened.

41506.q: What does a diplomat’s immunity mean?
a: They are exempt from the host country’s jurisdiction
They may take part in elections in the host country
They must do military service in the host country
They get a free flat in the host country
41506.e: Diplomats may not be arrested in the host country and usually cannot be put on trial. This lets them do their work without pressure from the host country.
41506.m: Thanks to immunity, a diplomat cannot be put on trial in the host country.

41507.q: Despite their immunity, must diplomats respect the laws of the host country?
a: Only if they were born there
41507.e: Article 41 obliges diplomats to respect the laws of the host country. Immunity only protects them from prosecution by the host country; it does not allow them to break the law.
41507.m: Diplomats too must keep to the laws of the host country.

41508.q: Must diplomats pay the usual taxes on their salary in the host country?
a: No, they are largely exempt from taxes
Only if they stay longer than a year
41508.e: According to Article 34 of the Convention, diplomats are exempt from most taxes of the host country. But they still pay indirect taxes included in the price of goods.
41508.m: In principle, diplomats pay no income tax in the host country.

41509.q: Which heads of mission belong to the highest class according to the Convention?
41509.e: The Convention divides heads of mission into three classes. Ambassadors belong to the first class, followed by envoys and chargés d’affaires.
41509.m: Ambassadors are in the highest class of diplomats.

41510.q: Who receives a foreign head of state on a state visit in Switzerland?
41510.e: Switzerland has no single head of state; the Federal Council performs this role together. That is why the whole Federal Council receives the state guest, led by the President of the Confederation.
41510.m: On a state visit, the whole Federal Council welcomes the guest.

41511.q: On which square in Bern does the ceremonial welcome often take place during state visits?
41511.e: The Bundesplatz is right in front of the Federal Palace. State guests are often received there with military honours.
41511.m: In Bern, state guests are often received on the Bundesplatz in front of the Federal Palace.

41512.q: What is the group of soldiers called that ceremonially welcomes a state guest on arrival?
41512.e: An army guard of honour stands ready at the welcome, and the guest inspects it with the host. This is part of the military honours of a state visit.
41512.m: A guard of honour gives the state guest military honours.

41513.q: What is meant by “protocol” in diplomacy?
a: The rules for how official events are run
A list of all embassies worldwide
41513.e: Protocol sets out who greets whom and how, who sits where and in which order things happen. At the FDFA a separate department deals with protocol.
41513.m: Diplomatic protocol governs the running and order of rank at official events.

41514.q: What is the formal dinner called that the host gives in honour of a state guest?
41514.e: The state banquet is a highlight of a state visit. The host and the guest usually each give a speech at the table.
41514.m: At a state banquet, a state guest is entertained festively.

41515.q: What is the order called that decides who comes before whom at official events?
41515.e: The order of precedence decides, for example, who is greeted first or who sits next to the host. It helps to avoid arguments about the guests’ honour.
41515.m: The order of precedence decides who goes first at official events.

41516.q: Which kind of visit by a head of state has the most ceremonial protocol?
41516.e: The state visit is the highest form of an official visit, with military honours and a banquet. On a working visit, by contrast, talks come first and the programme is simpler.
41516.m: A state visit is the most ceremonial form of visit between states.

41517.q: What is NOT one of the three classic features of a state?
41517.e: According to the three-element theory, a state needs a territory, a people and effective state authority. Its own currency is not necessary; Liechtenstein, for example, uses the Swiss franc.
41517.m: A state consists of territory, a people and state authority.

41518.q: What does it mean when a country “recognises” a new country?
a: It officially accepts it as a state
It closes the border with it
41518.e: By recognising it, a state says that it treats the new country as an equal state. Then the two can, for example, exchange ambassadors.
41518.m: Recognising means officially accepting a country as a state.

41519.q: What is the forcible incorporation of foreign territory into your own state called?
41519.e: An annexation breaks the ban on the use of force in the UN Charter. That is why most states do not recognise such changes of territory.
41519.m: Territory taken by annexation is usually not recognised internationally.

41520.q: Why is it important for a new country to be recognised by other states?
a: So that it can conclude treaties with them
So that it may have a flag
So that it may choose a capital
41520.e: Without recognition it is difficult to trade, open embassies or become a member of the UN.
41520.m: Recognised states can conclude treaties with other states.

41521.q: Which territory has its own government but is officially recognised as a state by only a few countries?
41521.e: The People’s Republic of China regards Taiwan as part of its territory. That is why only a few states officially recognise Taiwan, though many have unofficial relations.
41521.m: Despite its own government, Taiwan is officially recognised by only a few states.

41522.q: Which country in Europe is not recognised by all states?
41522.e: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Switzerland recognised Kosovo, but Serbia and some other states do not.
41522.m: Kosovo is not recognised by all states.

41523.q: Which country came into being in 1993 when Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two states?
41523.e: On 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia was divided into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Both states were recognised immediately.
41523.m: In 1993 Czechoslovakia became the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

41524.q: What does it mean when a state is sovereign?
a: It is ruled by a king
It is a member of the European Union
It has its own army with nuclear weapons
41524.e: Sovereignty means that a state has the highest authority internally and is independent of other states externally. No other state may give it orders.
41524.m: A sovereign state decides its own affairs.

41525.q: What is part of a state’s sovereignty?
a: It must adopt its neighbour’s laws
41525.e: A sovereign state decides for itself which laws apply in it. The term sovereignty was shaped by the French thinker Jean Bodin in the 16th century.
41525.m: A sovereign state makes its own laws.

41526.q: With which peace settlement of 1648 was the Swiss Confederation’s independence from the Holy Roman Empire recognised?
41526.e: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years’ War. It is also seen as the beginning of an order of equal sovereign states in Europe.
41526.m: Since the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, the Swiss Confederation has also been legally independent of the Empire.

41527.q: According to the Federal Constitution, the cantons are sovereign. What limits their sovereignty?
41527.e: Article 3 of the Federal Constitution says that the cantons are sovereign except where their sovereignty is limited by the Federal Constitution. Everything not assigned to the Confederation is regulated by the cantons themselves.
41527.m: The cantons are sovereign unless the Federal Constitution says otherwise.

41528.q: What is the principle called that states must not interfere in the internal affairs of other states?
41528.e: The principle of non-intervention follows directly from the sovereignty of states. It is set out in the UN Charter.
41528.m: No state should interfere in the internal affairs of another.

41529.q: How many votes does each member state have in the UN General Assembly?
a: As many as it has millions of inhabitants
Depending on the size of its contribution
41529.e: The UN is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all member states. That is why little Switzerland has as much voting power in the General Assembly as a big country.
41529.m: In the UN General Assembly, every state has exactly one vote.

41530.q: What is the idea called that all state power comes from the people?
41530.e: With popular sovereignty, the people are the highest holder of state power. In Switzerland this can be seen especially in referendums and initiatives.
41530.m: Popular sovereignty means that power in the state comes from the people.

41531.q: What is a state’s authority over all people and things on its territory called?
