41531.e: Territorial sovereignty means that the laws of a state apply on its own territory. Personal jurisdiction, by contrast, concerns the state’s own citizens, even abroad.
41531.m: Through territorial sovereignty, the laws of a state apply on its territory.

41532.q: What is the maximum width of a country's territorial sea?
41532.e: The territorial sea reaches at most 12 nautical miles out, measured from the coastline. There the coastal state has almost the same rights as on land.
41532.m: A country's territorial sea is at most 12 nautical miles wide.

41533.q: A nautical mile measures 1,852 metres. Roughly how many kilometres are 12 nautical miles?
41533.e: You calculate 12 times 1,852 metres, which makes 22,224 metres. Rounded, that is about 22 kilometres.
41533.m: A nautical mile is almost twice as long as a kilometre.

41534.q: What right do foreign ships have in a state’s territorial sea?
a: The right to fish freely there
The right to extract raw materials
The right to hold military exercises
41534.e: Foreign ships may pass through the territorial sea as long as they do not disturb the peace and security of the coastal state. They may not fish or extract raw materials there.
41534.m: Ships may pass peacefully through foreign territorial seas.

41535.q: Is a harbour on the sea part of the country’s territory?
a: No, the sea belongs to everyone
Only the seabed, not the water
Only when a ship is anchored there
41535.e: Harbours and bays count as internal waters. They belong entirely to the state, just like the land.
41535.m: Harbours and bays belong entirely to the state’s territory.

41536.q: According to which old rule was the territorial sea often only about three nautical miles wide in the past?
41536.e: In the past, the sea counted as state territory as far as a cannon could fire from the shore. That was about three nautical miles.
41536.m: In the past, the range of a cannon decided the width of the territorial sea.

41537.q: What is the open sea far out, which belongs to no state, called?
41537.e: No state has sovereignty on the high seas. All countries may, for example, sail ships there.
41537.m: The high seas belong to no state.

41538.q: Over what does a state exercise its sovereignty in its territorial sea?
a: Over the water, the seabed and the airspace
Only over the surface of the water
41538.e: The sovereignty of the coastal state extends to the water, the seabed and the subsoil. The airspace above the territorial sea is also included.
41538.m: The territorial sea includes the seabed and the airspace above it.

41539.q: What may a coastal state do in its territorial sea that foreign ships may not?
41539.e: In the territorial sea, fish and mineral resources belong to the coastal state. Foreign ships may only pass through peacefully.
41539.m: In the territorial sea, only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials.

41540.q: What does the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea regulate?
a: The rights and duties of states at sea
The prices of fish in shops
The building of harbours in Switzerland
41540.e: The Convention on the Law of the Sea was signed in 1982. It sets out, for example, which sea areas belong to a coastal state and which are open to all.
41540.m: The Convention on the Law of the Sea regulates who owns which parts of the sea.

41541.q: According to the Convention on the Law of the Sea, what are the high seas?
a: The open sea, which belongs to no state
The sea right in front of a beach
The sea around the North Pole only
41541.e: The high seas begin outside the zones of the coastal states. All states may sail and fish there. The convention was signed in Montego Bay in Jamaica.
41541.m: The high seas belong to no state and are open to all.

41542.q: What may only the coastal state do in its exclusive economic zone?
a: Fish and extract raw materials such as oil
Ban all foreign ships from passing through
Charge foreign ships an entrance fee
41542.e: The exclusive economic zone reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast. Only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials there, but foreign ships may pass through freely.
41542.m: In its economic zone, only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials.

41543.q: What is the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea responsible for?
a: Disputes between states about the law of the sea
Rowing boat accidents on Swiss lakes
41543.e: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea was created by the Convention on the Law of the Sea. It decides disputes about the law of the sea and is based in Hamburg.
41543.m: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides disputes about the law of the sea.

41544.q: What does the convention call the mineral resources on the seabed outside national zones?
a: The property of the nearest state
The possession of whoever comes first
The property of the veto powers
41544.e: The deep seabed of the high seas belongs to no single state. An international authority is meant to regulate its use for the benefit of all people.
41544.m: The treasures of the deep seabed are considered the common heritage of mankind.

41545.q: Which right does the Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantee to landlocked states such as Switzerland?
a: Access to the sea and use of the high seas
Its own territorial sea on the Mediterranean
A share of other states’ fishing
41545.e: States without a coast have the right to reach the sea through neighbouring states. Their ships may use the high seas just like the ships of coastal states.
41545.m: Countries without a coast may also use the sea and the high seas.

41546.q: Which city is the home port of ocean-going ships sailing under the Swiss flag?
41546.e: Although Switzerland has no coast, ocean-going ships sail under the Swiss flag. Their home port is Basel on the Rhine, via which you can reach the North Sea.
41546.m: Swiss ocean-going ships have Basel as their home port.

41547.q: What may foreign ships do in a coastal state’s economic zone?
a: Nothing at all, they may not enter
41547.e: The economic zone does not belong entirely to the coastal state. Only the fish and raw materials belong to it, but foreign ships may pass through freely.
41547.m: Ships may sail freely through a foreign economic zone.

41548.q: In which city does the Permanent Court of Arbitration have its seat?
41548.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration has worked in the Dutch seat of government since 1902. Other international courts are also based there.
41548.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration sits in The Hague.

41549.q: Which conference decided in 1899 to found the Permanent Court of Arbitration?
41549.e: At the First Hague Peace Conference, a convention for the peaceful settlement of international disputes was concluded. The Permanent Court of Arbitration grew out of it.
41549.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration was created after the First Hague Peace Conference of 1899.

41550.q: What is the building called where the Permanent Court of Arbitration and the International Court of Justice work?
41550.e: The Peace Palace opened in 1913 and was built with money from the industrialist Andrew Carnegie. It is seen as a symbol of peace through law.
41550.m: The Peace Palace is home to the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

41551.q: Who decides a dispute at the Permanent Court of Arbitration?
41551.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration is not a court with permanent judges. It keeps a list of experts from which the parties to a dispute choose their arbitrators for each case.
41551.m: At the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the parties choose their own arbitrators.

41552.q: Which sea was the well-known 2016 arbitration case Philippines versus China about?
41552.e: The Philippines challenged China’s territorial claims in the South China Sea. In 2016 the arbitral tribunal largely ruled in favour of the Philippines, but China does not recognise the decision.
41552.m: In 2016 an arbitration case decided about the South China Sea.

41553.q: What is the Permanent Court of Arbitration for?
a: It helps states settle disputes peacefully
It organises sports tournaments between countries
It hands out aid in war zones
41553.e: At the Permanent Court of Arbitration, states can have a dispute decided by arbitrators instead of going to war. About 130 states, including Switzerland, are parties to it.
41553.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration helps settle disputes between states peacefully.

41554.q: Is the Permanent Court of Arbitration older or younger than the UN?
a: Younger, it was created only around 2000
The same age, both were created in 1945
It was founded together with the EU
41554.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration was agreed in 1899 and has worked since 1902. The UN was created only in 1945.
41554.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration is older than the UN.

41555.q: What is meant by extradition in international law?
a: Handing over a wanted person to another state
41555.e: In an extradition, a state hands over a suspected or convicted person to another state. There the person is to be put on trial or serve their sentence.
41555.m: In an extradition, a wanted person is handed over to another state.

41556.q: May Swiss citizens be extradited to another state against their will?
a: Yes, but only to EU states
Yes, if the Federal Council agrees
41556.e: Article 25 of the Federal Constitution allows Swiss citizens to be extradited only with their consent. Instead, Switzerland can put them on trial itself.
41556.m: Switzerland extradites its own citizens only with their consent.

41557.q: What is the principle called that an act must be a crime in both states for extradition to happen?
41557.e: Switzerland usually extradites only if the act would also be a crime under Swiss law. That way nobody is prosecuted for something that is allowed here.
41557.m: Extradition happens only if the act is a crime in both states.

41558.q: According to the Federal Constitution, to which state may nobody be extradited?
a: To a state where they face torture
To a state without a coast
To a neighbouring state of Switzerland
41558.e: Article 25 of the Federal Constitution forbids extraditing people to a state where they face torture or other cruel treatment. This applies to everyone, not just Swiss citizens.
41558.m: Nobody may be extradited to a state where torture threatens.

41559.q: What does Switzerland demand before extraditing someone to a state with the death penalty?
a: An assurance that the death penalty will not be carried out
41559.e: Switzerland rejects the death penalty. It extradites only if the other state gives a binding assurance that the person will not be executed.
41559.m: Without a guarantee against the death penalty, Switzerland extradites nobody.

41560.q: Which federal office is responsible for extraditions in Switzerland?
41560.e: The Federal Office of Justice handles extradition requests from other states and makes such requests itself. It belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police.
41560.m: In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Justice deals with extraditions.

41561.q: Which Interpol notice is used to look for a person for arrest and extradition?
41561.e: With a Red Notice, a state asks police worldwide to provisionally arrest a wanted person. It can then request their extradition.
41561.m: The Interpol Red Notice seeks people for arrest and extradition.

41562.q: For which kind of offence is extradition usually not granted?
41562.e: Political offences are traditionally excluded from extradition. This is so that political opponents cannot be persecuted with the help of criminal law.
41562.m: Extradition is usually not granted for purely political offences.

41563.q: What colour is the cover of the Swiss passport?
41563.e: The Swiss passport is red and bears the white Swiss cross. Red is also the colour of the diplomatic and service passports.
41563.m: The Swiss passport is red with a Swiss cross.

41564.q: Which special passport do ambassadors receive for their work abroad?
41564.e: Ambassadors are diplomats. They travel with their own passport that shows their role.
41564.m: Diplomats travel with a special diplomatic passport.

41565.q: How long is a Swiss passport valid for children and young people under 18?
41565.e: Children’s appearance changes quickly. That is why their passport is valid for only five years, so that the photo stays up to date.
41565.m: Children’s passports are valid for a shorter time because children change quickly.

41566.q: For people aged 12 and over, what is stored on the chip of the Swiss passport in addition to the photo?
41566.e: Since 2010 the Swiss passport has had a chip. The photo and, from the age of 12, the fingerprints are stored on it.
41566.m: The chip in the passport stores the photo and fingerprints.

41567.q: What is shown on the visa pages of the new 2022 Swiss passport?
a: The members of the Federal Council
41567.e: The new passport was introduced on 31 October 2022. Each visa page is dedicated to a canton and shows its coat of arms and a typical motif.
41567.m: The 26 cantons are shown in the new Swiss passport.

41568.q: What is a visa, which sometimes goes into your passport?
a: Permission to enter a particular country
A receipt for the plane ticket
41568.e: Some countries require a visa. It shows that you may enter the country and stay there for a certain time.
41568.m: A visa allows you to enter a particular country.

41569.q: What is the area of letters and symbols at the bottom of a passport’s data page called, which machines can read?
41569.e: The machine-readable zone contains the name, passport number and date of birth in a fixed form. Border controls can quickly capture it with a reader.
41569.m: The machine-readable zone in the passport can be captured by readers.

41570.q: Which document is enough for Swiss people travelling to the countries of the Schengen area?
41570.e: For travel to Schengen states, a valid identity card is enough. For many countries outside Europe, on the other hand, you need a passport.
41570.m: You can travel to Schengen countries with the Swiss identity card.

41571.q: What is a visa called that you only get on arrival at the airport or border?
41571.e: Some countries issue travellers with a visa directly on entry. This is called a “visa on arrival”.
41571.m: For some countries, you get the visa only on arrival.

41572.q: What is a Schengen visa meant for?
a: Short trips into the Schengen area
41572.e: With a Schengen visa, people from certain countries may travel to the Schengen area for a short time, for example as tourists. Anyone who wants to stay longer needs a different permit.
41572.m: A Schengen visa is valid for short trips.

41574.q: Where do you normally apply for a visa for a foreign country?
a: At the destination country’s travel agency
41574.e: Visas are issued by the missions of the destination country, that is by embassies or consulates. Some countries also offer electronic visas today.
41574.m: You apply for a visa at the embassy or consulate of the destination country.

41575.q: In which country is the village of Schengen, after which the Schengen area is named?
41575.e: Schengen is a small wine village on the Moselle where three countries meet. The first agreement on removing border controls was signed there in 1985.
41575.m: The Schengen area is named after a village in Luxembourg.

41576.q: What does the Latin word “visum”, from which “visa” comes, mean?
41576.e: “Visum” is a form of the Latin verb “videre”, which means “to see”. In the past, an authority used this note to confirm that it had checked a document.
41576.m: The word visa comes from the Latin word for seen.

41577.q: What is the electronic travel authorisation called that you need for a visa-free trip to the USA?
41577.e: Anyone from Switzerland who wants to travel to the USA without a visa must first apply online for an ESTA authorisation. It is valid for short trips as a tourist or on business.
41577.m: For visa-free travel to the USA you need an ESTA authorisation.

41578.q: Who should a Swiss woman contact if she has lost her passport abroad?
a: The lost property office in Bern
The embassy of the neighbouring country
41578.e: Swiss missions abroad help Swiss citizens in emergencies. This includes help when identity documents are lost or stolen.
41578.m: Abroad, the Swiss embassy or consulate helps in emergencies.

41579.q: Which document can a Swiss mission issue if your passport has been stolen abroad?
41579.e: With a provisional passport you can continue your journey or return home. It is issued only for a short time.
41579.m: After losing a passport, the embassy can issue a provisional passport.

41580.q: According to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, what right does a person arrested abroad have?
a: Contact with the consulate of their home country
A trial in their home country
A journey home at state expense
41580.e: Under Article 36, the authorities must inform an arrested foreigner that they can have their consulate notified. Consular officials may then visit them.
41580.m: Anyone arrested abroad may contact their consulate.

41581.q: Which federal department is responsible for Swiss embassies and consulates?
41581.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) looks after relations with other countries. This includes the embassies and consulates.
41581.m: The FDFA is responsible for Switzerland’s missions abroad.

41582.q: What is a consul called who works unpaid and often lives in the host country?
41582.e: Honorary consuls are usually respected local people who work for a country alongside their main job. Switzerland has many honorary representations in places without its own embassy.
41582.m: An honorary consul represents a country on a voluntary basis.

41583.q: Does the Swiss embassy pay a fine that a Swiss tourist has received abroad?
a: No, the tourist must pay it
Yes, but only for young people
41583.e: Abroad, the principle of personal responsibility applies. The embassy helps in emergencies but does not pay fines, bail or lawyers’ fees.
41583.m: You have to pay fines abroad yourself.

41584.q: What is the FDFA’s information on the security situation in other countries called?
41584.e: In its travel advice, the FDFA informs about dangers such as unrest, crime or natural hazards. You should read it before every trip.
41584.m: Before a trip, it is worth checking the FDFA’s travel advice.

41585.q: Which mission abroad mainly looks after citizens’ passports and emergencies, not politics?
41585.e: Consulates carry out administrative tasks for their own citizens, for example identity documents or help in emergencies. Political relations, by contrast, are handled by the embassy.
41585.m: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad with practical matters.

41586.q: In which city did Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev meet for the first time in 1985?
41586.e: In November 1985 the US president and the Soviet party leader met in Geneva. The meeting is seen as the beginning of a thaw in the Cold War.
41586.m: Reagan and Gorbachev first met in Geneva in 1985.

41587.q: Which event happened in autumn 1989, shortly before the summit between Bush and Gorbachev in Malta?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The start of the Second World War
41587.e: The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. A few weeks later Bush and Gorbachev met in Malta. The summit is seen as a sign of the end of the Cold War.
41587.m: The Malta summit of 1989 stands for the end of the Cold War.

41589.q: What is the person called who prepares a summit for a head of state or government?
41589.e: Just as a mountain guide in the Himalayas prepares the way to the summit, the sherpa negotiates the texts and topics in advance. That way the leaders can decide quickly at the meeting.
41589.m: A sherpa prepares a summit for their leader.

41590.q: What is the summit of the heads of state and government of the EU member states called?
41590.e: In the European Council the leaders of the EU countries meet several times a year, usually in Brussels. The Council of Europe in Strasbourg, by contrast, is a separate organisation.
41590.m: The leaders of the EU states meet in the European Council.

41591.q: Which British prime minister coined the term “summit” for meetings of the powerful in 1950?
41591.e: In a speech in 1950 he spoke of a “parley at the summit” between the great powers. Since then meetings of heads of state and government have been called summits.
41591.m: Winston Churchill brought the word summit into politics.

41592.q: On which peninsula did the leaders of the USA, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union meet at Yalta in February 1945?
41592.e: The Yalta Conference took place on the Black Sea. There the three victorious powers discussed the order of Europe after the Second World War.
41592.m: The Yalta Conference took place in Crimea in 1945.

41594.q: What is a state of emergency?
a: A situation in which the government gets special powers
A particularly nice holiday across the country
A rule for behaviour in exams
A law on shop opening hours
41594.e: In a state of emergency the government gets special powers because of a crisis. Basic rights can be temporarily restricted.
41594.m: In a state of emergency the government gets special powers because of a crisis.

41595.q: Why do dictators like to misuse a state of emergency?
a: Because it lets them suspend basic rights
41595.e: In a state of emergency the government can restrict basic rights such as freedom of assembly. Dictators often extend it to persecute opponents more easily.
41595.m: A permanent state of emergency is a warning sign of dictatorship.

41596.q: After which event did France declare a state of emergency in November 2015?
a: After winning the football World Cup
41596.e: After the attacks of 13 November 2015 in Paris, France was in a state of emergency for around two years. During this time the police could search homes more easily.
41596.m: After the 2015 attacks France was in a state of emergency for around two years.

41597.q: After which event did Turkey declare a state of emergency in July 2016?
41597.e: After the failed coup attempt in July 2016, Turkey was in a state of emergency for two years. During this time tens of thousands of people were arrested or dismissed.
41597.m: Turkey was in a state of emergency for two years after the 2016 coup attempt.

41598.q: How long should a state of emergency really last?
a: Only as long as the crisis
41598.e: A state of emergency is only meant for emergencies. If it lasts very long, like around 30 years in Egypt, that is a warning sign.
41598.m: A state of emergency should only apply during the crisis.

41599.q: When, for example, can a state declare a state of emergency?
a: At the start of the summer holidays
41599.e: War, terrorism, epidemics or major natural disasters can justify a state of emergency. Then the state must be able to act quickly.
41599.m: A state of emergency is meant for severe crises.

41600.q: Why did the Federal Council declare the “extraordinary situation” in March 2020?
41600.e: Because of the coronavirus the Federal Council could order measures such as closing schools directly. The extraordinary situation lasted until June 2020.
41600.m: In the coronavirus crisis the Federal Council got special powers.

41601.q: Which basic right may never be restricted under the European Convention on Human Rights, even in an emergency?
41601.e: Article 15 of the ECHR allows some rights to be set aside in an emergency. But the ban on torture is one of the rights that always applies.
41601.m: The ban on torture applies even in the worst emergency.

41602.q: Which country declared martial law for a few hours in December 2024, until parliament lifted it?
41602.e: President Yoon Suk-yeol imposed martial law on 3 December 2024. Parliament voted against it that same night, and he had to withdraw it.
41602.m: In South Korea parliament stopped martial law in 2024 after a few hours.

41603.q: What could the President of the Weimar Republic do in emergencies?
41603.e: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution gave him this power. From 1930 Germany was governed almost entirely by emergency decrees.
41603.m: Emergency decrees made the Weimar Republic open to abuse.

41604.q: What happened after the Reichstag fire in February 1933?
a: There were free new elections without the NSDAP
The Reichstag was rebuilt straight away
41604.e: The day after the fire Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree. Among other things it abolished freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.
41604.m: After the Reichstag fire in 1933 basic rights in Germany were abolished.

41605.q: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler’s government to do?
41605.e: With the Enabling Act the government could pass laws itself, even against the constitution. In this way the Reichstag gave up its own power.
41605.m: With the Enabling Act the German parliament stripped itself of power in 1933.

41606.q: Why did many students in Germany protest against the emergency laws in 1968?
a: They feared abuse as in the Weimar period
41606.e: The emergency laws were passed in May 1968. Many people remembered how emergency powers had been abused before 1933.
41606.m: The German emergency laws of 1968 sparked big protests.

41607.q: What did the Swiss Federal Council receive in 1939 at the start of the Second World War?
41607.e: Parliament gave the Federal Council extraordinary full powers. This is known as the full powers regime. It could then regulate many things without parliament and the people.
41607.m: In the Second World War the Federal Council governed with special full powers.

41608.q: Which situation did the Federal Council declare under the Epidemics Act in March 2020 because of the coronavirus?
41608.e: On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation. This allowed it to order measures such as school closures across Switzerland.
41608.m: In March 2020 the extraordinary situation applied in Switzerland.

41609.q: How do emergency powers in a democracy differ from emergency powers in a dictatorship?
a: They are only used in secret
41609.e: In democracies emergency powers are limited in time, and parliament and the courts can review them. Dictatorships, by contrast, often use emergency powers permanently and without checks.
41609.m: Democratic emergency powers are time-limited and checked.

41610.q: During which event did the Federal Council use emergency powers in March 2023?
a: The takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS
The building of the Gotthard Base Tunnel
41610.e: To prevent Credit Suisse from collapsing, the Federal Council issued emergency decrees in March 2023. This allowed UBS to take over the bank quickly.
41610.m: The rescue of Credit Suisse in 2023 was done with emergency powers.

41611.q: How many candidates are usually on offer per constituency in elections in North Korea?
41611.e: In North Korea there is normally only one candidate per constituency on the ballot paper. Anyone who wants to vote against must cross out the name, which hardly anyone dares to do.
41611.m: In North Korea there is no real choice in elections.

41612.q: How could people usually vote in elections in East Germany?
a: Not at all; there were never elections
41612.e: In East Germany there was a single list of the National Front. Voters could only approve it, because the share of seats was already fixed.
41612.m: In East Germany there was only a single list to vote for.

41613.q: In East Germany, what did “folding the ballot” (Zettelfalten) mean at an election?
a: Putting the ballot paper in the box without reading it
Folding the ballot paper into a paper plane
Writing a letter to the government
41613.e: Anyone who simply folded the ballot paper and put it in approved the list. Anyone who used the voting booth made themselves look suspicious.
41613.m: In East Germany anyone who just folded the ballot openly approved the list.

41614.q: How did civil rights activists prove in 1989 that an East German election had been rigged?
a: They counted along themselves during the count
They asked the head of state
They read it in the newspaper
41614.e: Civil rights activists watched the count at the local elections in May 1989. Their figures showed that the official results had been rigged.
41614.m: The rigged local elections of 1989 strengthened the protests in East Germany.

41615.q: Which result is typical of a sham election in a dictatorship?
41615.e: In dictatorships the government often reports results of over 99 percent. In free elections such results are almost impossible.
41615.m: Almost 100 percent approval points to a sham election.

41616.q: Which Iraqi ruler had himself confirmed with officially 100 percent in a referendum in 2002?
41616.e: In the referendum of October 2002 the government claimed that every vote had been a yes vote. It was not a real election.
41616.m: Saddam Hussein had himself confirmed with supposedly 100 percent in 2002.

41617.q: How does the Guardian Council in Iran prevent a real choice in elections?
41617.e: The Guardian Council checks all candidates and rejects many of them. So often only people acceptable to the leadership can be voted for.
41617.m: In Iran the Guardian Council weeds out candidates before the election.

41618.q: Which organisation sends election observers in Europe to check that elections are fair?
41618.e: The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe observes elections in many countries. Its office for this is in Warsaw.
41618.m: The OSCE uses election observers to check whether elections are fair.

41619.q: Which feature of a free election is often missing in sham elections?
41619.e: In free elections nobody can see how someone votes. In dictatorships voting is often watched so that nobody votes against.
41619.m: Without a secret ballot an election is not free.

a: A party that alone controls the state and society
A party that only stands in one canton
A party that only collects taxes
41620.e: A state party is closely merged with the state. Important posts usually only go to its members.
41620.m: A state party dominates the whole state.

41621.q: What was the state party of East Germany called?
41621.e: The Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) dominated East Germany. It was formed in 1946 by the forced merger of the KPD and the SPD.
41621.m: The SED was the state party of East Germany.

41622.q: Were there other parties in East Germany besides the SED?
a: Yes, but they had to follow the SED
Yes, and they could vote the SED out
Yes, but only in West Germany
41622.e: Smaller parties, the so-called bloc parties, were not allowed to question the SED’s leadership. They gave East Germany a false appearance of variety.
41622.m: The other parties in East Germany had to follow the SED.

41623.q: What is the most important leadership body of a communist state party called?
41623.e: The Politburo makes the most important decisions of the party and therefore of the state. It has only a few members.
41623.m: The real power of a communist state party lies in the Politburo.

41624.e: The Communist Party of China has ruled the country alone since 1949. With around 100 million members it is one of the largest parties in the world.
41624.m: In China only the Communist Party rules.

41625.q: What was special about Mexico from 1929 to 2000?
a: The same party always provided the president
There was no president at all
A new party came to power every year
41625.e: The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) provided every president from 1929 to 2000. Only in 2000 did a candidate from another party win.
41625.m: The PRI dominated Mexico for over 70 years.

41626.q: Who led the state and society in the Soviet Union?
41626.e: The leading role of the Communist Party was even written into the constitution. This article was only removed in 1990.
41626.m: In the Soviet Union the Communist Party led the state.

41627.q: In communist states, who usually got the important posts in the state and the economy?
a: The best people in an open exam
41627.e: The party kept a list of important posts, the nomenklatura. It decided who got these jobs.
41627.m: In communist states loyal party members got the important posts.

41628.q: What is in the former Stasi headquarters in Berlin today?
41628.e: The headquarters of the Ministry for State Security was in Berlin-Lichtenberg. Today there is a museum about the Stasi there.
41628.m: The former Stasi headquarters is now a museum.

41629.e: The Stasi saw itself as the protection and weapon of the SED. So it served the party, not the citizens.
41629.m: The Stasi saw itself as the shield and sword of the SED.

41630.q: Besides its employees, who secretly helped the Stasi to spy on people?
41630.e: In 1989 the Stasi had around 91,000 employees. On top of that there were many unofficial collaborators who spied on neighbours, colleagues or even family members.
41630.m: Many people secretly informed for the Stasi.

41633.q: What came to light in Switzerland in 1989 in the Secret Files Scandal (Fichenskandal)?
a: The authorities had secretly registered hundreds of thousands of people
The army had secretly built a tunnel
41633.e: A parliamentary commission of inquiry revealed that around 900,000 files had been created since 1900. Those recorded were often left-wingers, trade unionists and foreigners.
41633.m: The Secret Files Scandal showed that there was excessive surveillance in Switzerland too.

41634.q: What did many people in Switzerland demand after the Secret Files Scandal?
41634.e: On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people protested in Bern against the “snooping state”. Many wanted to see what had been collected about them.
41634.m: After the Secret Files Scandal many people wanted to see their own files.

41636.q: Where can people today see the files the Stasi kept on them?
a: At the Federal Palace in Bern
41636.e: Since 1992 those affected have been allowed to read their Stasi files. Since 2021 the records have been part of the German Federal Archives.
41636.m: At the Stasi Records Archive people can see what was collected about them.

a: An arrest without legal grounds or a trial
An arrest after a theft with evidence
41637.e: In an arbitrary arrest someone is locked up without legal grounds or a fair trial. Dictatorships often do this to critics.
41637.m: Arbitrary arrest means locking someone up without legal grounds.

41638.q: What does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights forbid?
41638.e: Article 9 says: no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.

41639.q: Under an old English law of 1679, what should quickly happen to a prisoner?
a: He is brought before a judge
He is sent out of the country
He has to pay a fine
41639.e: Under the Habeas Corpus Act a prisoner had to be brought before a judge quickly. The judge then checked whether the detention was lawful.
41639.m: A judge should check whether detention is lawful.

41640.q: What could the French king do with a sealed letter before 1789?
a: Have people locked up without trial
Pay off all the country’s debts
41640.e: With a lettre de cachet, a sealed order from the king, people were sent to the Bastille, for example, without any court judgement.
41640.m: In old France the king could have people locked up without trial.

41641.q: What does “enforced disappearance” mean in dictatorships?
a: People are secretly arrested and their whereabouts kept secret
Files are taken to the archive
41641.e: With an enforced disappearance relatives do not know where the person is or whether they are still alive. It is considered a serious crime against human rights.
41641.m: With enforced disappearances families are left not knowing what happened to their relatives.

41642.q: Why is it dangerous if a prisoner is not allowed contact with a lawyer and family?
a: Because nobody notices if he is mistreated
Because he then eats too much
Because he then gets out sooner
Because he then gets too loud
41642.e: If a prisoner is completely cut off from the outside world, this is called incommunicado detention. Then the risk of torture and mistreatment rises.
41642.m: Prisoners need contact with a lawyer and family.

41643.q: In Switzerland, who decides whether someone has to stay in pre-trial detention?
41643.e: The public prosecutor applies for pre-trial detention. An independent court, the compulsory measures court, decides on it.
41643.m: In Switzerland a court decides on pre-trial detention.

41644.q: In which Swiss city does the UN work especially for human rights?
41644.e: The UN human rights system is based in Geneva. There, for example, a working group examines complaints about arbitrary detention.
41644.m: In Geneva the UN works for human rights.

41645.q: Which organisation adopted a worldwide agreement against torture in 1984?
41645.e: The UN adopted the Convention against Torture in 1984. It came into force in 1987.
41645.m: The UN adopted an agreement against torture in 1984.

a: Yes, if a judge allows it
41646.e: The European Convention on Human Rights forbids torture without exception. Switzerland is bound by it too.
41646.m: Torture is always forbidden in Switzerland.

41647.q: Which important document from 1948 says that nobody may be tortured?
a: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
41647.e: Article 5 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights forbids torture and cruel treatment.
41647.m: The 1948 Declaration of Human Rights already forbids torture.

41648.q: Why do independent experts visit prisons in Switzerland?
a: They check whether prisoners are treated well
41648.e: Since 2010 the National Commission for the Prevention of Torture has inspected places where people are detained. It writes reports with recommendations.
41648.m: In Switzerland a commission checks how prisoners are treated.

41649.q: In which Swiss city was a well-known organisation against torture founded in 1977?
41649.e: The Geneva banker Jean-Jacques Gautier founded the Association for the Prevention of Torture in Geneva. His idea of prison visits found its way into international treaties.
41649.m: An organisation against torture works from Geneva.

41650.q: For whom is there a UN day of remembrance every year on 26 June?
41650.e: The UN chose 26 June because the Convention against Torture came into force on that day in 1987.
41650.m: On 26 June the victims of torture are remembered worldwide.

41651.q: May experts from the Council of Europe also visit prisons in Switzerland?
41651.e: A Council of Europe committee may visit prisons, police stations and clinics in all member states, including Switzerland. Afterwards it writes reports.
41651.m: The Council of Europe checks whether prisoners are treated well.

41652.q: In the 18th century, during the Enlightenment, what happened to torture in many European countries?
a: It was only used on children
41652.e: During the Enlightenment the idea spread that torture is inhumane. Many rulers abolished it, for example Maria Theresa in 1776.
41652.m: During the Enlightenment torture was abolished in many countries.

41653.q: What is the system that China uses to block many foreign websites called?
41653.e: The “Great Firewall” blocks sites such as Google, YouTube or Facebook. The name is a play on the Great Wall of China.
41653.m: The Great Firewall cuts the Chinese internet off from many foreign sites.

41654.q: How do many people in dictatorships get round internet blocks?
41654.e: A VPN sends data in encrypted form via a server abroad. That way blocked sites can often still be opened.
41654.m: A VPN can get round internet blocks.

41655.q: Instead of the global internet, what may most people in North Korea use?
41655.e: North Korea has its own network called Kwangmyong, which only works inside the country. The global internet is forbidden for almost all residents.
41655.m: In North Korea most people only have a sealed-off national network.

a: The government switches the internet off completely or partly
A computer goes into sleep mode
41656.e: Governments sometimes switch off the internet during protests. That makes it harder for demonstrators to coordinate, and pictures do not get abroad.
41656.m: In an internet shutdown the government cuts the connection to the world.

41657.q: Which online encyclopedia was blocked in Turkey from 2017 to 2019?
41657.e: Turkey blocked Wikipedia in April 2017. Only after a ruling by the Constitutional Court was the site unblocked at the end of 2019.
41657.m: Turkey blocked Wikipedia for almost three years.

41658.q: Which platforms did Russia block in March 2022, shortly after attacking Ukraine?
41658.e: Russia blocked Facebook and Instagram in March 2022. The government wanted to limit critical information about the war this way.
41658.m: Russia blocked Facebook and Instagram in 2022.

41659.q: In which country was the internet heavily restricted during the protests after the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in 2022?
41659.e: After the young woman died in the custody of the morality police, there were big protests. The government blocked Instagram and WhatsApp and slowed down the network.
41659.m: Iran heavily restricted the internet during protests in 2022.

41660.q: Which country switched off the internet almost completely in January 2011 during the protests on Tahrir Square?
41660.e: At the end of January 2011 the Mubarak government cut almost all internet connections for several days. But it could not stop the protests that way.
41660.m: Egypt switched off the internet in 2011 to slow down protests.

41661.q: What distinguishes state media in a dictatorship from free media?
a: They spread what the government wants
They always belong to private individuals
41661.e: State media in dictatorships are controlled by the government. Critical reports are not allowed there.
41661.m: State media in dictatorships are the mouthpiece of the government.

41662.q: What does the name of the Soviet party newspaper “Pravda” mean in English?
41662.e: “Pravda” was the newspaper of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Despite its name it mainly spread propaganda.

41663.q: What was the SED’s most important daily newspaper in East Germany called?
41663.e: “Neues Deutschland” was the central newspaper of the SED. It printed what the party leadership told it to.
41663.m: “Neues Deutschland” was the SED’s party newspaper.

41664.q: Are there independent newspapers and broadcasters in North Korea?
a: No, the state controls all media
Yes, they belong to foreign companies
41664.e: In North Korea all media spread the leadership’s announcements, such as the state news agency KCNA. There are no independent media.
41664.m: There are no independent media in North Korea.

41665.q: Whose view does the Chinese state news agency Xinhua spread?
41665.e: Xinhua means “New China”. The agency is under state control and spreads the government’s view.
41665.m: Xinhua is China’s state news agency.

41666.q: Which Russian state broadcaster did the EU ban in March 2022?
41666.e: The EU banned RT and Sputnik after Russia attacked Ukraine. It justified this with targeted disinformation.
41666.m: In 2022 the EU banned the Russian state broadcaster RT.

41667.q: Which organisation publishes the press freedom ranking every year?
41667.e: Reporters Without Borders is based in Paris and compares 180 countries. Countries with strong state media and censorship end up near the bottom.
41667.m: Reporters Without Borders rates press freedom every year.

41668.q: What distinguishes the SRG in Switzerland from state media in a dictatorship?
a: Its programmes are independent of the government
It may only broadcast government announcements
It is run by the military
41668.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees the independence of radio and television. The government may not tell the SRG what to report.
41668.m: Despite the licence fee, the SRG is independent of the government.

41669.q: What does the Greek word “autocracy” literally mean?
41669.e: “Autos” means self, “kratos” means power. So an autocrat rules alone and without checks.

41670.q: What was the sole ruler of old Russia called?
41670.e: The Russian tsars ruled as autocrats. Until 1905 their power was not limited by any constitution.
41670.m: The Russian tsar ruled as an autocrat.

a: A government made up of officers
A parliament made up of farmers
41671.e: A military junta is a group of officers who rule after a coup. It is a form of autocracy.
41671.m: Under a military junta officers rule instead of elected politicians.

41672.q: What do you call rule by a few rich and powerful people?
41672.e: In an oligarchy power lies with a small group. The word comes from the Greek “oligoi”, meaning “few”.
41672.m: Oligarchy is rule by the few.

a: A mixture of democracy and dictatorship
41673.e: In a hybrid regime there are elections, but they are not really fair. The opposition and the media are obstructed.
41673.m: A hybrid regime mixes democratic and authoritarian features.

41674.q: What is often obstructed in a hybrid regime?
a: The work of the opposition and free media
41674.e: In a hybrid regime there are elections, but the opposition and the media are obstructed. That is why the elections are not really fair.
41674.m: In hybrid regimes the opposition and the media are obstructed.

41675.q: What is meant by an “illiberal democracy”?
a: There are elections, but freedoms are restricted
There are no elections any more
The people vote on every law
41675.e: The term became well known through the Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán. It means a state with elections in which the media, courts and opposition are weakened.
41675.m: In an illiberal democracy people vote, but freedom is restricted.

41676.q: What do you call a state where elections are held but the opposition has no fair chance?
41676.e: In an electoral autocracy elections take place, but without real competition. The government makes sure it always wins.
41676.m: An electoral autocracy has elections but no real freedom.

41677.q: What is typical of elections in a hybrid regime?
a: The opposition may stand but has hardly any fair chance
There are no elections at all
All parties have exactly equal chances
41677.e: The opposition may take part. But because the media, money and the authorities are on the government’s side, it can hardly win.
41677.m: In a hybrid regime elections are not really fair.

41678.q: Which magazine publishes the well-known Democracy Index through its research division?
41678.e: The Economist Intelligence Unit publishes the Democracy Index. It first appeared in 2006.
41678.m: The Democracy Index comes from the magazine “The Economist”.

41679.q: What does the Democracy Index compare?
a: How democratic the countries of the world are
How many inhabitants the countries have
41679.e: The index rates almost every country in the world. It shows whether a country is a democracy or an authoritarian regime.
41679.m: The Democracy Index compares how democratic countries are.

41680.q: According to the Democracy Index, what share of the world’s population lives in a full democracy (as of 2025)?
41680.e: According to the 2025 Democracy Index only about 6.6 percent of people live in a full democracy. Many large countries count as flawed democracies or authoritarian regimes.
41680.m: Only a few people in the world live in a full democracy.

41681.q: What does it mean if a country has very few points in the Democracy Index?
41681.e: Countries with few points count as authoritarian regimes. There are hardly any free elections or freedoms there.
41681.m: Few points in the Democracy Index mean little democracy.

41682.q: Which country has been ranked first in the Democracy Index for years (as of 2025)?
41682.e: Norway scored around 9.8 out of 10 points in the 2025 index. It has topped the ranking since 2010.
41682.m: According to the Democracy Index Norway is the most democratic country in the world.

41683.q: Which country is ranked last in the 2025 Democracy Index?
41683.e: Afghanistan under the Taliban scored only around 0.25 points. There are neither elections nor freedoms there.
41683.m: According to the Democracy Index Afghanistan is the least democratic country.

41684.q: Which type of regime does Switzerland belong to in the Democracy Index (as of 2025)?
41684.e: Switzerland scores around 9.3 out of 10 points. That makes it one of the full democracies.
41684.m: In the Democracy Index Switzerland counts as a full democracy.

41685.q: Which of these areas is rated in the Democracy Index?
41685.e: As well as civil liberties, the electoral process and political participation also count, for example. Economic data is not rated.
41685.m: The Democracy Index rates civil liberties, among other things.

a: The monarch has all power, with no constitution to limit him
Parliament elects a new king every year
The king only has ceremonial duties
The people vote on every law
41686.e: In an absolute monarchy the ruler combines lawmaking, government and the courts. Nobody can keep him in check.
41686.m: In an absolute monarchy the ruler has all the power.

41687.q: Which French king is seen as the very model of absolutism?
41687.e: Louis XIV, the “Sun King”, reigned from 1643 to 1715. The sentence “I am the state” is attributed to him.
41687.m: Louis XIV is the best-known example of an absolute ruler.

41688.q: Which palace did Louis XIV have expanded as a sign of his power?
41688.e: From 1661 Versailles was magnificently expanded and became the seat of the court. The nobility had to live there and so were kept under control.
41688.m: Versailles showed the power of the absolute king.

41689.q: What did an absolute ruler appeal to in order to justify his power?
41689.e: According to the divine right of kings, the king gets his power directly from God. So he does not have to answer to anyone.
41689.m: Absolute rulers appealed to the divine right of kings.

41690.q: Which country is an absolute monarchy today (as of 2025)?
41690.e: In Saudi Arabia the king has supreme power, and there is no elected parliament. Sweden, Spain and the United Kingdom are parliamentary monarchies.
41690.m: Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy today.

41691.q: Which smallest state in the world is an absolute elective monarchy?
41691.e: The Pope is head of state of Vatican City and holds all state power. He is elected by the cardinals.
41691.m: Vatican City is an absolute elective monarchy.

41692.q: What form of government does the United Kingdom have today?
41692.e: The United Kingdom has a king, but the elected parliament makes the laws. The king mainly has ceremonial duties.
41692.m: In a parliamentary monarchy the elected parliament governs.

41693.q: Which event of 1789 ended absolute monarchy in France?
41693.e: In 1789 the people of France rose up against the king. After that the king no longer had all the power.
41693.m: The French Revolution ended absolutism in France.

41694.q: Which President of the Reich appointed Hitler Chancellor in 1933?
41694.e: President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor. Conservative politicians believed at the time that they could control Hitler.

41695.q: Which building in Berlin burned on 27 February 1933?
41695.e: Late in the evening of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building burned. The Nazis used the fire to move against their opponents.
41695.m: The Reichstag fire served the Nazis as an excuse.

41696.q: Whom did the Nazis blame for the Reichstag fire and persecute first?
41696.e: The Nazis claimed that the communists had set fire to the Reichstag. Thousands of members of the KPD were arrested.
41696.m: After the Reichstag fire the communists were persecuted first.

41697.q: Which workers' organisations were broken up on 2 May 1933?
41697.e: On 2 May 1933 the SA and SS occupied trade union buildings all over the country. They were replaced by the German Labour Front of the Nazi Party.
41697.m: In May 1933 the free trade unions were dissolved.

41698.q: What did the Enabling Act of 1933 allow Hitler's government to do?
a: Rule only with the people's permission
41698.e: With the Enabling Act the government could make laws on its own. Only the SPD voted against it in the Reichstag.
41698.m: The Enabling Act switched parliament off.

41699.q: What is the name for the way the Nazis brought states, clubs and associations under their control in 1933?
41699.e: During Gleichschaltung every part of society was placed under the party. Clubs and associations were given Nazi leaders.
41699.m: Gleichschaltung means that everything was made subordinate to the party.

41700.q: What title did Hitler hold from August 1934?
41700.e: After the Reich President died in August 1934, Hitler combined the two highest offices. He now called himself “Führer and Reich Chancellor”.
41700.m: From 1934 Hitler held all power in his own hands.

41701.q: In which city did the Nazi Party (NSDAP) begin?
41701.e: In 1920 the party grew out of the German Workers' Party, which had been founded in Munich. Munich was later called the “Capital of the Movement”.
41701.m: The Nazi Party was founded in Munich.

41702.q: How did Hitler's attempted coup in Munich in 1923 end?
a: It failed and Hitler went to prison
41702.e: The Beer Hall Putsch of 8 and 9 November 1923 failed. Hitler was convicted and sent to prison.

41703.q: Which book did Hitler write while he was in prison in Landsberg?
41703.e: In “Mein Kampf” Hitler set out his antisemitic and racist ideas. The book came out in 1925 and 1926.

41704.q: Which sign was the symbol of the Nazi Party?
41704.e: The swastika was the party symbol of the Nazis. In Germany today it is banned as an unconstitutional symbol.
41704.m: The swastika was the sign of the Nazis.

41705.q: How did the Nazi Party become the largest party in the Reichstag in 1932?
41705.e: In the Reichstag election of July 1932 the Nazi Party won about 37 per cent of the vote. However, that did not give it a majority.
41705.m: In 1932 the Nazi Party became the largest party through elections.

41706.q: How many parties were allowed in Germany from July 1933?
41706.e: A law of July 1933 banned the founding of new parties. The Nazi Party was therefore the only party allowed.
41706.m: From 1933 there was only one party in Germany.

41707.q: What was the name of the Nazi Party's fighting troop with the brown shirts?
41707.e: The SA (Storm Detachment) protected party events and terrorised opponents in the streets. Because of their uniform its members were called “Brownshirts”.
41707.m: The SA was the Nazi Party's brown-shirted gang of thugs.

41708.q: From what age did boys join the German Young People, the section of the Hitler Youth for younger boys?
41708.e: Boys aged 10 to 14 belonged to the German Young People. After that they moved into the Hitler Youth proper.
41708.m: Even ten-year-olds were drawn into the Hitler Youth.

41709.q: What was the name of the Hitler Youth organisation for girls?
41709.e: Girls aged 14 to 18 belonged to the League of German Girls (BDM). Above all, they were supposed to be prepared for the role of mother.
41709.m: Girls were organised in the League of German Girls.

41710.q: What did membership of the Hitler Youth become from 1939?
41710.e: From 1939 youth service was compulsory. All young people had to belong to the Hitler Youth.
41710.m: From 1939 the Hitler Youth was compulsory for all young people.

41711.q: What happened to the other youth groups in Germany besides the Hitler Youth from 1933?
41711.e: The Nazis wanted all young people in the Hitler Youth. Other youth groups were banned or absorbed into the Hitler Youth.
41711.m: Apart from the Hitler Youth, other youth groups were banned.

41712.q: What was the main aim of the Hitler Youth?
a: To bring up young people in Nazi ideology
To prepare young people for university
To teach young people foreign languages
To train young people as musicians
41712.e: The Hitler Youth was meant to turn young people into loyal followers of Hitler. Camps, marches and field games also prepared them for war.
41712.m: The Hitler Youth was meant to raise children as followers of Hitler.

41713.q: What did nonconformist youth groups who resisted the Hitler Youth call themselves?
41713.e: The Edelweiss Pirates met mainly in the Rhineland and the Ruhr. They wanted to be free and were persecuted for it.
41713.m: The Edelweiss Pirates resisted the Hitler Youth.

41714.q: What were Hitler Youth boys also used for towards the end of the war?
a: As anti-aircraft helpers and in the Volkssturm
41714.e: Towards the end of the war even teenagers had to operate anti-aircraft guns and fight in the Volkssturm. Many of them were killed.
41714.m: At the end of the war even children were sent into battle.

41715.q: Did girls also have to take part in the Hitler Youth?
41715.e: The younger girls belonged to the Young Girls' League. At 14 they moved into the League of German Girls.
41715.m: Even the youngest girls were taken into the Hitler Youth.

41716.q: In which year were the Nuremberg Laws passed?
41716.e: The Nuremberg Laws were passed in September 1935. They made the exclusion of Jews law.

41717.q: What did Jewish people lose through the Reich Citizenship Law?
41717.e: Only “Reich citizens” had full political rights. Jews now counted only as nationals without the right to vote.
41717.m: The Reich Citizenship Law made Jews second-class citizens.

41718.q: What did one of the Nuremberg Laws forbid?
41718.e: The so-called “Blood Protection Law” forbade such marriages. It was based on a false racial theory.
41718.m: The Nuremberg Laws forbade marriages between Jews and non-Jews.

41719.q: Which flag became the only national flag of the Reich with the Nuremberg Laws?
41719.e: The Reich Flag Law was one of the three Nuremberg Laws. It made the party flag the national flag.
41719.m: With the Nuremberg Laws the swastika flag became the national flag.

41720.q: How did the Nazis decide who counted as a Jew?
41720.e: What mattered most was how many grandparents had belonged to the Jewish religion. A person's own faith hardly played any role.
41720.m: The Nazis sorted people by their descent.

41721.q: What were people with Jewish and non-Jewish ancestors called under the Nuremberg Laws?
41721.e: The Nazis contemptuously called them “Mischlinge of the first or second degree”. They too were discriminated against.
41721.m: The Nuremberg Laws divided people into degrading groups.

41722.q: Which false theory were the Nuremberg Laws based on?
41722.e: The Nazis claimed that people belonged to different valuable and inferior “races”. This racial ideology is scientifically wrong.
41722.m: The racial ideology of the Nazis is false and inhuman.

41723.q: On which night did the worst of the November pogroms take place?
41723.e: On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938 Jews were attacked all over the German Reich. The violence continued in the following days.
41723.m: The November pogroms began on 9 November 1938.

41724.q: Which name that plays down the November pogroms was widely used for a long time?
41724.e: The term “Kristallnacht” (Night of Broken Glass) plays down the violence. That is why people today speak of the November pogroms.
41724.m: Instead of “Kristallnacht”, people now say November pogroms.

41725.q: What did the Nazis use as a pretext for the November pogroms of 1938?
a: An assassination attempt on a German diplomat
41725.e: The young Jewish man Herschel Grynszpan shot a German diplomat in Paris. The Nazis used the act as a pretext for the violence.
41725.m: An assassination in Paris served as a pretext for the pogroms.

41726.q: Which places of worship were set on fire during the November pogroms?
41726.e: More than 1,000 synagogues and prayer rooms were destroyed or set on fire. The fire brigade was only supposed to stop the fire spreading to neighbouring houses.
41726.m: During the November pogroms the synagogues burned.

41727.q: About how many Jewish men were taken to concentration camps after the November pogroms?
41727.e: After the pogrom more than 30,000 Jewish men were arrested. They were sent to the camps at Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen.
41727.m: After the pogroms tens of thousands of Jewish men were deported.

41728.q: Who had to pay for the damage after the November pogroms?
41728.e: The victims were blamed for the damage. On top of that they had to pay one billion Reichsmarks.
41728.m: After the pogroms the victims were robbed as well.

41729.q: Who gave the inflammatory speech in Munich on the evening of 9 November 1938 that set off the pogrom?
41729.e: At a party meeting in Munich the propaganda minister called for violence. After that the orders went out to party offices throughout the Reich.
41729.m: The pogroms were planned by the party leadership and were not spontaneous.

41730.q: Where does the word “Kristall” (crystal) in the old name for the pogrom night come from?
a: From the broken panes of glass
41730.e: Countless shop windows of Jewish shops and homes were smashed. The broken glass on the streets gave the night its glossed-over name.
41730.m: The shards of smashed shop windows lay on every street.

41731.q: Which office did Joseph Goebbels hold from 1933?
41731.e: Goebbels was Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. He controlled newspapers, radio and films.

41732.q: Which action took place on 10 May 1933 in Berlin and many university towns?
41732.e: Students burned books by Jewish authors and critics of the regime. In Berlin Goebbels gave a speech at the event.
41732.m: During the book burning unwanted books were destroyed.

41733.q: Which question did Goebbels ask in his famous speech at the Berlin Sportpalast in 1943?
41733.e: After the defeat at Stalingrad Goebbels wanted to push the population into an even greater war effort. The hand-picked audience cheered on command.
41733.m: In the Sportpalast speech Goebbels called for total war.

41734.q: What was the cheap radio set that brought propaganda into many homes called?
41734.e: The People's Receiver (Volksempfänger) was cheap so that as many families as possible could afford a radio. That way millions heard the speeches of the party leaders.
41734.m: The People's Receiver brought propaganda into people's living rooms.

41735.e: With propaganda Goebbels tried to win people over to the Nazis. He used newspapers, radio, films and parades to do so.
41735.m: Propaganda influences people in a one-sided way.

41736.q: Which media did Goebbels mainly use for his propaganda?
41736.e: In the 1930s there was no internet yet and hardly any television. So Goebbels controlled radio, newspapers and cinema.
41736.m: Goebbels spread propaganda through radio, newspapers and films.

41737.q: What happened to artists and journalists the Nazis did not like?
a: They were no longer allowed to work in their profession
They were allowed to earn more
41737.e: Anyone who wanted to work had to be a member of Goebbels' Reich Chamber of Culture. Jews and critics were not admitted and lost their jobs.
41737.m: Goebbels controlled who was allowed to make art and culture.

41738.q: How did Joseph Goebbels' life end?
a: He took his own life in Berlin in May 1945
He was sentenced to death in Nuremberg
41738.e: On 1 May 1945, shortly before the end of the war, Goebbels took his own life in the Führer's bunker in Berlin. So he never had to answer for his actions in court.
41738.m: At the end of the war Goebbels escaped all responsibility.

41739.q: What does the abbreviation SS stand for?
41739.e: The SS was founded in 1925 as a protection troop for Hitler. Later it became the most powerful organisation in the Nazi state.
41739.m: The SS was the Protection Squadron of the Nazi Party.

41740.e: Heinrich Himmler built the SS up into a huge apparatus of power. He was one of those chiefly responsible for the Holocaust.
41740.m: Heinrich Himmler was the head of the SS.

41741.q: Who was the SS originally a protection troop for?
41741.e: The SS was founded in 1925 as a bodyguard for Hitler. Later it became the most powerful organisation in the Nazi state.
41741.m: The SS began as a protection troop for Hitler.

41742.q: What colour was the well-known uniform the SS wore from 1932?
41742.e: Before that the SS wore the brown SA shirt with a black cap and tie. With the black uniform it wanted to set itself apart from the SA as an elite.
41742.m: From 1932 the SS wore black uniforms.

41743.q: Which organisation ran and guarded the concentration camps?
41743.e: The camps were run by SS units, the so-called Death's Head units. The SS was therefore responsible for countless crimes.
41743.m: The SS ran the concentration camps.

41744.q: What does the word “Gestapo” stand for?
41744.e: Gestapo is short for Geheime Staatspolizei, the Secret State Police. It was the political police of the Nazi state.
41744.m: The Gestapo was the Secret State Police.

41745.q: What was the main task of the Gestapo?
a: Tracking down and persecuting political opponents
Collecting customs duties at the border
41745.e: The Gestapo watched the population and persecuted everyone regarded as an opponent. It tortured prisoners and sent them to camps.
41745.m: The Gestapo persecuted opponents of the regime.

41746.q: Could the Gestapo lock people up without a court ruling?
a: Yes, for as long as it liked
41746.e: With so-called protective custody the Gestapo could imprison people without a verdict. No court could review this.
41746.m: The Gestapo could imprison people without a verdict.

41747.q: Where did the Gestapo get a great many of its tip-offs from?
41747.e: The Gestapo had relatively few officers. Many arrests came from denunciations by neighbours, colleagues or acquaintances.
41747.m: Denunciations helped the Gestapo persecute people.

41748.q: What stands today in Berlin where the Gestapo headquarters used to be?
a: A museum about the Nazis' crimes
41748.e: Today the Topography of Terror on the site informs visitors about the crimes of the Gestapo and the SS.
41748.m: In Berlin a museum remembers the Gestapo perpetrators.

41749.q: About how many European Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
41749.e: The Nazis murdered about six million Jews. That was about two thirds of the Jews in Europe.
41749.m: About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.

41750.q: What is the Holocaust called in Hebrew?
41750.e: Shoah means “catastrophe” or “great disaster” in Hebrew. Many Jewish people use this word.
41750.m: Shoah is the Hebrew word for the Holocaust.

41751.q: At which conference in January 1942 did senior Nazi officials organise the mass murder of the Jews?
41751.e: On 20 January 1942 representatives of ministries and the SS met in a villa on Berlin's Wannsee lake. They discussed carrying out the so-called “Final Solution”.
41751.m: The genocide was organised at the Wannsee Conference.

41752.q: In which city was the largest Jewish ghetto in occupied Europe?
41752.e: At times more than 400,000 people were crammed into the Warsaw Ghetto. In 1943 the inhabitants fought back in the ghetto uprising.
41752.m: The Warsaw Ghetto was the largest ghetto.

41753.q: Which sign did Jews in the German Reich have to wear on their clothes from September 1941?
41753.e: The yellow star with the word “Jude” (Jew) had to be worn where it could be seen. In this way Jews were publicly marked and excluded.
41753.m: The yellow star marked Jews in public.

41754.q: Which group, besides the Jews, was also the victim of a Nazi genocide?
41754.e: Hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma were persecuted and murdered. Many Roma call this genocide the Porajmos.
41754.m: The Sinti and Roma were also victims of genocide.

41755.q: Which St Gallen police commander saved Jewish refugees in 1938 and was later honoured as “Righteous Among the Nations”?
41755.e: Paul Grüninger let hundreds of refugees into Switzerland despite a ban. He was dismissed and convicted, and only cleared in 1995.
41755.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees and was punished for it.

41756.q: Which Swiss diplomat saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest with letters of protection?
41756.e: Carl Lutz was vice consul in Budapest and issued letters of protection in 1944. In this way he saved tens of thousands of people from deportation.
41756.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of lives in Budapest.

41757.q: In which present-day country is the Auschwitz memorial?
41757.e: Auschwitz is near the town of Oświęcim in southern Poland. At that time the area was occupied by Germany.

41758.q: Who liberated the Auschwitz camp in January 1945?
41758.e: Soviet soldiers reached the camp and found about 7,000 survivors. The SS had driven most of the prisoners away on death marches beforehand.

41759.q: On which day is International Holocaust Remembrance Day?
41759.e: 27 January is the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz in 1945. The UN declared it a day of remembrance in 2005.
41759.m: On 27 January the victims of the Holocaust are remembered worldwide.

41760.q: What was the part of Auschwitz called where most people were murdered in gas chambers?
41760.e: Auschwitz II, called Birkenau, was an extermination camp. Most of the victims there were murdered straight after they arrived.
41760.m: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest extermination camp.

41761.q: Which words are written over the gate of the Auschwitz main camp?
41761.e: The sentence “Arbeit macht frei” was a cruel lie. It was meant to deceive and mock the prisoners.
41761.m: Over the gate of Auschwitz stood “Arbeit macht frei”.

41762.q: About how many people were murdered in Auschwitz?
41762.e: About 1.1 million people were murdered in Auschwitz, the vast majority of them Jews. No other camp had so many victims.
41762.m: Auschwitz has become the symbol of the Holocaust.

41763.q: What was tattooed on the forearm of many prisoners in Auschwitz?
41763.e: Auschwitz was the only camp where prisoners were systematically tattooed with numbers. People were meant to be nothing but numbers.
41763.m: In Auschwitz people were turned into numbers.

41764.q: Which Nazi organisation ran the Auschwitz camp?
41764.e: The SS ran the concentration and extermination camps. The first commandant of Auschwitz was Rudolf Höss.
41764.m: The SS ran the Nazis' camps.

41765.q: Who formed the core of the resistance group White Rose?
41765.e: The White Rose consisted mainly of young students at the University of Munich. They wanted to call on people to resist.
41765.m: The White Rose was a group of young students.

41766.q: What was the name of Sophie Scholl's brother, who also belonged to the White Rose?
41766.e: Hans Scholl studied medicine and founded the group with Alexander Schmorell. His younger sister Sophie joined later.
41766.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl fought the regime together.

41767.q: By what means did the White Rose resist?
41767.e: The group wrote, printed and handed out leaflets against Hitler. It wanted to make people think.
41767.m: The White Rose fought with words.

41768.q: What did the White Rose leaflets call for?
41768.e: Six leaflets were produced between 1942 and 1943. They urged people to stand up against Hitler and the war.
41768.m: The White Rose used leaflets to call for resistance.

41769.q: Where were Hans and Sophie Scholl discovered and arrested in February 1943?
a: At a printing works in Vienna
41769.e: On 18 February 1943 they threw leaflets into the atrium of the university. A caretaker saw them and reported them to the police.
41769.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested at their university.

41770.q: How old was Sophie Scholl when she was executed in February 1943?
41770.e: Sophie Scholl was born on 9 May 1921 and executed on 22 February 1943. So she was 21 years old.

41771.q: What was Sophie Scholl when she joined the White Rose?
41771.e: Sophie Scholl began studying biology and philosophy in Munich in 1942. There she joined her brother's group.
41771.m: Sophie Scholl was a student in Munich.

41772.q: What did the Allies do with the last leaflet of the White Rose?
a: They dropped millions of copies over Germany
They banned it in their countries
They sold it as a book
41772.e: The leaflet reached England. In 1943 British planes dropped it over Germany as the “Manifesto of the Munich Students”.
41772.m: In this way the White Rose's message reached millions of people.

41773.q: Who helped the White Rose students with the last leaflet?
41773.e: Kurt Huber was a professor of philosophy and musicology in Munich. He helped write the last leaflet and was executed in 1943.
41773.m: A professor also belonged to the White Rose.

41774.q: Which officer planted a bomb on 20 July 1944 to kill Hitler?
41774.e: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg placed the bomb at a briefing meeting. He wanted to end the war and the crimes.
41774.m: Stauffenberg dared to try to assassinate Hitler.

41775.q: What was the name of the Führer's headquarters where the bomb of 20 July exploded?
41775.e: The Wolf's Lair was in East Prussia, in present-day Poland. Hitler stayed there for much of the war.
41775.m: The assassination attempt took place at the Wolf's Lair.

41776.q: What did Stauffenberg hide the bomb in?
41776.e: At the meeting Stauffenberg put the bag with the explosives near Hitler. Then he left the room on a pretext.
41776.m: The bomb was hidden in a briefcase.

41777.q: What was the name of the plan the conspirators meant to use to take power after the assassination?
41777.e: The “Valkyrie” plan was really meant for an emergency at home. The conspirators wanted to use it to take over the government.
41777.m: Operation Valkyrie was meant to seize power.

41778.q: What protected Hitler from the full force of the explosion?
41778.e: The explosive was behind a solid table support. Also, the meeting was held in a wooden hut, so the blast could escape.
41778.m: Hitler survived the assassination attempt with only slight injuries.

41779.q: What did the conspirators of 20 July 1944 want to achieve?
a: Kill Hitler and end the war
41779.e: The conspirators wanted to get rid of Hitler, take power and end the war. The plan failed.
41779.m: The conspirators of 20 July wanted to overthrow Hitler.

41780.q: What happened to Stauffenberg after the failed assassination attempt?
a: He was shot that same night
41780.e: Stauffenberg was arrested in Berlin and shot during the night. Today a memorial there remembers the resistance.
41780.m: Stauffenberg was shot that same night.

41781.q: How did the Nazi regime react to the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944?
a: It had many of those involved arrested and executed
41781.e: After the assassination attempt thousands were arrested. Many were sentenced to death in show trials.
41781.m: The Nazi regime took brutal revenge on the conspirators.

41782.q: When did the main war crimes trial in Nuremberg begin?
41782.e: The trial began on 20 November 1945. The verdicts were announced on 1 October 1946.
41782.m: The Nuremberg trials began in autumn 1945.

41783.q: How many victorious powers together formed the court in Nuremberg?
41783.e: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France formed the International Military Tribunal. Each country provided judges and prosecutors.
41783.m: Four victorious powers sat in judgement in Nuremberg.

41784.q: Which highest-ranking defendant took his own life before his execution?
41784.e: Hermann Göring was commander-in-chief of the air force and was sentenced to death. Shortly before the execution he poisoned himself in his cell.

41785.q: What was the harshest sentence the Nuremberg court imposed on several of the main defendants?
41785.e: The court passed twelve death sentences. Others received prison sentences, and three were acquitted.
41785.m: In Nuremberg several of the main defendants were sentenced to death.

41786.q: In which building did the trial in Nuremberg take place?
41786.e: The Palace of Justice had hardly been damaged in the war and had a prison. Courtroom 600 is a memorial today.
41786.m: The trial took place in the Nuremberg Palace of Justice.

41787.q: Which charge was used for the first time in an international trial at Nuremberg?
41787.e: For the first time leading politicians had to answer for crimes against humanity. That was a milestone in international law.
41787.m: In Nuremberg crimes against humanity were charged for the first time.

41788.q: Which present-day court in The Hague follows in the tradition of the Nuremberg trials?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
41788.e: The International Criminal Court has been working since 2002. Like the court in Nuremberg, it prosecutes individuals for the most serious crimes.
41788.m: The Nuremberg trials are a model for today's international criminal law.

41789.q: Which deputy of Hitler stayed in prison after the Nuremberg trials until his death in 1987?
41789.e: Rudolf Hess was sentenced to life imprisonment. In the end he was the only prisoner in Berlin's Spandau prison. Goebbels, Hitler and Göring were no longer alive in 1946.
41789.m: Rudolf Hess stayed in prison until his death.

41790.q: What did the Fascists want to achieve with the March on Rome in 1922?
41790.e: At the end of October 1922 Mussolini's supporters headed towards Rome. Shortly afterwards Mussolini became head of government.
41790.m: The March on Rome brought Mussolini to power.

41791.q: Who led the movement that organised the March on Rome?
41791.e: Benito Mussolini was the leader of the Italian Fascists. With the March on Rome he put pressure on the government.
41791.m: Mussolini used the March on Rome to come to power.

41792.q: Who appointed Mussolini head of government in 1922?
41792.e: King Victor Emmanuel III asked Mussolini to form a government instead of using the army against the Fascists.
41792.m: In 1922 the king handed the government to Mussolini.

41793.q: Why did the Italian army not stop the March on Rome?
a: The king gave no order to do so
The Fascists were already in Rome
41793.e: The government wanted to use the army against the Fascists. But the king did not sign the necessary state of emergency.
41793.m: Because the king did not act, nobody stopped the Fascists.

41794.q: How did Mussolini himself travel to Rome to become head of government?
a: On foot at the head of the march
41794.e: Mussolini waited in Milan to see how things would develop. Only when the king summoned him did he travel to Rome in a sleeping car.
41794.m: Mussolini did not march himself but came to Rome by train.

41795.q: What were Mussolini's supporters called because of their clothes?
41795.e: The fighting squads of the Italian Fascists wore black shirts. The Nazis' SA later wore brown shirts.

41796.q: Which German coup attempt of 1923 took the March on Rome as its model?
41796.e: In November 1923 Adolf Hitler wanted to march from Munich to Berlin, much as Mussolini had marched on Rome. However, the putsch failed in Munich itself.
41796.m: Hitler's putsch of 1923 copied the March on Rome but failed.

41797.q: Which title did Mussolini give himself as leader of the Fascists?
41797.e: “Duce” comes from the Latin “dux”, which means leader. In propaganda Mussolini was only ever called “il Duce”.

41798.q: Which job, among others, had Mussolini done before he became a politician?
41798.e: Mussolini was a teacher and above all a journalist. He edited the socialist newspaper “Avanti!” and later founded “Il Popolo d'Italia”.
41798.m: Before his dictatorship Mussolini was a newspaper journalist.

41799.q: What colour were the shirts of the Italian Fascist fighting squads?
41799.e: The Fascist gangs of thugs wore black shirts. That is why they are called Blackshirts.
41799.m: The Blackshirts were the fighting squads of the Italian Fascists.

41800.q: Who was the leader of the Italian Fascists and their Blackshirts?
