42913.e: In 2018 the limit of two terms was removed from the constitution. This allowed Xi Jinping to start a third term as President in 2023.
42913.m: Since 2018 the Chinese President’s time in office is no longer limited.

42914.q: What is the big infrastructure project that Xi Jinping announced in 2013 called?
42914.e: The New Silk Road is meant to create trade routes with ports, railways and roads to Asia, Africa and Europe. Its official name is the “Belt and Road Initiative”.
42914.m: The New Silk Road is Xi Jinping’s big trade project.

42915.q: What is the capital of the country that Xi Jinping governs?
42915.e: Beijing is the capital of China. Xi Jinping’s government is based there. Xi Jinping was also born in Beijing.

42916.q: Where did the young Xi Jinping have to live and work for several years during the Cultural Revolution?
a: In a village in the countryside
At a university in the USA
42916.e: Like millions of other young people, Xi was sent to the countryside. From 1969 he lived in a village in Shaanxi province.
42916.m: As a young man Xi Jinping lived in a village in the countryside.

42917.q: What is one of Xi Jinping’s best-known campaigns at home?
42917.e: Since 2012 hundreds of thousands of officials have been punished in the fight against corruption. Critics say that political opponents have also been removed this way.
42917.m: Xi Jinping leads a big campaign against corruption.

42918.q: What does the Party call Xi Jinping’s political ideas, which were written into the constitution?
42918.e: “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era” has been in the Party constitution since 2017 and in the state constitution since 2018. No Party leader since Mao has been honoured like this during his lifetime.
42918.m: Xi Jinping Thought is in China’s constitution.

42919.q: What is the National People’s Congress?
a: The parliament of the People’s Republic of China
42919.e: According to the constitution, the National People’s Congress is the highest organ of state power. In reality, however, the Communist Party decides policy.
42919.m: The National People’s Congress is China’s parliament.

42920.q: Roughly how many members does the National People’s Congress have?
42920.e: The People’s Congress has just under 3,000 members. This makes it one of the biggest parliaments in the world.
42920.m: The National People’s Congress has around 3,000 members.

42921.q: In which building in Beijing does the National People’s Congress meet?
a: In the Great Hall of the People
42921.e: The Great Hall of the People stands on Tiananmen Square. It was completed in 1959.
42921.m: The People’s Congress meets in the Great Hall of the People.

42922.q: How often does the National People’s Congress meet in full session?
42922.e: The full session takes place every year in March and lasts only about a week. Between sessions the Standing Committee does the work.
42922.m: The National People’s Congress meets once a year.

42923.q: Who really decides policy in China, even though the National People’s Congress is the parliament?
42923.e: In China only one party has real power, the Communist Party. The People’s Congress usually approves its plans.
42923.m: In China the Communist Party decides policy.

42924.q: Who officially elects the President in China?
42924.e: According to the constitution, the People’s Congress elects the President. But the Party has already chosen the candidate beforehand.
42924.m: The National People’s Congress elects China’s President.

42925.q: Why is the National People’s Congress often called a “rubber-stamp parliament”?
a: It almost always approves the Party’s proposals
It has no voting rights at all
It is made up only of foreigners
42925.e: Votes usually end with very large majorities for the Party leadership’s proposals. There is no real opposition in the People’s Congress.
42925.m: The National People’s Congress almost always approves the Party’s plans.

42926.q: What is the body called that passes laws between the sessions of the National People’s Congress?
42926.e: The Standing Committee has about 170 members and meets regularly. It does a large part of the law-making.
42926.m: The Standing Committee works between the sessions of the People’s Congress.

42927.q: When was North Korea founded as a separate state?
a: Shortly after the Second World War
42927.e: North Korea was founded in 1948, three years after the end of the Second World War. Kim Il-sung became its first ruler.
42927.m: North Korea was created shortly after the Second World War.

42928.q: Which great power helped Kim Il-sung come to power after the Second World War?
42928.e: After 1945 the Soviet Union occupied the north of Korea. It supported Kim Il-sung as leader of the new state.
42928.m: Kim Il-sung came to power with the help of the Soviet Union.

42929.q: Which war did Kim Il-sung start in 1950 with an attack on the South?
42929.e: In June 1950 North Korea attacked South Korea. The war ended in 1953 with a ceasefire but without a peace treaty.
42929.m: Kim Il-sung started the Korean War in 1950.

42930.q: How long did Kim Il-sung rule North Korea?
42930.e: Kim Il-sung ruled from the founding in 1948 until his death in 1994. There are no free elections in North Korea.
42930.m: Kim Il-sung ruled North Korea until his death.

42931.q: Who followed Kim Il-sung as ruler of North Korea?
42931.e: After Kim Il-sung’s death, his son Kim Jong-il took power. Today his grandson, Kim Jong-un, is already in charge.
42931.m: Kim Il-sung founded a family dynasty in North Korea.

42932.q: What title did Kim Il-sung receive in North Korea’s constitution after his death?
42932.e: In 1998 Kim Il-sung was declared “Eternal President” in the constitution. This was meant to keep him at the head of the state for ever.
42932.m: In North Korea Kim Il-sung is regarded as the “Eternal President”.

42933.q: Which day is a big holiday in North Korea, known as the “Day of the Sun”?
42933.e: Kim Il-sung was born on 15 April 1912. His birthday is celebrated every year in North Korea with big festivities.
42933.m: In North Korea Kim Il-sung’s birthday is celebrated as the “Day of the Sun”.

42934.q: What is the exaggerated worship of Kim Il-sung in North Korea called?
42934.e: All over the country there are statues and pictures of Kim Il-sung. People have to bow in front of his monuments.
42934.m: There is a strong personality cult around Kim Il-sung.

42935.q: Roughly what does the Korean word “Juche” mean?
42935.e: Juche means something like “self-reliance” or “independence”. According to this idea, a country should provide for itself politically, economically and militarily.

42936.q: In which country is the Juche ideology the official state ideology?
42936.e: The Juche ideology is written into North Korea’s constitution. It shapes politics, school and art there.
42936.m: The Juche ideology is North Korea’s state idea.

42937.q: Who is regarded as the founder of the Juche ideology?
42937.e: Kim Il-sung put the Juche idea in the foreground from the 1950s. His successors later developed it further.
42937.m: Kim Il-sung founded the Juche ideology.

42938.q: Roughly how tall is the Juche Tower in Pyongyang?
42938.e: The Juche Tower was opened in 1982 for the 70th birthday of the state’s founder. Including the flame at the top, it is about 170 metres tall.
42938.m: The Juche Tower in Pyongyang is about 170 metres tall.

42939.q: With which year does the Juche calendar in North Korea start counting?
a: The year North Korea was founded
The end of the Korean War
42939.e: 1912, the year Kim Il-sung was born, is year 1 in the Juche calendar. The calendar was introduced in 1997.
42939.m: The Juche calendar starts with Kim Il-sung’s year of birth, 1912.

42940.q: What economic effect did the Juche policy of isolation have on North Korea?
a: The country stayed poor and isolated
The country became Asia’s biggest exporter
The country became a magnet for tourists
42940.e: North Korea trades very little with other countries and has hardly any contact with the outside world. In the 1990s the country suffered a severe famine.
42940.m: Isolation has made North Korea poor and cut off.

42941.q: What was given priority in North Korea under the Songun policy from the 1990s?
42941.e: Songun means “military first”. The army got the most money and resources, while many people went hungry.
42941.m: In North Korea Songun means “military first”.

42942.q: According to the Juche ideology, what should people in North Korea mainly follow?
42942.e: According to the Juche ideology, the people need a great leader to guide them. In this way it justifies the power of the Kim family.
42942.m: The Juche ideology justifies the power of the Kim family.

42943.q: Which country carried out the reforms called “Doi Moi”?
42943.e: The Communist Party of Vietnam decided on Doi Moi in 1986. The country’s economy was in a serious crisis at the time.
42943.m: Doi Moi were economic reforms in Vietnam.

42944.q: What does the Vietnamese term “Doi Moi” mean?
42944.e: Doi Moi translates as “renewal”. It refers to the restructuring of the economy.

42945.q: What mainly changed in Vietnam because of Doi Moi?
a: The economy opened up to the market
42945.e: Farmers and businesses were again allowed to make more of their own decisions and to make profits. Politically, however, the Communist Party stayed alone in power.
42945.m: Doi Moi opened up Vietnam’s economy, but the Party stayed in power.

42946.q: Which country served Vietnam as a model for the Doi Moi reforms?
42946.e: China had been successful with market reforms since 1978. Vietnam followed a similar path.
42946.m: For Doi Moi, Vietnam followed China’s example.

42947.q: How did things change for Vietnam with rice after the Doi Moi reforms?
a: It became one of the biggest rice exporters
It had to import even more rice
It gave up growing rice completely
It was no longer allowed to sell rice
42947.e: Before the reforms, Vietnam had to import rice. A few years later it was one of the world’s biggest rice exporters.
42947.m: After Doi Moi Vietnam became a big rice exporter.

42948.q: With which former enemy in war did Vietnam restore diplomatic relations in 1995?
42948.e: In the Vietnam War the USA had fought against North Vietnam. In 1995 the two countries normalised their relations, which brought Vietnam more trade.
42948.m: Vietnam and the USA have had diplomatic relations again since 1995.

42949.q: Which international trade organisation did Vietnam join in 2007?
42949.e: Joining the WTO was an important step in opening up. It made it easier for Vietnam to export all over the world.
42949.m: Vietnam has been a member of the WTO since 2007.

42950.q: What happened to poverty in Vietnam in the decades after Doi Moi?
42950.e: The economy grew quickly for many years. The share of very poor people fell considerably.
42950.m: After Doi Moi poverty in Vietnam fell sharply.

42951.q: What happened in Cuba on New Year’s Day 1959?
a: The dictator fled and the revolutionaries won
Cuba became part of the USA
42951.e: On New Year’s Eve 1959 the dictator left the country. This meant Fidel Castro and his fighters had won.
42951.m: The Cuban Revolution triumphed on 1 January 1959.

42952.q: Who did the Cuban revolutionaries overthrow?
42952.e: The dictator Fulgencio Batista ruled Cuba harshly and unjustly. The revolutionaries led by Fidel Castro drove him out.
42952.m: The Cuban Revolution overthrew a dictator.

42953.q: What are fighters called who, like Castro’s rebels, fight an army in small groups from mountains and forests?
42953.e: Guerrilla means “little war” in Spanish. Castro’s rebels attacked the army and then withdrew to the mountains again.
42953.m: Castro’s rebels fought a guerrilla war.

42954.q: How did Fidel Castro and his fighters get from Mexico to Cuba in 1956?
42954.e: 82 fighters crossed the sea to Cuba on the small yacht “Granma”. The journey was very cramped and dangerous.
42954.m: Castro’s fighters came to Cuba on a small boat.

42955.q: Where did Castro’s rebels hide from 1956?
a: In the mountains in the east of Cuba
In the presidential palace in Havana
In a city in the USA
42955.e: The rebels withdrew into the Sierra Maestra mountains. There they were hard to find and built up their army.
42955.m: The Cuban rebels hid in the mountains.

42956.q: How did the USA respond economically to the confiscations in Cuba from 1960?
42956.e: The new government also nationalised companies from the USA. In response the USA imposed an embargo that is still largely in force today.
42956.m: The USA imposed a trade embargo on Cuba.

42957.q: How did the Cuban Revolution end?
42957.e: At the end of 1958 the rebels won the decisive battles. At the beginning of 1959 Fidel Castro took power.
42957.m: The Cuban Revolution ended with the rebels’ victory.

42958.q: Which country became Cuba’s most important ally after the revolution?
42958.e: Cuba bought oil from the Soviet Union and sold it sugar. After the end of the Soviet Union in 1991, Cuba fell into a severe economic crisis.
42958.m: After the revolution the Soviet Union was Cuba’s most important partner.

42959.q: How was Raúl Castro related to Fidel Castro?
42959.e: Raúl Castro was born in 1931 and was five years younger than Fidel. Both fought together in the revolution.
42959.m: Raúl Castro is Fidel Castro’s younger brother.

42960.q: Which office did Raúl Castro hold for almost 50 years before he became President?
42960.e: Raúl Castro was Minister of Defence from 1959 to 2008. He built up the Cuban army.
42960.m: Raúl Castro was Cuba’s Minister of Defence for decades.

42961.q: Why did Raúl Castro temporarily take over Fidel’s duties in 2006?
42961.e: Fidel Castro had to have an operation in 2006. Raúl then ran things and officially became President in 2008.
42961.m: Raúl Castro took over the leadership in 2006 because Fidel was ill.

42962.q: Until which year was Raúl Castro President of Cuba?
42962.e: In 2018 Raúl Castro gave up the presidency. For the first time since 1976, no Castro was head of state.
42962.m: Raúl Castro was President of Cuba until 2018.

42963.q: Who followed Raúl Castro as President of Cuba in 2018?
42963.e: Miguel Díaz-Canel was born in 1960, so only after the revolution. Before that he was First Vice-President of Cuba.
42963.m: Miguel Díaz-Canel followed Raúl Castro in 2018.

42964.q: With which US president did Raúl Castro improve relations with the USA?
42964.e: At the end of 2014 both announced a rapprochement. In 2015 embassies opened again, and in 2016 Obama visited Havana.
42964.m: Raúl Castro and Barack Obama improved relations between Cuba and the USA.

42965.q: What did Raúl Castro increasingly allow Cubans to have from 2010?
a: A separate currency for each province
42965.e: Under Raúl Castro more people were allowed to work for themselves, for example with small restaurants or taxis. One-party rule remained.
42965.m: Raúl Castro allowed more small private businesses in Cuba.

42966.q: From which year did the one-child policy apply in China?
42966.e: The rules were announced in 1979 and enforced across the country from 1980. They were meant to slow down the fast growth of the population.
42966.m: The one-child policy applied in China from 1980.

42967.q: What was the main aim of the one-child policy?
a: To get more children into school
42967.e: At the end of the 1970s China had almost a billion inhabitants. The government feared that there would not be enough food and work for everyone.
42967.m: The one-child policy was meant to slow down population growth.

42968.q: From which year were all couples in China allowed to have two children?
42968.e: At the end of 2015 China decided on the two-child policy, which applied from January 2016. The population was getting older and there was a shortage of young workers.
42968.m: Since 2016 all couples in China have been allowed two children.

42969.q: How many children has China allowed each couple since 2021?
42969.e: In 2021 the limit was raised to three children. Later the penalties for having more children were abolished completely.
42969.m: Since 2021 China has allowed three children per couple.

42970.q: What effect did the one-child policy have on the balance of boys and girls in China?
a: There are clearly more men than women
There are clearly more women than men
There are exactly the same number
42970.e: Many families wanted a son. That is why fewer girls were born, and today there are millions of women missing.
42970.m: Because of the one-child policy there are more men than women in China.

42971.q: Which group was usually exempt from the one-child policy?
42971.e: Many of the 55 recognised minorities were allowed to have more children. Farming families also often got a second child if the first was a girl.
42971.m: National minorities were often exempt from the one-child policy.

42972.q: Which problem did the one-child policy make worse in the long run?
a: The number of people who cannot read
42972.e: Because fewer children were born, there are now many older people and fewer young ones. Since 2022 China’s population has been shrinking.
42972.m: The one-child policy made China’s population age faster.

42973.q: How were families punished who broke the one-child policy?
42973.e: Anyone who had too many children often had to pay heavy fines and could even lose their job. The state put great pressure on families.
42973.m: Breaking the one-child policy was punished with heavy fines.

42974.q: Which doctor from Argentina became a comandante in the Cuban Revolution and later Cuba’s Minister of Industry?
42974.e: Che Guevara had studied medicine in Buenos Aires. After the victory he ran the National Bank and the Ministry of Industry, among other things.
42974.m: Che Guevara was a doctor and became a minister in Cuba.

42975.q: What is Shenzhen known for around the world today?
42975.e: A great many mobile phones, computer parts and drones are developed and built in Shenzhen. That is why the city is often called “China’s Silicon Valley”.
42975.m: Shenzhen is a centre for electronics and technology.

42976.q: What were spoilt only children in China called informally?
42976.e: Because parents and four grandparents looked after a single child, people spoke of “little emperors”. The expression describes spoilt only children.
42976.m: In China spoilt only children were called “little emperors”.

42977.q: Where does Kim Il-sung’s embalmed body lie today?
42977.e: His former palace in the capital Pyongyang was converted into a mausoleum. His son Kim Jong-il also lies there.
42977.m: Kim Il-sung lies in a mausoleum in Pyongyang.

42978.e: In Cuba only the Communist Party is allowed. Raúl Castro led it until 2021.
42978.m: Cuba is governed by the Communist Party.

42979.q: What status did the cantons have in the Helvetic Republic?
a: They had a right of veto
42979.e: The cantons lost their sovereignty and became administrative units of the central state. At their head was a prefect appointed by the central government.
42979.m: In the Helvetic Republic the cantons no longer had their own sovereignty.

42980.q: Which educator looked after orphans in Stans for the Helvetic government after the fighting of 1798?
42980.e: The Helvetic government asked Pestalozzi to run an orphanage in Stans for the children of the victims. He described his experiences there in the “Letter from Stans”.
42980.m: In 1799 Pestalozzi cared for war orphans in Stans.

42981.q: Which Helvetic canton combined Uri, Schwyz, Zug and Unterwalden in 1798?
42981.e: To weaken the rebellious rural cantons, they were combined in 1798 into the canton of Waldstätten. Only the Malmaison Constitution divided it up again.
42981.m: The Helvetic Republic merged the Central Swiss cantons into the canton of Waldstätten.

42982.q: To which city did the Helvetic councils move in October 1798 as their new seat of government?
42982.e: Aarau had only been the provisional capital. In October 1798 the government and councils moved to Lucerne, and in 1799 on to Bern.
42982.m: The Helvetic Republic changed its seat of government several times.

42983.q: How were those who did not vote counted in the vote on the second Helvetic Constitution of 1802?
a: Half as yes and half as no
42983.e: Following the principle “silence seems to mean consent”, those who did not vote were added to the supporters. Only in this way was there a majority, as the no votes outnumbered the yes votes.
42983.m: In the constitutional vote of 1802, silence counted as consent.

42984.q: Which French general defeated the Russian troops at the Second Battle of Zurich in September 1799?
42984.e: André Masséna beat the Russians under Korsakov on 25 and 26 September 1799. At that time the Helvetic Republic was a battleground of the War of the Second Coalition.
42984.m: In 1799 Switzerland became a battlefield for foreign armies.

42985.q: Over which pass did the Russian general Suvorov retreat from Switzerland in autumn 1799?
42985.e: Suvorov had come from Ticino over the Gotthard and marched through the Muota valley, over the Pragel and through Glarus. He reached the Grisons over the snow-covered Panix Pass.
42985.m: Suvorov's Alpine march of 1799 ended over the Panix Pass.

42986.q: Which levies did the first Helvetic Constitution abolish in principle?
42986.e: The first constitution did away with tithes, feudal rights and the guild system. Because the state's coffers were empty, however, old ground rents were reintroduced in 1800.
42986.m: The Helvetic Republic wanted to free the farmers from the old feudal dues.

42987.q: Which patriot from Vaud, a former tutor of the Russian Tsar Alexander I, became a Helvetic Director in 1798?
42987.e: Frédéric-César de La Harpe had campaigned for Vaud's liberation from Bern. In June 1798 he joined the Directory and was removed in January 1800.
42987.m: La Harpe from Vaud was a leading figure of the Helvetic Republic.

42988.q: Which canton was NOT created by the Act of Mediation of 1803?
42988.e: Valais had been a separate republic since 1802 and was annexed by France in 1810. It only joined the Confederation as a canton in 1815.
42988.m: Valais was not part of Switzerland during the Mediation period.

42989.q: What was the highest office of the Confederation called during the Mediation period?
42989.e: The office rotated every year among six cantons together with the leading canton (Vorort). The chief magistrate or mayor of the leading canton became Landammann of Switzerland.
42989.m: In the Mediation period the Landammann of Switzerland was at the head.

42990.q: What did Switzerland commit itself to towards France in the Mediation period?
a: To introduce French as the only official language
To hand over its taxes to Paris
42990.e: Under the military agreement of 1803, France was allowed to recruit 16,000 soldiers in Switzerland. Many Swiss later died in Napoleon's Russian campaign, for example at the Berezina.
42990.m: Mediation Switzerland had to provide France with soldiers.

42991.q: Which years does the Mediation period cover?
42991.e: The Mediation period began with the Act of Mediation of 1803. With the collapse of Napoleonic rule at the end of 1813 it lost its basis.
42991.m: The Mediation period lasted from 1803 to 1813.

42992.q: In which city did Swiss delegates discuss a new order in the winter of 1802/03 in the so-called Consulta?
42992.e: The Helvetic Consulta met in Paris on 10 December 1802. Most delegates were Unitarians (centralists), a minority were Federalists.
42992.m: The Act of Mediation was negotiated in Paris.

42993.q: What status did Neuchâtel have during the Mediation period?
a: A canton of the Confederation with equal rights
Part of the canton of Bern
42993.e: Neuchâtel belonged to the King of Prussia until 1806; after that Napoleon made his Marshal Berthier its prince. Neuchâtel only became a canton in 1815.
42993.m: In the Mediation period Neuchâtel was a principality, not a canton.

42994.q: Which state did Geneva belong to during the Mediation period?
42994.e: Geneva had been annexed by France in 1798 and was the capital of the Léman department. It only joined the Confederation as a canton in 1815.

42995.q: Which event abroad sparked the Regeneration in Switzerland in 1830?
42995.e: The July Revolution of 1830 in France encouraged the Liberals in many cantons. They demanded new constitutions and an end to the Restoration.
42995.m: The July Revolution in Paris triggered the Regeneration in 1830.

42996.q: What did the thousands of people at the Uster Day of 22 November 1830 mainly demand?
a: A return to the Helvetic Republic
42996.e: At the Uster Day, country people from the canton of Zurich demanded a constitution with fair representation of the countryside and liberal freedoms. The canton of Zurich got a new constitution in 1831.
42996.m: The Uster Day of 1830 was a milestone of the liberal movement in Zurich.

42997.q: What is the conservative uprising called that overthrew the liberal Zurich government in 1839?
42997.e: It was triggered by the appointment of the Bible-critical theologian David Friedrich Strauss to the University of Zurich. In September 1839 the outraged rural population overthrew the liberal government.
42997.m: The dispute over David Friedrich Strauss led to the Züriputsch in 1839.

42998.q: What was the 1832 alliance of seven liberal cantons, which guaranteed each other's new constitutions, called?
a: League of the Four Forest Cantons
42998.e: In the Concordate of the Seven, Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn, St Gallen, Aargau and Thurgau guaranteed each other's liberal constitutions. They also aimed to revise the Federal Treaty.
42998.m: In the Concordate of the Seven, liberal cantons protected each other.

42999.q: What was the association of conservative cantons called that joined forces in 1832 against liberal renewal?
42999.e: Conservative cantons such as Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Basel-City joined together in the League of Sarnen in 1832. It was dissolved by the Diet in 1833.
42999.m: The League of Sarnen was a conservative counter-alliance to the Regeneration.

43000.q: Which conflict of 1841 sharpened the opposition between Liberals and Catholic Conservatives?
43000.e: In 1841 the canton of Aargau closed all its monasteries, which the Catholic cantons saw as a breach of the Federal Treaty. The dispute contributed to the split in the Confederation.
43000.m: The Aargau monastery dispute of 1841 deepened the religious divide.

43001.q: With which programme did liberal cantons want to place the Catholic Church under greater state supervision in 1834?
43001.e: The Baden Articles of 1834 provided, among other things, for state approval of church decrees. The Pope condemned them, and the tensions grew.
43001.m: The Baden Articles were an attempt by liberal cantons to control the Church.

43002.q: Which general led the Diet's troops against the Sonderbund in 1847?
43002.e: General Dufour ended the war in less than a month with few deaths. He is also regarded as a co-founder of the Red Cross.
43002.m: General Dufour led the Diet's army in the Sonderbund War.

43003.q: In which year did the Catholic Conservative cantons join together in Lucerne to form the Sonderbund?
43003.e: The Sonderbund was founded in Lucerne on 11 December 1845 as a defensive alliance. The majority of the Diet saw it as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815.
43003.m: The Sonderbund was formed in 1845 as a defensive alliance.

43004.q: From which great power did the Sonderbund cantons hope for military support?
43004.e: The Sonderbund cantons counted on help from Austria. However, internal problems of the conservative powers prevented them from intervening.
43004.m: Foreign help for the Sonderbund never came.

43005.q: What did the Diet decide in Bern on 4 November 1847?
a: To dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms
43005.e: After the Sonderbund had refused to dissolve, the majority of the Diet decided to use armed force. This started the civil war.
43005.m: On 4 November 1847 the Diet decided to take military action.

43006.q: What are the armed expeditions of radical volunteers against Lucerne in 1844 and 1845 called?
43006.e: Radical volunteers from cantons such as Bern and Aargau wanted to bring a liberal government to power in Lucerne. Both volunteer raids failed and made the conflict worse.
43006.m: The volunteer raids against Lucerne failed.

43007.q: Which appointment by Lucerne sharpened the conflict before the Sonderbund War in 1844?
a: Calling in the Jesuits to run the higher schools
43007.e: For the Liberals and Radicals the Jesuit order was a hated enemy. Calling in the Jesuits led to the volunteer raids and to the founding of the Sonderbund.
43007.m: Calling the Jesuits to Lucerne fuelled the conflict.

43008.q: Roughly how large was the Diet's army in the Sonderbund War?
43008.e: The Diet raised almost 100,000 men with over 170 guns. The Sonderbund had far fewer troops and cannons.
43008.m: The Diet's army was clearly superior to the Sonderbund.

43009.q: Into which canton did Sonderbund troops advance over the Gotthard in November 1847?
43009.e: At the battle of Airolo on 17 November 1847, Sonderbund troops pushed into the Leventina valley. The advance did not change the outcome of the war.
43009.m: The Sonderbund tried to advance into Ticino over the Gotthard.

43010.q: Under the Federal Constitution of 1848, from what age could Swiss men take part in National Council elections?
43010.e: Every Swiss man who had reached the age of 20 and was not excluded from active citizenship was entitled to vote. Women had no right to vote.

43011.q: What could no longer be concluded under the Federal Constitution of 1848?
43011.e: Military capitulations were contracts by which cantons provided foreign powers with mercenary troops. The constitution of 1848 banned new contracts of this kind.
43011.m: From 1848 no new mercenary contracts could be concluded.

43012.q: Which order was not allowed to operate in Switzerland under the Federal Constitution of 1848?
43012.e: The constitution of 1848 forbade the Jesuits and their affiliated societies any activity in state and church. The ban was a result of the Sonderbund conflict.
43012.m: The ban on Jesuits was already in the first Federal Constitution.

43013.q: Which city did the Federal Assembly choose in November 1848 as the seat of the federal authorities?
43013.e: After the founding of the federal state, the Federal Assembly chose Bern as the federal city. Zurich and Lucerne lost out.
43013.m: Bern has been the federal city since 1848.

43014.q: Which war came immediately before the Federal Constitution of 1848?
43014.e: In November 1847 the liberal cantons defeated the Sonderbund of the Catholic Conservative cantons. After that the way was clear for the federal state.
43014.m: After the Sonderbund War the federal state was created in 1848.

43015.q: Who could vote on the new Federal Constitution in 1848?
43015.e: Women's suffrage only came at federal level in 1971. So only men voted on the constitution of 1848.
43015.m: Only men voted on the constitution of 1848.

43016.q: Which form of state did the Federal Constitution of 1848 replace?
a: The unitary state of the Helvetic Republic
43016.e: Before 1848 Switzerland was a loose confederation of states with the Diet. The constitution turned it into a federal state with a common government.
43016.m: In 1848 the confederation of states became a federal state.

43017.q: For whom did the Federal Constitution of 1848 guarantee the free practice of worship?
43017.e: In 1848 freedom of worship only applied to the recognised Christian denominations. Only the constitution of 1874 extended it to all religious communities.
43017.m: The freedom of worship of 1848 only applied to Christians.

43018.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in 1848 as the first person from Ticino?
43018.e: Stefano Franscini was a member of the first Federal Council and represented Italian-speaking Switzerland. Among other things, he promoted federal statistics.
43018.m: Stefano Franscini was the first Federal Councillor from Ticino.

43019.q: Which system of power did the Democratic Movement in the canton of Zurich fight against?
43019.e: The business leader and politician Alfred Escher combined posts in politics, railways and banks. The Democrats criticised this liberal web of power as the “Escher system”.
43019.m: The Zurich Democrats fought against the power of the Escher system.

43020.q: Which epidemic in 1867 increased discontent in the canton of Zurich?
43020.e: In the summer of 1867 cholera raged in Zurich. The epidemic increased criticism of the liberal government and brought the movement broad support.
43020.m: The cholera of 1867 gave the Democratic Movement a boost.

43021.q: Which people's rights did the Zurich cantonal constitution of 1869 introduce?
a: The legislative referendum and the initiative
43021.e: The constitution of 1869 brought the mandatory legislative referendum and the popular initiative. Zurich thus became a model of direct democracy.
43021.m: The Zurich constitution of 1869 strengthened direct democracy.

43022.q: Under the Zurich constitution of 1869, who elected the cantonal government?
43022.e: The Democrats pushed through the election of the government by the people. Before that, parliament had elected the government.
43022.m: Since 1869 the people of Zurich have elected their government themselves.

43023.q: What was one of the mottos of the Democratic Movement?
a: “Everything for the people, everything through the people!”
43023.e: The motto stressed that the people themselves should decide on laws and authorities. The Democrats wanted to add direct people's rights to representative democracy.
43023.m: The Democrats wanted everything for the people and everything through the people.

43024.q: Which social groups mainly supported the Democratic Movement?
a: The rural and small-town middle classes
43024.e: The movement relied on craftsmen, farmers, small business owners and workers in the countryside and small towns. Teachers, priests and newspaper editors often took the lead.
43024.m: The Democratic Movement was mainly a movement of the countryside.

43025.q: In which canton did the Democratic Movement begin in 1861 with a dispute about reunification with the city?
43025.e: A decision by the cantonal parliament on reunification with Basel-City sparked protests in Basel-Country. The opposition then pushed through a total revision of the cantonal constitution.
43025.m: In Basel-Country the Democratic Movement began as early as 1861.

43026.q: Which town was the stronghold of the Zurich Democrats?
43026.e: The Democrats had their centre in Winterthur, among other things with the newspaper “Der Landbote”. The town was a counterweight to the liberal city of Zurich.
43026.m: Winterthur was a centre of the Democratic Movement.

43027.q: Which ban did the Federal Constitution of 1874 newly introduce during the Kulturkampf?
43027.e: During the Kulturkampf the constitution of 1874 banned the founding of new monasteries and orders and the re-establishment of closed ones. This exceptional article was only removed by the people and the cantons in 1973.
43027.m: The constitution of 1874 banned the founding of new monasteries.

43028.q: What did the Federal Constitution of 1874 lay down for primary school education?
a: Compulsory, free of charge, religiously neutral
Voluntary, fee-paying, run by the church
43028.e: The cantons had to provide sufficient primary education, which was compulsory and free of charge in state schools. The schools had to be open to members of all faiths.
43028.m: Since 1874 primary school has been compulsory and free.

43029.q: Which people's right did the Federal Constitution of 1874 newly introduce at federal level?
a: The popular initiative for partial revision
Election of the Federal Council by the people
43029.e: With 30,000 signatures you could now demand a vote on federal acts. The popular initiative for partial revision only came in 1891.
43029.m: The optional referendum has existed since 1874.

43030.q: Under the Federal Constitution of 1874, which group could not be elected to the National Council?
43030.e: In the spirit of the Kulturkampf, the constitution excluded clergy from election to the National Council. The rule applied to clergy of all denominations.
43030.m: After 1874 clergy were not allowed to sit in the National Council.

43031.q: Under the Federal Constitution of 1874, what could only be established with the Confederation's approval?
43031.e: The diocese article required the Confederation's consent for every new diocese. As the last exceptional article on religion, it was only abolished in 2001.
43031.m: The diocese article dates from the Kulturkampf.

43032.q: In which area of law did the Confederation gain the power to legislate in 1874?
43032.e: The Confederation could now regulate, among other things, the law of obligations, commercial law, the law on bills of exchange and debt enforcement law. A general power over criminal and civil law was removed from the draft.
43032.m: Since 1874 the Confederation can regulate the law of obligations.

43033.q: With the Federal Constitution of 1874, what became a matter for the Confederation in military affairs?
a: The citizens' militias of the towns
43033.e: Legislation on the army passed to the Confederation, but the cantons kept their units. In this way the army became more uniform.
43033.m: Since 1874 the Confederation has regulated military matters by law.

43034.q: Under the constitution of 1874, how many cantons together could demand a referendum against a federal act?
43034.e: As well as voters, the cantons also got the right to demand a referendum. This requires eight cantons.
43034.m: Eight cantons together can also call a referendum.

43035.q: Compared with the failed proposal of 1872, which cantons tipped the balance in 1874?
a: French-speaking cantons such as Vaud and Geneva
Central Swiss cantons such as Uri and Zug
43035.e: The revised draft met the Federalists of French-speaking Switzerland halfway. Vaud, Neuchâtel and Geneva, which had said no in 1872, now voted in favour.
43035.m: French-speaking Switzerland helped the constitution of 1874 to succeed.

43036.q: In which two forms can a federal popular initiative be submitted?
a: General proposal or fully drafted text
43036.e: An initiative can contain a fully worded constitutional text or a general proposal. With a general proposal, Parliament drafts the text.
43036.m: A popular initiative is either fully worded or a general proposal.

43037.q: From which political camp did the push to introduce the initiative for partial revision come?
43037.e: A motion by Catholic Conservative members of Parliament in 1884 gave the push. The minority hoped the initiative would give it more influence against the Radical majority.
43037.m: The popular initiative was originally a tool of the minority.

43038.q: Which drink was banned in 1908 by a popular initiative that was accepted?
43038.e: The initiative for a ban on absinthe was accepted in 1908 with about 63.5 per cent yes. It was one of the few successful early popular initiatives.
43038.m: The absinthe ban entered the constitution through a popular initiative in 1908.

43039.q: Which kind of popular initiative still does not exist at federal level today?
43039.e: At federal level popular initiatives are aimed at the constitution. Several attempts to introduce a legislative initiative failed, and the general popular initiative adopted in 2003 was abolished again unused in 2009.
43039.m: At federal level an initiative can only change the constitution.

43040.q: Who decides whether a federal popular initiative is valid?
43040.e: Parliament checks the unity of form, the unity of subject matter and compatibility with mandatory international law. Declarations of invalidity are very rare.
43040.m: Parliament decides whether a popular initiative is valid.

43041.q: Roughly how many of the federal popular initiatives put to the vote from 1891 to 2020 were accepted?
43041.e: From 1891 to 2020 only 22 initiatives were accepted, while about 200 were rejected. That is about a tenth of the initiatives put to the vote.
43041.m: Most popular initiatives are rejected at the ballot box.

43042.q: Where in Switzerland did the popular initiative first exist?
43042.e: Cantons such as Vaud had the right of initiative from 1845. At federal level the initiative for partial revision of the constitution was only introduced in 1891.
43042.m: The cantons led the way for the Confederation with the popular initiative.

43043.q: Why were the 50,000 signatures for a popular initiative in 1891 a higher hurdle than today's 100,000?
a: There were far fewer people entitled to vote
You could only sign in Bern
43043.e: In 1891, 50,000 signatures were about 7.6 per cent of those entitled to vote, who were then only men. Today 100,000 signatures are only about 2 per cent.
43043.m: Measured against the number of voters, an initiative was harder to achieve in 1891.

43044.q: Roughly what share of yes votes did the proportional representation initiative receive when it was accepted in 1918?
43044.e: About 300,000 yes votes faced about 149,000 no votes, so about 67 per cent yes. A majority of the cantons was also clearly reached.
43044.m: The proportional representation initiative was clearly accepted in 1918.

43045.q: Which party lost its absolute majority in the National Council at the first proportional election of 1919?
43045.e: Under the majority system the Radicals had dominated the National Council for a long time. With proportional representation they fell from over 100 to 60 seats in 1919.
43045.m: Proportional representation ended the Radical majority in the National Council in 1919.

43046.q: Why did the proportional representation initiative of 1910 fail?
a: It missed the popular majority despite a majority of cantons
It missed the cantonal majority despite a popular majority
43046.e: In 1910 about 265,000 voters said no and 240,000 yes. A majority of the cantons, however, had agreed.
43046.m: The proportional representation initiative of 1910 narrowly missed a popular majority.

43047.q: In which year was the National Council first elected by proportional representation?
43047.e: The people accepted the proportional representation initiative in October 1918. The first election under the new system took place in October 1919.
43047.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

43048.q: Why did the proportional representation initiative launched in 1913 only come to a vote in 1918?
a: Because of the First World War
Because of a Federal Supreme Court ruling
43048.e: The initiative was launched again in 1913. The First World War delayed the popular vote until October 1918.
43048.m: The First World War delayed the vote on proportional representation.

43049.q: What was special about the timing of the first proportional election of the National Council?
a: It was brought forward by a year
It was postponed by two years
It took place in the middle of winter
It took place on National Day
43049.e: The sitting National Council would normally have stayed in office until 1920. The new election under the new system was therefore brought forward.
43049.m: The first proportional election took place earlier than normally planned.

43050.q: Which political force, a forerunner of today's SVP, entered the National Council with about 30 seats in 1919?
43050.e: Thanks to proportional representation, the new farmers' parties won about 30 seats straight away in 1919. They gave rise to the BGB, the forerunner of the SVP.
43050.m: The farmers' parties benefited greatly from proportional representation in 1919.

43051.q: In which chamber did the Radicals keep their absolute majority after the 1919 elections?
43051.e: Proportional representation only applied to the National Council; members of the Council of States were still mostly elected by majority vote. There the Radicals were able to defend their majority in 1919.
43051.m: Proportional representation mainly changed the National Council.

43052.q: In which month and year was the Federal Council first composed according to the “magic formula”?
43052.e: The Federal Assembly elected the new composition on 17 December 1959. It then lasted for over four decades.
43052.m: The magic formula was created in December 1959.

43053.q: How were the seven Federal Council seats divided under the magic formula of 1959?
43053.e: The Radicals, the Catholic Conservatives (later CVP) and the Social Democrats each got two seats. The Farmers', Traders' and Citizens' Party (later SVP) got one seat.
43053.m: The magic formula divided the seats in the ratio two to two to two to one.

43054.q: What aim did the Catholic Conservatives pursue with the magic formula of 1959?
a: To bring the SP in with two seats and weaken the FDP
To push the SP out of the Federal Council completely
To enlarge the Federal Council to nine seats
To make the BGB the strongest force
43054.e: Their general secretary Martin Rosenberg planned the return of the Social Democrats with two seats. This was meant to push back Radical influence.
43054.m: Martin Rosenberg is regarded as the inventor of the magic formula.

43055.q: Which official SP candidate was not elected by the Federal Assembly in 1959?
43055.e: Walther Bringolf, mayor of Schaffhausen, was controversial because of his Communist past. The Federal Assembly elected a different Social Democrat in his place.
43055.m: Walther Bringolf failed in 1959 despite his official nomination.

43056.q: What changed the magic formula in 2003?
a: The SVP won a second seat at the expense of the CVP
The Greens entered the Federal Council for the first time
The SP lost a seat to the FDP
The Federal Council was enlarged to nine members
43056.e: In December 2003 Christoph Blocher was elected instead of the sitting Federal Councillor Ruth Metzler. The SVP then had two seats and the CVP only one.
43056.m: In 2003 the magic formula ended with the SVP's second seat.

43057.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in December 2007 instead of Christoph Blocher?
43057.e: On 12 December 2007 the Federal Assembly elected the SVP politician Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf from the Grisons instead of the sitting Federal Councillor Blocher. The SVP group then declared itself in opposition for a time.
43057.m: In 2007 Christoph Blocher was not re-elected as a Federal Councillor.

43058.q: Why was the SP not represented in the Federal Council between 1954 and 1959?
a: Its Federal Councillor Max Weber had resigned
It had boycotted the Federal Council
It had never had a seat
43058.e: Max Weber resigned at the end of 1953 after his finance proposal was rejected, and the SP went into opposition. It only returned with the new composition of 1959.
43058.m: Before the magic formula the SP was not in the Federal Council for a few years.

43059.q: How did the Federal Supreme Court interpret the term “Landleute” (citizens of the canton) in the Appenzell Innerrhoden constitution in 1990?
43059.e: The court chose an interpretation in line with the constitution: “Landleute” includes both men and women. So no change to the cantonal constitution was needed.
43059.m: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court counted women as part of the “Landleute”.

43060.q: According to the 1990 ruling, what applied to earlier decisions taken without women?
a: They only applied for one more year
43060.e: The ruling only took effect from when it was announced. Earlier elections and votes without women did not become invalid afterwards.
43060.m: The 1990 ruling applied to the future, not retrospectively.

43061.q: In which year was the equality article, on which the 1990 ruling was based, added to the Federal Constitution?
43061.e: On 14 June 1981 the people and the cantons added the sentence “Men and women have equal rights” to the constitution. Nine years later the Federal Supreme Court based its ruling on it.

43062.q: How did Appenzell Innerrhoden vote on federal women's suffrage in 1971?
a: It did not vote at all
43062.e: In 1971 Innerrhoden was one of the cantons that rejected women's suffrage at federal level. Across Switzerland as a whole it was accepted all the same.
43062.m: Innerrhoden rejected federal women's suffrage in 1971.

43063.q: On what were women in Appenzell Innerrhoden already allowed to vote between 1971 and 1990?
43063.e: From 1971 women's suffrage applied at federal level throughout Switzerland. But in Innerrhoden cantonal matters remained men's business until 1990.
43063.m: From 1971 women in Innerrhoden voted federally, but not in the canton.

43064.q: Which argument by the canton did the Federal Supreme Court reject in 1990?
a: That the cantons could regulate the cantonal right to vote freely
That women already had the right to vote
That the Federal Supreme Court was not responsible for elections
43064.e: The canton relied on the provision that the cantonal right to vote is a matter for the cantons. The court did not see this as a real exception to the requirement of equality.
43064.m: Equality also applies to the cantonal right to vote.

43065.q: Apart from women from Innerrhoden, who was among the successful appellants in 1990?
43065.e: As well as over 50 women, almost 50 men from the canton had also lodged an appeal. Both appeals were upheld.
43065.m: In 1990 men from Innerrhoden also fought for women's suffrage.

43066.q: How did women in Appenzell Innerrhoden get the cantonal right to vote in 1990?
a: Through a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court
Through a decision of the Landsgemeinde
Through a decision of the Federal Council
43066.e: The Landsgemeinde had still rejected women's suffrage in 1990. In November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that excluding women breached the Federal Constitution.
43066.m: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court brought women's suffrage to Innerrhoden.

43067.q: What new feature regarding fundamental rights did the Federal Constitution of 1999 bring?
a: A systematic catalogue of fundamental rights
Fundamental rights only in the cantons
43067.e: Many fundamental rights had previously been unwritten and only recognised by the Federal Supreme Court. The new constitution brought them together in a chapter of their own.
43067.m: The 1999 constitution contains a complete catalogue of fundamental rights.

43068.q: Which Federal Councillor, as justice minister, led the total revision up to the vote in 1999?
43068.e: Arnold Koller from Appenzell headed the Federal Department of Justice and Police and drove the constitutional reform forward. Shortly after the vote he left the Federal Council.
43068.m: Federal Councillor Arnold Koller is seen as the father of the 1999 constitution.

43069.q: What does a new Federal Constitution need in order to be accepted?
a: A majority of the people and a majority of the cantons
43069.e: Constitutional amendments are subject to the mandatory referendum. They need a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons.
43069.m: Constitutional amendments need the people and the cantons.

43070.q: Under which Federal Councillor did an expert commission present a first draft for a total revision in 1977?
43070.e: The expert commission under Federal Councillor Kurt Furgler presented a far-reaching draft in 1977. It met with a lot of criticism and was not put into practice.
43070.m: The first draft of a new constitution in 1977 failed.

43071.q: Which reform followed in 2000 as a further package of the constitutional reform?
43071.e: On 12 March 2000 the people and the cantons accepted the judicial reform. Among other things, it brought the guarantee of access to the courts and the basis for new federal courts.
43071.m: The judicial reform of 2000 added to the new Federal Constitution.

43072.q: What does Article 3 of the Federal Constitution of 1999 state about the cantons?
a: They are sovereign insofar as the constitution does not limit this
They may not pass their own laws
They are directly under the Federal Council
43072.e: Article 3 states that the cantons exercise all rights not assigned to the Confederation. This is a core principle of Swiss federalism.
43072.m: The cantons are sovereign unless the Federal Constitution says otherwise.

43073.q: Which term does the Federal Constitution of 1999 no longer use?
43073.e: The 1999 constitution lists 26 cantons as equals. Instead of half-cantons, it speaks of cantons that have half a cantonal vote in the count of cantons.
43073.m: Today's Federal Constitution has 26 cantons and no more half-cantons.

43075.q: In which session is the whole Federal Council elected after the National Council elections?
43075.e: National Council elections take place in October, and the new legislative period begins with the winter session. There, in December, the United Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.
43075.m: The Federal Council is re-elected as a whole in the winter session.

43076.q: Where did the National Council and the Council of States meet in May and June 2020?
43076.e: Because of the Covid-19 pandemic, distancing could not be kept in the Federal Palace. The extraordinary session and the summer session were therefore held on the Bernexpo site.
43076.m: During the 2020 pandemic Parliament met on the Bernexpo site.

43077.q: What is a parliamentary group in the Federal Assembly?
a: An alliance of members from the same or similar parties
An electoral district of the National Council
43077.e: A parliamentary group needs at least five members from one of the two chambers. Only parliamentary groups get seats on the committees.
43077.m: In a parliamentary group, members with similar views work together.

43078.q: Which parliamentary group do the representatives of the Lega dei Ticinesi sit in at the Federal Palace?
43078.e: The Lega has too few seats for a group of its own and joins the SVP group. The EDU and MCG do the same.
43078.m: In the Federal Palace the Lega dei Ticinesi belongs to the SVP group.

43079.q: How does the Confederation fund the parliamentary groups of the Federal Assembly?
a: With a basic contribution and a contribution per member
Only with donations from the parties
With a contribution per vote received
43079.e: Each group receives a basic contribution every year plus an amount per member for its secretariat. Parliamentary groups have received state support since 1972.
43079.m: Parliamentary groups get a basic contribution and an amount per member from the Confederation.

43080.q: Who must approve the formation of a new parliamentary group in the National Council?
43080.e: New groups are recognised by the Coordination Conference. It is made up of the bureaus of both chambers.
43080.m: A new parliamentary group must be recognised by the Coordination Conference.

43081.q: Which parliamentary group was the largest in the Federal Assembly at the start of the 52nd legislative period in 2023?
43081.e: The SVP group is by far the largest group. It is followed by the SP, the Centre and the FDP.
43081.m: The SVP has the largest group in the Federal Palace (as of 2023).

43082.q: What is the first phase of dealing with a parliamentary initiative called?
43082.e: In the preliminary examination, the responsible committee decides whether the initiative should be taken further. Only then is a draft act prepared.
43082.m: A parliamentary initiative first goes through a preliminary examination.

43083.q: Who may submit a parliamentary initiative in the federal parliament?
43083.e: A parliamentary initiative can be submitted by a member, a parliamentary group or a committee. Cantons, on the other hand, submit a cantonal initiative.
43083.m: Parliamentary initiatives come from Parliament itself.

43084.q: What is special about a parliamentary initiative compared with a motion?
a: It always goes to the people
It only applies to the cantons
43084.e: With a motion, the Federal Council has to draw up a proposal. With a parliamentary initiative, a parliamentary committee writes the draft itself.
43084.m: With a parliamentary initiative, Parliament makes a law itself.

43085.q: What role does the Federal Council have in a parliamentary initiative?
a: It can give its opinion on the draft
It can stop it with a veto
It has no say at all
43085.e: The committee presents its draft to the Federal Council for its opinion. The Federal Council can propose changes but cannot decide.
43085.m: The Federal Council may only give its opinion on a parliamentary initiative.

43086.q: Which proposal goes back to a parliamentary initiative by the Green Liberals in 2013?
43086.e: The Green Liberal group submitted the parliamentary initiative “Marriage for all” in 2013. The law was accepted in a popular vote in 2021.
43086.m: Marriage for all came from a parliamentary initiative.

43087.q: In which two forms can a parliamentary initiative be submitted?
a: As a general proposal or a fully drafted text
43087.e: A parliamentary initiative can propose the act in general terms or already contain a fully worded draft. In both cases a committee then draws up the proposal.
43087.m: A parliamentary initiative is a general proposal or a finished draft.

43088.q: Over what do the Control Committees exercise oversight?
a: The Federal Council, the federal administration and the federal courts
Only the National Bank and the stock exchange
43088.e: Based on Article 169 of the Federal Constitution, the Control Committees supervise the conduct of business of the Federal Council, the administration and the federal courts. Other bodies carrying out federal tasks are included too.
43088.m: The Control Committees oversee the Federal Council, the administration and the federal courts.

43089.q: By which three main criteria do the Control Committees examine the conduct of business?
43089.e: The Control Committees mainly check whether the authorities act lawfully, appropriately and effectively. They also look at efficiency and proportionality.
43089.m: The Control Committees check legality, appropriateness and effectiveness.

43090.q: Which delegation of the Control Committees supervises state security and the intelligence services?
43090.e: The Control Delegation (GPDel) has three members from each of the two Control Committees. It has particularly far-reaching rights to information in the field of intelligence.
43090.m: The Control Delegation oversees the intelligence service.

43091.q: Which service supports the Control Committees with scientific evaluations?
a: The Parliamentary Control of the Administration
43091.e: The Parliamentary Control of the Administration (PCA) carries out evaluations on behalf of the Control Committees. It is part of the Parliamentary Services.
43091.m: The PCA carries out evaluations for the Control Committees.

43092.q: How do the powers of the Control Committees differ from those of a parliamentary investigation committee (PUK)?
a: They have less far-reaching investigative rights
They have no access to files at all
43092.e: The Control Committees have far-reaching rights to information, but a PUK has additional investigative powers. That is why a PUK is only set up for events of great significance.
43092.m: A PUK has stronger investigative rights than the Control Committees.

43093.q: How do the Control Committees usually exercise their oversight?
a: After the event, with reports and recommendations
43093.e: Oversight usually takes place after the event. The Control Committees publish reports with recommendations, on which the authority must give its opinion.
43093.m: The Control Committees mostly check afterwards and make recommendations.

43094.q: Which annual reports do the Control Committees examine each year?
a: Those of the Federal Council and the federal courts
Those of the cantons and municipalities
Those of the parties and associations
43094.e: One of the regular tasks of the Control Committees is examining the annual reports of the Federal Council and the federal courts. The chambers then approve them.
43094.m: Every year the Control Committees examine the annual reports of the Federal Council and the federal courts.

43095.q: How many members does the Finance Delegation of the federal chambers have?
43095.e: Each of the two Finance Committees elects three members to the Finance Delegation. There are also substitute members.
43095.m: The Finance Delegation has six members from both Finance Committees.

43096.q: When must the Finance Delegation approve a Federal Council credit before Parliament decides on it?
a: When the spending is urgent and cannot be delayed
Only for spending by the cantons
43096.e: If a larger item of spending cannot be delayed, the Federal Council obtains the approval of the Finance Delegation. Parliament then approves the credit afterwards.
43096.m: For urgent credits the Finance Delegation decides first.

43097.q: What role did the Finance Delegation play in the rescue of Credit Suisse in March 2023?
a: It approved guarantees of 109 billion francs
It chose the new CS management
It bought CS shares for the Confederation
43097.e: On 19 March 2023 the Finance Delegation approved urgent commitment credits totalling 109 billion francs. The National Council rejected the credits afterwards in the extraordinary session in April, with no legal effect.
43097.m: In March 2023 the Finance Delegation urgently approved the guarantees for the CS takeover.

43098.q: Which body is the Confederation's supreme financial supervisory body and supports the Finance Delegation?
43098.e: The Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO) independently examines the Confederation's finances. Its director usually attends the meetings of the Finance Delegation.
43098.m: The SFAO is the Confederation's supreme financial supervisory body.

43099.q: Which main items do the Finance Committees prepare every year?
a: The budget and the federal accounts
43099.e: The Finance Committees prepare the budget and the federal accounts for the chambers. They also examine supplementary credits and financial planning.
43099.m: The Finance Committees prepare the Confederation's budget and accounts.

43100.q: From which committees do the members of the Finance Delegation come?
a: From the Finance Committees of both chambers
Only from the National Council's Finance Committee
43100.e: The Finance Committees of the National Council and the Council of States each elect three members to the Finance Delegation. In this way both chambers are represented.
43100.m: The Finance Delegation consists of members of both Finance Committees.

43101.q: How are the Finance Delegation's rights to information described?
a: As unlimited, even towards the Federal Council
As usable only with a court order
43101.e: The Finance Delegation has very far-reaching rights to information. It even receives documents that serve the Federal Council's immediate decision-making.
43101.m: The Finance Delegation may also see confidential Federal Council documents.

43102.q: Apart from the general finances, which area does the Finance Delegation particularly supervise?
a: The finances of state security and the intelligence services
43102.e: The Finance Delegation's oversight also covers the financial aspects of state security and the intelligence services. Spending there is often secret.
43102.m: The Finance Delegation also checks the spending of the intelligence services.

43103.q: On which right of the Federal Assembly is a parliamentary investigation committee (PUK) based?
a: Oversight of the Federal Council and the administration
The right to remove federal judges
43103.e: The Federal Constitution gives the Federal Assembly oversight of the Federal Council, the administration and the courts. For events of great significance it can set up a PUK for this purpose.
43103.m: A PUK is based on Parliament's oversight.

43104.q: Who must agree to setting up a PUK?
a: The National Council and the Council of States
43104.e: Both chambers decide to set up a PUK. Its mandate and budget are laid down in this decision.
43104.m: A PUK is set up by both chambers.

43105.q: Which right does a PUK have that the standing committees lack?
a: To put laws into force immediately
43105.e: A PUK can question witnesses, see all files and appoint investigators. Official secrecy cannot be used against it.
43105.m: A PUK may formally question witnesses.

43106.q: Which affair did the PUK on the Federal Department of Justice and Police uncover in 1989?
43106.e: After Elisabeth Kopp's resignation, the PUK under Moritz Leuenberger investigated the Department of Justice and Police. It revealed that the federal police had been keeping watch on hundreds of thousands of people.
43106.m: The 1989 PUK uncovered the secret files scandal.

43107.q: Which secret organisations did the PUK on the Military Department investigate in 1990?
43107.e: The PUK on the Military Department investigated the intelligence services and the secret groups P-26 and P-27. It found that they worked without a sufficient legal basis or control.
43107.m: The 1990 PUK on the Military Department revealed the secret organisations P-26 and P-27.

43108.q: Which purchase led to the first major parliamentary investigation of this kind in 1964?
a: The purchase of Mirage fighter jets
The building of the Gotthard road tunnel
The purchase of the Swissair fleet
43108.e: The costs of the Mirage fighter aircraft rose massively, and the Federal Council needed an additional credit of almost 580 million francs. The investigation under Kurt Furgler led to a reduction to 57 aircraft.
43108.m: The Mirage affair of 1964 is seen as the origin of the PUK.

43109.q: Who chaired the PUK on the collapse of Credit Suisse?
43109.e: Isabelle Chassot, member of the Council of States (Centre, Fribourg), led the PUK; Franziska Ryser was vice-chair. The report appeared on 20 December 2024.
43109.m: Isabelle Chassot chaired the PUK on Credit Suisse.

43110.q: In which cases does the federal parliament set up a PUK?
43110.e: A PUK is Parliament's strongest supervisory tool. It is only set up for events of great significance, such as the collapse of Credit Suisse.
43110.m: A PUK only exists for exceptionally important events.

43111.q: How are the chair and vice-chair of a PUK filled?
a: Always by two members of the National Council
By the President of the Confederation
43111.e: Both chambers provide the same number of members. The chair and vice-chair must come from different chambers.
43111.m: The chair and vice-chair of a PUK come from different chambers.

43112.q: What is the minimum number of yes votes needed in the National Council to declare a law urgent?
43112.e: A majority of the 200 members is required, so 200 / 2 + 1 = 101. Abstentions and absent members therefore count in effect like no votes.
43112.m: In the National Council urgency needs at least 101 votes.

43113.q: Which referendum applies to an urgent federal act without a constitutional basis?
a: Mandatory, with the people and the cantons
Optional, with only a popular majority
43113.e: An urgent federal act without a constitutional basis must be accepted by the people and the cantons within one year. Otherwise it ceases to apply.
43113.m: Without a constitutional basis an urgent law needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

43114.q: According to the Federal Constitution, which time requirement always applies to urgent federal acts?
a: They apply for exactly ten years
They only apply during the session
43114.e: Article 165 of the Federal Constitution expressly requires that their period of validity be limited. Urgent law is meant to remain an exception.
43114.m: Urgent federal acts must always be time-limited.

43115.q: Which popular initiative restricted Parliament's emergency law-making in 1949?
43115.e: In the 1930s and 1940s Parliament had declared many decisions urgent and in this way avoided the referendum. The initiative “Return to direct democracy”, accepted in 1949, made urgent acts subject to a referendum afterwards.
43115.m: Since 1949 urgent acts can be put to the people afterwards.

43116.q: Where must important rules such as the basic features of a tax be laid down in Switzerland?
a: In a directive of a federal office
43116.e: The Federal Constitution requires that important law-making provisions be laid down in an act. A referendum can be called against acts, but not against ordinances.
43116.m: Important rules belong in an act, not in an ordinance.

43117.q: Which procedure comes before an important bill by the Federal Council?
43117.e: In the consultation, cantons, parties, associations and other interested groups can comment on a draft. The Federal Council then adopts a dispatch to Parliament.
43117.m: Before a bill, the Federal Council holds a consultation.

43118.q: What is a simple federal decree?
a: A federal decree that is not subject to a referendum
A decision of the National Council only
A decision of the Federal Council
A decision without a final vote
43118.e: Article 163 paragraph 2 of the Federal Constitution calls a federal decree that is not subject to a referendum a simple federal decree. It must still be passed by both chambers.
43118.m: A simple federal decree cannot be challenged with a referendum.

43119.q: In what form does Parliament approve the Confederation's annual budget?
43119.e: The budget is approved with a simple federal decree. So at federal level there is no financial referendum against the budget.
43119.m: The federal budget is approved by simple federal decree.

43120.q: What form does the Confederation's guarantee of an amended cantonal constitution take?
43120.e: The Federal Assembly guarantees cantonal constitutions with a simple federal decree. It checks whether the constitution complies with federal law.
43120.m: Cantonal constitutions are guaranteed with a simple federal decree.

43121.q: What distinguishes a federal decree from a simple federal decree?
a: The federal decree is subject to a referendum
The simple one is decided by the people
The federal decree only needs one chamber
The simple one only applies to cantons
43121.e: A federal decree in the narrower sense is subject to an optional or mandatory referendum. The simple federal decree is not.
43121.m: Only the federal decree, not the simple one, is subject to a referendum.

43122.q: In what form do the chambers approve the federal accounts?
43122.e: Like the budget, the federal accounts are approved with a simple federal decree.
43122.m: The federal accounts are approved with a simple federal decree.

43123.q: What form does the decision on the Federal Council's legislative programme take?
43123.e: The Federal Assembly decides on the legislative programme with a simple federal decree. It can change goals and measures in it.
43123.m: The legislative programme is adopted with a simple federal decree.

43124.q: In what form does Parliament approve a commitment credit, for example for a building programme?
43124.e: Credits such as commitment credits and spending ceilings are approved with simple federal decrees. The Federal Council requests them each time with a dispatch.
43124.m: Parliament approves commitment credits with simple federal decrees.

43125.q: What distinguishes a Federal Council ordinance from a federal act?
a: There is no referendum against an ordinance
An ordinance only applies in one canton
An ordinance needs a popular vote
An ordinance ranks above the constitution
43125.e: Federal acts are passed by Parliament, and the people can call a referendum. Ordinances are issued by the Federal Council itself, with no possibility of a referendum.
43125.m: No referendum can be called against ordinances.

43126.q: Which body used to be responsible for the Parliamentary Services as well?
a: The Office of the Attorney General
43126.e: Originally the Federal Chancellery also did the clerical work for Parliament. With the Federal Constitution of 1999 the Parliamentary Services became fully independent.
43126.m: The Parliamentary Services separated from the Federal Chancellery.

43127.q: Who are the Parliamentary Services of the Confederation there to serve?
43127.e: The Federal Constitution states that the Federal Assembly has Parliamentary Services. It can also call on units of the federal administration.
43127.m: The Parliamentary Services work for Parliament.

43128.q: In the National Council, debates are interpreted simultaneously by the Parliamentary Services. Into which languages?
a: All four national languages and English
43128.e: In the National Council, interpreters from the Parliamentary Services provide simultaneous interpretation into German, French and Italian. In the Council of States there is no simultaneous interpretation.
43128.m: The Parliamentary Services interpret National Council debates into three languages.

43129.q: Who became Switzerland's first female Federal Chancellor in 1999?
43129.e: Annemarie Huber-Hotz was Secretary General of the Federal Assembly and thus head of the Parliamentary Services before she was elected Federal Chancellor in December 1999. Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman in the Federal Council.
43129.m: Annemarie Huber-Hotz moved from the Parliamentary Services to the Federal Chancellery.

43130.q: Which publication, which records the debates in the chambers word for word, is looked after by the Parliamentary Services?
a: The Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce
43130.e: The Official Bulletin of the Federal Assembly contains the verbatim records of the debates in the National Council and the Council of States. It is published by the Information section of the Parliamentary Services.
43130.m: The debates in the chambers are recorded in the Official Bulletin.

43131.q: Which of these is not one of the tasks of the Parliamentary Services?
a: Passing laws on behalf of Parliament
43131.e: The Parliamentary Services are the staff of the Federal Assembly: they plan, take minutes, translate, advise and document. But only the chambers themselves make decisions.
43131.m: The Parliamentary Services support Parliament but decide nothing.

43132.q: Which body, together with the presidency, runs the business of the National Council?
43132.e: The Bureau plans the sessions, sets up committees and allocates business. It is led by the presidency of the chamber.
43132.m: The Bureau organises the work of the National Council.

43133.q: What office does the person hold who ranks second in protocol after the President of the National Council?
a: President of the Council of States
President of the Federal Supreme Court
43133.e: The order is: President of the National Council, President of the Council of States, then President of the Confederation. The leadership of Parliament thus ranks above the government.
43133.m: In protocol the President of the Council of States comes directly after the President of the National Council.

43134.q: Why must questions for question time be submitted a few days in advance?
a: So that the administration can prepare the answers
So that the people can vote on them
So that the Council of States can agree
So that they can be translated and printed
43134.e: The questions are submitted in writing in the week before question time. This lets the Federal Council and the administration prepare precise answers.
43134.m: Questions for question time are submitted in advance.

43135.q: What happens to questions that are not answered in question time because there is not enough time?
a: The Federal Council answers them in writing
They are read out in the next session
They go to the Council of States
43135.e: The Federal Council answers unanswered questions in writing, following the rules for urgent questions.
43135.m: Questions not dealt with are answered in writing.

43136.q: Who answers the members' questions in question time in the National Council?
43136.e: In question time, members of the National Council ask the government short questions. The responsible Federal Councillors answer orally.
43136.m: In question time the Federal Council answers.

43137.q: In which session do the chambers usually approve the previous year's federal accounts?
43137.e: The accounts for the past year are ready in spring and are approved in the summer session in June. The budget for the following year only comes in winter.
43137.m: The federal accounts are approved in the summer session.

43138.q: How long does an ordinary session of the Federal Assembly normally last?
43138.e: There are four ordinary sessions a year, each lasting three weeks. Special sessions are added when needed.
43138.m: An ordinary session lasts three weeks.

43139.q: How many ordinary sessions does the Federal Assembly hold each year?
43139.e: The four ordinary sessions are the spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions. In between, the committees work.
43139.m: Parliament meets in four ordinary sessions a year.

43140.q: Why does the Federal Assembly meet in separate sessions instead of all year round?
a: Because it is organised as a militia parliament
Because the Federal Palace is otherwise rented out
Because the Federal Council decides so
43140.e: Most members have a job alongside their mandate. That is why Parliament only meets for a few weeks a year, with the committees working in between.
43140.m: As a militia parliament, the Federal Assembly meets in sessions.

43141.q: In which city did the first session of the Federal Assembly outside Bern take place in 1993?
43141.e: The autumn session of 1993 was held in Geneva. Later, further sessions followed in other parts of the country.
43141.m: The first session away from Bern took place in Geneva in 1993.

43142.q: What do the parliamentary groups use the contribution they receive from the Confederation every year for?
a: For the salaries of the Federal Council
43142.e: Each group receives a basic contribution and an amount per member. The money covers the costs of its secretariat.
43142.m: The Confederation's contributions fund the groups' secretariats.

43143.q: Which body of the National Council do the presidents of the parliamentary groups belong to by virtue of their office?
43143.e: The presidents of the parliamentary groups sit ex officio in the National Council's Bureau and in the Coordination Conference. This lets them help plan the work of the chamber.
43143.m: The presidents of the parliamentary groups sit in the National Council's Bureau.

43144.q: Who can form a parliamentary group in the Federal Palace?
a: Members of the same or similar parties
Only the members of the Federal Council
43144.e: The Federal Constitution allows members of the Federal Assembly to form parliamentary groups. Usually members of the same party join together, and small parties join larger ones.
43144.m: Parliamentary groups are alliances of members of Parliament.

43145.q: Which political force dominated the federal state in the first decades after 1848?
43145.e: The Radicals and Liberals, known as the Freisinn, founded the federal state and provided all the Federal Councillors until 1891. In 1878 they also formed the first formal parliamentary group.
43145.m: The Radicals shaped the first decades of the federal state.

43146.q: Who decides if the committee of the second chamber does not want to take a parliamentary initiative further?
43146.e: If the committee of the other chamber does not agree, the initiative is put to the chamber, which votes on it. In the end the full chamber has the last word on the preliminary examination.
43146.m: When the committees disagree, the full chamber decides on a parliamentary initiative.

43147.q: Which benefit came from the parliamentary initiative by National Councillor Pierre Triponez and was accepted by the people in 2004?
