43147.e: The Triponez initiative extended the income compensation scheme to working mothers. After the yes vote in September 2004, paid maternity leave of 14 weeks has applied since 2005.
43147.m: Maternity allowance goes back to a parliamentary initiative.

43148.q: By which principle do the Control Committees work politically?
a: Independently of party and by consensus
Following instructions from the Federal Council
Following the will of the majority of cantons
43148.e: The Control Committees aim for unanimous findings that are independent of party. Only in exceptional cases is a significant minority opinion published.
43148.m: The Control Committees work independently of party and seek consensus.

43149.q: In which year did the Control Delegation start work as a result of the secret files scandal?
43149.e: The PUKs of 1989 and 1990 had uncovered serious failings in the control of state security and the intelligence services. As a consequence, the Control Delegation met for the first time in March 1992.
43149.m: The Control Delegation has existed since 1992.

43150.q: Why can the Finance Delegation also meet at very short notice?
a: Because it has to decide on urgent credits
Because it replaces the Federal Supreme Court
Because it elects the Federal Council
43150.e: As well as its regular meetings, the Finance Delegation meets at short notice when needed. This was the case, for example, during the rescue of Credit Suisse in March 2023.
43150.m: For urgent credits the Finance Delegation meets at short notice.

43151.q: Which chamber rejected a PUK on the financial crisis and the UBS rescue in 2010?
43151.e: The National Council agreed to a PUK on the financial crisis, but the Council of States rejected it. Since both chambers must agree, no PUK was set up.
43151.m: A PUK needs the approval of both chambers.

43152.q: What is the minimum number of votes needed in the Council of States to declare a law urgent?
43152.e: A majority of the 46 members is required, so 46 / 2 + 1 = 24. What counts is not the majority of those present.
43152.m: In the Council of States urgency needs at least 24 votes.

43153.q: According to Article 165 of the Federal Constitution, what applies to an urgent federal act that has been rejected in a popular vote?
a: It can be passed again at once
It continues to apply to the cantons
It goes to the Federal Supreme Court
43153.e: Article 165 paragraph 4 of the Federal Constitution forbids renewing a rejected urgent federal act. This way Parliament cannot get round the people's decision.
43153.m: An urgent law rejected by the people may not be renewed.

43154.q: Which federal act, declared urgent in 2020, did the people accept in a referendum vote in June 2021?
43154.e: Parliament declared the Covid-19 Act urgent in September 2020 so that it could come into force at once. A referendum was called against the act, and on 13 June 2021 the people accepted it.
43154.m: The urgent Covid-19 Act was accepted by the people in 2021.

43155.q: Which condition does Article 165 of the Federal Constitution set for declaring a federal act urgent?
a: Its coming into force cannot be delayed
It costs less than a million
43155.e: According to the constitution, a federal act may be declared urgent if its coming into force cannot be delayed. Typical cases are crises such as pandemics or financial emergencies.
43155.m: A law only becomes urgent if it cannot be delayed.

43156.q: Who issues most federal ordinances in Switzerland?
43156.e: The Federal Council issues ordinances to put laws into practice in detail. For this it needs a basis in an act or in the constitution.
43156.m: Ordinances are mostly issued by the Federal Council.

43157.q: What is the document called with which the Federal Council explains a draft law to Parliament?
43157.e: With the dispatch, the Federal Council presents a draft and explains its reasons in detail. The responsible committees then discuss it first.
43157.m: The Federal Council explains draft laws in a dispatch.

43158.q: In which official publication do Federal Council dispatches and proposals subject to referendum appear?
a: The Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce
43158.e: The Federal Gazette publishes, among other things, dispatches, draft laws and proposals adopted by Parliament. The referendum period begins with publication.
43158.m: Dispatches and proposals subject to referendum appear in the Federal Gazette.

43159.q: What is the official online platform for publishing federal law called?
43159.e: The Federal Gazette and the Official and Classified Compilations are published electronically on Fedlex. Since 2021 the electronic version has been the authoritative one.
43159.m: Federal law is published on the Fedlex platform.

43160.q: Which principle in Article 5 of the Federal Constitution requires that state action has a legal basis?
43160.e: Article 5 paragraph 1 of the Federal Constitution says, in essence, that the law is the basis and the limit of state action. It also follows that ordinances need a basis in an act or in the constitution.
43160.m: Under the principle of legality, all state action needs a legal basis.

43161.q: According to Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, what must Swiss courts do even if a federal act contradicts the constitution?
a: Pass the case to the Federal Council
43161.e: In Switzerland there is no constitutional review of federal acts. Here Parliament and the people have the last word, not the courts.
43161.m: Courts in Switzerland must always apply federal acts.

43162.q: In what form does the Federal Assembly approve a larger deployment of the army in support of civil authorities?
43162.e: A support deployment with more than 2000 members of the armed forces or lasting more than three weeks must be approved by Parliament. This is done with a simple federal decree, without a referendum.
43162.m: Parliament approves larger army deployments at home by simple federal decree.

43163.q: What is the Federal Assembly's business database with all parliamentary procedural requests and items of business called?
43163.e: All items of business, procedural requests and their status are recorded in Curia Vista. The database is run by the Parliamentary Services.
43163.m: All parliamentary business can be found in Curia Vista.

43164.q: Who decides on the head of the Parliamentary Services today?
43164.e: Until 2000 the Federal Council elected the head of the Parliamentary Services. Since then Parliament itself has decided who leads its services.
43164.m: Since 2000 Parliament itself has chosen the head of its services.

43165.q: Who was the first President of the National Council in 1848?
43165.e: Ulrich Ochsenbein from Bern chaired the National Council in its first session in 1848. Shortly afterwards he was elected to the first Federal Council.
43165.m: Ulrich Ochsenbein was the first President of the National Council.

43166.q: Who, at 32, was the youngest President of the National Council in history?
43166.e: Pascale Bruderer, an SP politician from Aargau, was elected in 2009 at the age of 32. Irène Kälin was also very young at 34 in 2021.
43166.m: Pascale Bruderer is the youngest President of the National Council.

43167.q: When does the National Council elect its new presidency each time?
a: At the start of the winter session
At the end of the summer session
43167.e: The new presidency is elected on the first day of the winter session and serves for one year. Usually the previous first vice-president is elected.
43167.m: The presidency of the chamber is newly elected at the start of the winter session.

43168.q: Who was President of the Council of States in the year of office 2024/25?
43168.e: Andrea Caroni, FDP member of the Council of States from Appenzell Ausserrhoden, was elected on 2 December 2024 and succeeded Eva Herzog. At the same time an FDP politician became President of the National Council.
43168.m: Andrea Caroni was President of the Council of States in 2024/25.

43169.q: Which tradition follows the election of a new President of the National Council?
a: A celebration in her home canton
A journey through all the cantons
43169.e: After the election, Parliament, guests and the public travel to a reception in the home canton of the newly elected president. There the “highest Swiss” is celebrated.
43169.m: A new President of the National Council is celebrated in her home canton.

43170.q: What happens to a question in question time if the person asking it is not present?
a: It goes to the Council of States
It is turned into a motion
43170.e: If there is time but the questioner is absent, the question is not answered. The Official Bulletin notes this.
43170.m: In question time the person asking must be present.

43171.q: In question time, what may the person asking do after the Federal Council's answer?
43171.e: After the answer, the person asking may put a short supplementary question. There is no debate in question time.
43171.m: One supplementary question is allowed in question time.

43172.q: How does the Federal Council deal with identical questions in question time?
a: It answers only the first one
43172.e: Identical questions or questions on the same topic are answered together. This often happens with current topics.
43172.m: Similar questions are answered together in question time.

43173.q: What is question time in the National Council mainly for?
a: For quick information on current topics
For the final vote on laws
43173.e: In question time, members quickly get information from the Federal Council on current issues. It is a tool for keeping a check on the government.
43173.m: Question time brings quick answers on current topics.

43174.q: How must questions for question time be worded?
a: As a yes or no question to the people
43174.e: Article 31 of the National Council's Rules of Procedure requires short questions without reasons. For more detailed concerns there are interpellations and written questions.
43174.m: Questions for question time are short and give no reasons.

43175.q: What does the abbreviation UVEK (in English DETEC) stand for?
43175.e: UVEK is the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. It is responsible for infrastructure, environmental protection and media regulation.
43175.m: UVEK covers four areas: environment, transport, energy and communications.

43176.q: Which present-day department was called the “Federal Political Department” until 1979?
43176.e: The Political Department had been responsible for foreign relations since 1848. In 1979 it was renamed the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
43176.m: The foreign affairs department used to be called the Political Department.

43177.q: By what name was today's Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research (EAER) known until the end of 2012?
43177.e: From 2013 the Federal Department of Economic Affairs became the Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research. At that time education and research were brought together in this department.
43177.m: The EAER is the successor of the former Department of Economic Affairs.

43178.q: What does the “B” in the German abbreviation VBS (Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport) stand for?
43178.e: VBS stands for the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. Civil protection includes, for example, the civil defence service and disaster relief.
43178.m: In VBS the B stands for civil protection.

43179.q: What does Article 178 of the Federal Constitution lay down about the leadership of the departments?
a: Each department is headed by a member of the Federal Council
The departments choose their own heads
Each department is run by two Federal Councillors
Parliament appoints the heads of department
43179.e: The federal administration is divided into departments, each led by a member of the Federal Council. In this way every member is both a member of the government and head of an administration.
43179.m: Each Federal Councillor heads exactly one department.

43180.q: Which unit in every department supports the head of department as a staff and coordination unit?
43180.e: Each department has a General Secretariat that handles planning, coordination and resources. It also prepares the department's business for the Federal Council.
43180.m: The General Secretariat is the staff of a head of department.

43181.q: Which department is the presidential department in 2026?
43181.e: The presidential department is always the department of the President of the Confederation. In 2026 this is Guy Parmelin's department.
43181.m: The presidential department changes every year with the presidency.

43182.q: What role does the Federal Chancellor have in meetings of the Federal Council?
a: An advisory voice without a vote
A full vote like a Federal Councillor
The casting vote in a tie
43182.e: The Federal Chancellor attends the meetings and can make proposals and take part in the discussion. But the Chancellor may not vote, not being a member of the Federal Council.
43182.m: The Federal Chancellor takes part in Federal Council discussions but does not vote.

43183.q: What task does the Federal Chancellery carry out in the field of people's rights?
a: It checks whether popular initiatives and referendums have succeeded
It decides whether popular initiatives are valid
It collects signatures for referendums itself
It judges initiatives before the Federal Supreme Court
43183.e: The Federal Chancellery checks the signatures submitted and rules on whether the initiative or referendum has succeeded. It also makes sure federal elections and votes are carried out correctly.
43183.m: The Federal Chancellery decides whether a popular initiative has gathered enough signatures.

43184.q: Who elects the Federal Chancellor of Switzerland?
43184.e: Like the Federal Council, the Federal Chancellor is elected by the United Federal Assembly for four years.
43184.m: The Federal Assembly elects the Federal Chancellor.

43185.q: What is the main task of the Federal Council spokesperson?
a: To explain the Federal Council's decisions to the public
To represent the Federal Council in Parliament
To chair the Federal Council's meetings
43185.e: After Federal Council meetings, the spokesperson informs the media. The role is based in the Federal Chancellery.
43185.m: The Federal Council spokesperson informs the public about the Federal Council's decisions.

43186.q: What is the Federal Chancellery often called because it supports the Federal Council?
43186.e: The Federal Chancellery prepares the Federal Council's meetings and coordinates the work. It is not a department but the government's staff office.
43186.m: The Federal Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office.

43187.q: From which round of voting in a Federal Council election are new candidates no longer possible?
43187.e: In the first two rounds any eligible person can receive votes. After that, only people who have already received votes can be elected.
43187.m: After two open rounds, no new names are allowed in a Federal Council election.

43188.q: How are the members of the Federal Council elected?
a: Individually and by secret ballot by the United Federal Assembly
As a list by the people
By the Council of States alone
43188.e: The National Council and the Council of States, sitting together as the United Federal Assembly, elect each seat individually. The election is secret.
43188.m: The Federal Assembly elects each Federal Councillor individually and by secret ballot.

43189.q: What is a “magic formula” in Swiss politics?
a: A key for dividing the Federal Council seats among the parties
A procedure for electing the President of the Confederation
43189.e: From 1959 to 2003 the FDP, CVP, SP and SVP divided the seven seats in the ratio 2:2:2:1. This division was called the magic formula.
43189.m: The magic formula divides the Federal Council seats among the large parties.

43190.q: Which ballot papers are not taken into account when calculating the absolute majority in a Federal Council election?
a: Ballot papers of members of the Council of States
Ballot papers with names of non-members of Parliament
43190.e: The absolute majority is more than half of the valid ballot papers. Blank and invalid ones do not count.
43190.m: Only valid, filled-in ballot papers count for the absolute majority.

43191.q: In what order are the seats filled when the whole Federal Council is re-elected?
a: By length of service of the sitting members
By the size of the parties
By the alphabetical order of names
By the age of the candidates
43191.e: First the seats of the sitting members are filled, starting with the longest-serving. Then the seats becoming vacant follow.
43191.m: In the full re-election, the longest-serving Federal Councillor is confirmed first.

43192.q: In a full re-election, when do newly elected members of the Federal Council take office?
a: On 1 January of the following year
On 1 March of the following year
43192.e: Those elected start on 1 January, and the outgoing members stay in office until 31 December. For by-elections a different deadline applies.
43192.m: New Federal Councillors from the full re-election start on New Year's Day.

43193.q: According to Article 175 of the Federal Constitution, who can be elected to the Federal Council?
a: Anyone who can be elected to the National Council
Only members of a cantonal government
43193.e: The Federal Assembly elects the members of the Federal Council from all Swiss citizens who are eligible for the National Council. A party nomination or a seat in Parliament is not legally required.
43193.m: Anyone who could be elected to the National Council can be elected to the Federal Council.

43194.q: What does Article 176 of the Federal Constitution expressly rule out for the President of the Confederation?
a: Election as Vice-President for the following year
Taking part in Federal Council meetings
43194.e: The President can neither be re-elected for the following year nor elected Vice-President for the following year. This ensures rotation.
43194.m: Anyone who was President cannot become Vice-President the following year.

43195.q: By tradition, which office does the Vice-President take on in the following year?
a: The presidency of the National Council
43195.e: The Federal Assembly usually elects the previous Vice-President as President of the Confederation. But it is not legally obliged to do so.
43195.m: The Vice-President usually becomes President the following year.

43196.q: What is the main task of the Vice-President of the Federal Council?
a: To stand in for the President when the President is unable to act
To chair the United Federal Assembly
43196.e: If the President is absent, the Vice-President chairs the meetings and takes over representative duties. Otherwise the Vice-President runs a department as normal.
43196.m: The Vice-President steps in when the President cannot act.

43197.q: By tradition, what principle decides who becomes Vice-President?
a: Length of service in the Federal Council
43197.e: The offices rotate according to the seniority principle. Whoever has gone longest without being President, or has never been President, moves forward in the queue.
43197.m: The vice-presidency is given out according to seniority.

43198.q: Who presents the Federal Assembly with the dispatch on the legislative programme at the start of each legislative period?
a: The Bureau of the National Council
43198.e: In this dispatch the government sets out its political guidelines and goals for four years. Parliament discusses it and decides on it.
43198.m: The legislative programme is proposed by the Federal Council.

43199.q: What does the Federal Council lay down in the legislative programme?
a: Guidelines and goals for the four-year legislative period
The dates of all popular votes
The constituencies for the National Council
43199.e: The legislative programme for 2023 to 2027 contains four guidelines and 25 goals with concrete measures. The budget for one year, on the other hand, is the annual budget.
43199.m: The legislative programme contains the Federal Council's goals for four years.

43200.q: How many political guidelines does the legislative programme for 2023 to 2027 include?
43200.e: The Federal Council arranges its goals for the legislative period under four political guidelines. In the 2019 to 2023 period there were still three.
43200.m: The legislative programme for 2023 to 2027 has four guidelines.

43201.q: Which topic is one of the guidelines of the legislative programme for 2023 to 2027?
a: Protecting the climate and natural resources
43201.e: One guideline says, in essence, that Switzerland protects the climate and takes care of natural resources. The other answers are not guidelines.
43201.m: Climate protection is one guideline of the current legislative programme.

43202.q: With which tool does the Federal Council put the legislative programme into concrete terms for each individual year?
a: The report on the federal accounts
43202.e: Every year the Federal Council sets concrete goals derived from the legislative programme. Later it shows in the annual report whether they were achieved.
43202.m: The annual objectives turn the legislative programme into concrete steps for one year.

43203.q: In which report does the Federal Council give an annual account of whether it has achieved its goals?
43203.e: The annual report is presented to Parliament and dealt with by the Control Committees. It compares goals and results.
43203.m: In the annual report the Federal Council shows what it has achieved.

43204.q: Which plan complements the legislative programme on the financial side?
43204.e: The legislative financial plan shows how the planned projects will be financed. It is coordinated with the goals of the legislative programme.
43204.m: The legislative programme comes with a legislative financial plan.

43205.q: How long is a legislative period at federal level?
43205.e: The National Council and the Federal Council are renewed as a whole every four years. The legislative programme covers exactly this period.
43205.m: A federal legislative period lasts four years.

43206.q: When may the Federal Council issue an emergency ordinance based directly on the constitution?
a: In the event of serious disturbances to public order or security
When a popular initiative is submitted
43206.e: Under Article 185 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Council may issue ordinances when serious disturbances have occurred or are imminent. These must be time-limited.
43206.m: Emergency ordinances are only allowed in the event of serious disturbances.

43207.q: In which other area may the Federal Council also issue ordinances based directly on the constitution?
43207.e: Article 184 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution gives the Federal Council its own power to issue ordinances in foreign policy, for example for sanctions. These ordinances must also be time-limited.
43207.m: The Federal Council also has its own power to issue ordinances in foreign policy.

43208.q: What condition does the Federal Constitution set for emergency ordinances of the Federal Council?
a: They only apply in one canton
43208.e: The constitution expressly requires that such ordinances be limited in time. Emergency law should not become a permanent state of affairs.
43208.m: Emergency ordinances of the Federal Council always apply for a limited time only.

43209.q: What must the Federal Council do if an emergency ordinance is to apply for longer?
a: Present Parliament with a legal basis
Ask the Federal Supreme Court for permission
43209.e: Emergency law should not become a permanent state. If the Federal Council does not present Parliament with a draft within six months, the emergency ordinance ceases to apply.
43209.m: Emergency ordinances soon need a legal basis from Parliament.

43210.q: Who can replace an emergency ordinance of the Federal Council with an ordinance of its own?
43210.e: Parliament can replace an emergency ordinance of the Federal Council with its own ordinance. This also applies for three years at most.
43210.m: Parliament can take over from the Federal Council's emergency law.

43211.q: With which instrument did the Federal Council make the takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS possible in March 2023?
a: With a Federal Supreme Court ruling
43211.e: The Federal Council relied on its emergency powers to make guarantees and liquidity support possible quickly. Parliament could only discuss it afterwards.
43211.m: The 2023 CS takeover was secured with the Federal Council's emergency law.

43212.q: From which date did the Federal Council govern in the “extraordinary situation” during the Covid-19 pandemic?
43212.e: The Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation on 16 March 2020. Until 19 June 2020 it issued many emergency ordinances.
43212.m: The extraordinary situation in the pandemic began on 16 March 2020.

43213.q: What must be the case for the Federal Council to be allowed to issue an emergency ordinance to protect security?
a: A serious disturbance that has occurred or is imminent
A decision by at least twelve cantons
43213.e: The danger must concern public order or internal or external security. Mere political urgency is not enough.
43213.m: Emergency ordinances require a serious, acute disturbance.

43214.q: What are the far-reaching special powers that Parliament gave the Federal Council in 1939 during the Second World War called?
43214.e: With the full powers decree of August 1939, the Federal Council was allowed to govern largely without Parliament. This emergency law stood outside the normal constitutional order.
43214.m: In the Second World War the Federal Council governed with full powers.

43215.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in 2007 instead of the sitting SVP Federal Councillor?
43215.e: The member of the Grisons cantonal government accepted the election the day after the vote. She was a Federal Councillor from 2008 to 2015.
43215.m: Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf entered the Federal Council unexpectedly in 2007.

43216.q: Which Federal Councillor was the first not to be re-elected, in 1854?
43216.e: Ulrich Ochsenbein from Bern was a member of the first Federal Council of 1848. He had lost support in Parliament.
43216.m: In 1854 Ulrich Ochsenbein was the first Federal Councillor to be voted out.

43217.q: Which party was created in 2008 as a result of the 2007 Federal Council election?
43217.e: The SVP expelled its Grisons cantonal party because the newly elected Federal Councillor belonged to it. This gave rise to the BDP, which merged with the CVP in 2021 to form the Centre.
43217.m: The BDP was born in 2008 out of the dispute over the Federal Council election.

43218.q: Which department did Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf take over in 2008 after her election?
43218.e: She took over the Department of Justice and Police left vacant by her predecessor. In November 2010 she moved to the Finance Department.

43219.q: Can the Federal Assembly vote a member of the Federal Council out during the current term of office?
a: No, there is no vote of no confidence
Yes, with a simple majority of both chambers
Only at the request of the Federal Supreme Court
43219.e: The members are elected for a fixed term of four years. They can only be removed at the next full re-election, by not being re-elected.
43219.m: Federal Councillors cannot be brought down by a vote of no confidence.

43220.q: Which department does the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) belong to?
43220.e: The FOPH is part of the Federal Department of Home Affairs. Social insurance and statistics are also based there.
43220.m: The FOPH belongs to the Department of Home Affairs.

43221.q: Which department does the Federal Roads Office (FEDRO) belong to?
43221.e: FEDRO is responsible for the national roads. It belongs to the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications.
43221.m: FEDRO is a federal office within DETEC.

43222.q: Which department is the Federal Office of Police (fedpol) assigned to?
43222.e: Fedpol fights serious and organised crime and works with Interpol and Europol. It belongs to the Department of Justice and Police.
43222.m: Fedpol is the federal police within the FDJP.

43223.q: Which federal office produces the official national maps of Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office for Spatial Development
43223.e: The Federal Office of Topography, swisstopo, surveys Switzerland and publishes the national maps. It belongs to the DDPS.
43223.m: Switzerland's national maps come from swisstopo.

43224.q: What has the former Federal Customs Administration been called since 2022?
a: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security
Federal Office for Border Protection and Trade
43224.e: The renaming reflects the merger of customs and the border guard. The office belongs to the Finance Department.
43224.m: Since 2022 the customs administration has been the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.

43225.q: Which federal office started work in 2024 as successor to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)?
43225.e: The new office was assigned to the DDPS. It coordinates the protection of Switzerland against cyberattacks.
43225.m: Since 2024 there has been a separate Federal Office for Cyber Security.

43226.q: Which federal office belongs to the Department of Home Affairs?
43226.e: The Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology is part of the FDHA. Energy belongs to DETEC, agriculture to the EAER and sport to the DDPS.
43226.m: The national weather service MeteoSwiss belongs to the FDHA.

43227.q: Which department does the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) belong to?
43227.e: SECO is the Confederation's centre of expertise for economic policy and the labour market. It belongs to the Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research.
43227.m: SECO is a State Secretariat within the EAER.

43228.q: What is the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) responsible for?
43228.e: The SEM regulates residence, asylum procedures and naturalisation at federal level. It belongs to the Department of Justice and Police.
43228.m: The SEM is the federal authority for migration and asylum.

43229.q: Which State Secretariat belongs to the Federal Department of Finance?
43229.e: The SIF represents Switzerland's interests in international financial, tax and currency matters. It was created in 2010.
43229.m: The SIF deals with international financial matters within the Finance Department.

43230.q: Which State Secretariat was created in the DDPS in 2024?
43230.e: SEPOS is meant to coordinate the Confederation's security policy strategically. It started work at the beginning of 2024.
43230.m: Since 2024 the DDPS has had a State Secretariat for Security Policy.

43231.q: What does the abbreviation SBFI (in English SERI) stand for?
a: State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation
Swiss Federal Office for Research and Industry
Foundation for Vocational Training, Research and Integration
Federal Secretariat for Finance and Investment
43231.e: SERI is responsible, among other things, for vocational training, universities and the funding of research. It also looks after cooperation in European research programmes.
43231.m: SBFI is the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation.

43232.q: Who leads a federal State Secretariat?
a: A member of the Federal Council
The President of the National Council
43232.e: State Secretaries lead important federal offices and often represent Switzerland in international negotiations. They report to a member of the Federal Council.
43232.m: State Secretariats are led by State Secretaries.

43233.q: What does Article 175 paragraph 4 of the Federal Constitution require for the composition of the Federal Council?
a: The regions and language areas should be fairly represented
Each national language must get exactly one seat
At least three members must be women
Each canton must be represented once a decade
43233.e: The provision is a guideline for the Federal Assembly, not a fixed quota. It is meant to reflect Switzerland's diversity in the government.
43233.m: In Federal Council elections all regions and language areas should be fairly taken into account.

43234.q: Which rule was replaced in 1999 by today's requirement on the representation of the regions?
43234.e: Until 1999 no more than one member of the Federal Council could come from the same canton. The people and the cantons abolished this rule.
43234.m: The cantonal clause was abolished in 1999.

43235.q: Who was elected in 2017 as the first Italian-speaking member of the Federal Council since 1999?
43235.e: The Radical from Ticino ended a long period without representation for Italian-speaking Switzerland. He took over the Department of Foreign Affairs.
43235.m: With Ignazio Cassis, Italian-speaking Switzerland returned to the Federal Council in 2017.

43236.q: Which Federal Councillor from Ticino resigned in 1999, after which Italian-speaking Switzerland was no longer represented until 2017?
43236.e: The CVP politician was in the Federal Council from 1987 to 1999, finally as foreign minister. After that came a long gap without an Italian-speaking member.
43236.m: Until 1999 Flavio Cotti was the last Federal Councillor from Ticino before the long gap.

43237.q: Who is regarded as the only Romansh member in the history of the Federal Council?
43237.e: The Radical from the Grisons was a Federal Councillor from 1913 to 1920 and President of the Confederation in 1918. Since then Romansh-speaking Switzerland has not been represented by a native speaker.
43237.m: Felix Calonder was the only Romansh speaker in the Federal Council.

43238.q: How many members of the Federal Council come from French-speaking Switzerland in 2026?
43238.e: Guy Parmelin from Vaud and Elisabeth Baume-Schneider from Jura represent the Romandie. Four members are German-speaking and one is Italian-speaking.
43238.m: In 2026 the Romandie has two members of the Federal Council.

43239.q: Who was elected in 2022 as the first member of the Federal Council from the canton of Jura?
43239.e: The SP politician beat Eva Herzog in December 2022. The canton of Jura has only existed since 1979.
43239.m: Elisabeth Baume-Schneider is the first Federal Councillor from Jura.

43240.q: Which region was long seen as under-represented in the Federal Council before Beat Jans was elected in 2023?
43240.e: Before Beat Jans, Basel-City had only provided two Federal Councillors, and Basel-Country none. Zurich, Bern and the Romandie, on the other hand, are almost always represented.
43240.m: Beat Jans is only the third Federal Councillor from Basel-City.

43241.q: Who allocates the departments among the members after a Federal Council election?
a: The presidents of the parliamentary groups
43241.e: Parliament only elects the people, not the departments. The allocation is decided internally by the government as a body.
43241.m: The Federal Council divides the departments among its members.

43242.q: What happens if the Federal Council cannot agree on how to allocate the departments?
a: The Federal Council takes a vote
43242.e: If there is disagreement, the Federal Council takes a majority decision. Newly elected members sometimes have to take on a department they did not want.
43242.m: In a dispute over departments, the majority in the Federal Council decides.

43243.q: May a member of the Federal Council refuse the department allocated to them?
a: No, they are obliged to take it on
Yes, at any time without giving reasons
Yes, but only in their first year in office
43243.e: The Government and Administration Organisation Act obliges every member to take on the department allocated. A change is only possible when the departments are next allocated.
43243.m: A Federal Councillor must take on the department allocated to them.

43244.q: Which department did Elisabeth Baume-Schneider receive after her election in December 2022?
43244.e: At the start of 2023 she took over the Department of Justice and Police. In 2024, after Alain Berset's resignation, she moved to his department.
43244.m: Baume-Schneider began in the Federal Council as justice minister.

43245.q: When must a member of the Federal Council withdraw from dealing with an item of business?
a: When they have a direct personal interest in it
When they hold a different political opinion
When the business concerns another department
When they proposed the business themselves
43245.e: The duty to withdraw is meant to prevent conflicts of interest. What matters is a direct personal interest in the business.
43245.m: If they have a personal interest, a Federal Councillor withdraws.

43246.q: What does it mean when a member of the Federal Council “withdraws” (tritt in den Ausstand)?
a: They take no part in the discussion and decision on that item
They give up their office permanently
They vote publicly against the decision
They hand over their department for a year
43246.e: The member leaves the discussion of this one item and does not vote on it. For all other business they take part as normal.
43246.m: Anyone who has withdrawn plays no part in that item.

43247.q: Why is there a duty to withdraw for members of the Federal Council?
a: To share out the work evenly
43247.e: Anyone with a personal interest in an item should not help decide on it. This keeps the Federal Council's decisions independent.

43248.q: Which principle in Article 177 of the Federal Constitution requires the Federal Council to decide as a body?
43248.e: The Federal Council decides as a collegial authority, and all members support the decisions. The departments only prepare the business.
43248.m: The Federal Council decides together by the principle of collegiality.

43249.q: What does the principle of collegiality mean for a Federal Councillor who was outvoted internally?
a: They still support the decision in public
They may campaign against it in public
They can overturn the decision alone
43249.e: The Federal Council decides as a body. Even those who were against it support the decision in public.
43249.m: Federal Councillors support joint decisions even if they personally disagree.

43250.q: After how many years do the minutes of the Federal Council usually become publicly accessible?
43250.e: Minutes have been kept since 1848 and are subject to a protection period of 30 years. After that they can be consulted in the Federal Archives.
43250.m: Federal Council minutes can be seen after a protection period of 30 years.

43251.q: Apart from the responsible Federal Councillors, who gives information at the press conference after the Federal Council meeting?
a: The President of the National Council
The President of the Federal Supreme Court
43251.e: The Federal Council spokesperson leads the press conferences and reports on further decisions. The spokesperson is also Vice-Chancellor.
43251.m: The Federal Council's press conferences are led by its spokesperson.

43252.q: Where do the Federal Council's press conferences in Bern usually take place?
a: In the Federal Palace Media Centre
43252.e: The Federal Palace Media Centre is next to the Federal Palace in Bern. The conferences are also streamed on the internet.
43252.m: The Federal Council informs the media in the Federal Palace Media Centre.

43253.q: What does the principle of collegiality expect of a Federal Councillor who presents a decision at the press conference that they themselves opposed?
a: They represent the decision of the whole Federal Council
They make their vote against it public
They leave the information to the opposition
43253.e: The members present decisions to the public together, even if they lost internally. Differing opinions usually remain confidential.
43253.m: Federal Councillors support collegial decisions even against their own opinion.

43254.q: How often does the Federal Council usually meet, with information on its decisions given afterwards?
43254.e: The Federal Council normally meets every week in the Federal Palace in Bern. Afterwards the most important decisions are announced publicly.
43254.m: The Federal Council usually holds a meeting every week.

43255.q: Which department is responsible for the Confederation's agricultural policy?
43255.e: The Federal Office for Agriculture belongs to the Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research. Direct payments to farms, for example, are regulated there.
43255.m: Agricultural policy belongs to the EAER.

43256.q: Which department does the Federal Tax Administration belong to?
43256.e: The Federal Tax Administration collects, among other things, VAT, withholding tax and direct federal tax. It is part of the Finance Department.
43256.m: The Federal Tax Administration is part of the Finance Department.

43257.q: Which department is responsible for the AHV (old-age insurance) and the other social insurances?
43257.e: The Federal Social Insurance Office belongs to the Department of Home Affairs. It looks after the AHV, disability insurance, supplementary benefits and occupational pensions.
43257.m: The Department of Home Affairs is responsible for the AHV and social insurance.

43258.q: May the Federal Chancellor belong to a party?
a: Yes, like the members of the Federal Council
Only the SP or the FDP
43258.e: Federal Chancellors usually belong to a party; Walter Thurnherr, for example, belonged to the CVP. But the office is carried out with party-political restraint.
43258.m: The Federal Chancellor can also be a party member.

43259.q: Who is responsible for the “Federal Council explanations” for federal popular votes?
43259.e: The Federal Chancellery produces the so-called voting booklet on behalf of the Federal Council. It is sent to all voters with the voting papers.
43259.m: The voting booklet is produced by the Federal Chancellery.

43260.q: Roughly how many people does the Federal Chancellery employ (as of 2025)?
43260.e: Compared with the departments, the Federal Chancellery is small. It has about 340 employees.
43260.m: The Federal Chancellery has about 340 employees.

43261.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what must members of the Federal Council give up after their election?
a: Any other federal or cantonal office and any other gainful activity
Only their seat in Parliament, but not board memberships
Their residence outside the canton of Bern
43261.e: Article 144 of the Federal Constitution sets out these incompatibilities. Federal Councillors are meant to devote themselves fully to their office and be independent.
43261.m: Federal Councillors may not hold any other office or have any other job.

43262.q: When is there a by-election to the Federal Council?
a: When a member resigns or dies during the term of office
When a party loses the elections
43262.e: If a Federal Councillor leaves early, the United Federal Assembly elects a successor for the rest of the term.
43262.m: By-elections fill gaps in the Federal Council during the legislative period.

43263.q: Which department does the Vice-President of the Federal Council lead in 2026?
43263.e: The Vice-President in 2026 is Ignazio Cassis. He has headed the Department of Foreign Affairs since 2017.
43263.m: The Vice-President in 2026 is also foreign minister.

43264.q: When does the Federal Assembly elect the Vice-President of the Federal Council for the coming year?
a: In the winter session in December
In the spring session in March
In the summer session in June
In the autumn session in September
43264.e: The President and Vice-President are elected each December for the following year. The election takes place in the United Federal Assembly.
43264.m: The vice-presidency is elected each December.

43265.q: How many times so far has a sitting member of the Federal Council not been re-elected in a full re-election?
43265.e: Those not re-elected were Ulrich Ochsenbein in 1854, Jean-Jacques Challet-Venel in 1872, Ruth Metzler in 2003 and Christoph Blocher in 2007. Otherwise the Federal Assembly almost always confirms Federal Councillors.
43265.m: Voting out Federal Councillors is very rare in Switzerland.

43266.q: Who was elected in December 2003 in place of the Federal Councillor who was not re-elected?
43266.e: The Federal Assembly elected the SVP politician from Zurich in the third round. This gave the SVP a second seat in the Federal Council.
43266.m: Christoph Blocher entered the Federal Council in 2003.

43267.q: Which party declared itself in opposition after the non-re-election of 2007?
43267.e: The party did not see the newly elected member as its representative. Its role in opposition ended with the election of Ueli Maurer at the end of 2008.
43267.m: The SVP went into opposition for a time in 2008.

43268.q: Which department did Albert Rösti take over after his election in December 2022?
43268.e: At the start of 2023 he took over the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. His predecessor there was Simonetta Sommaruga.
43268.m: Albert Rösti has headed DETEC since 2023.

43269.q: Is abstaining allowed in votes in the Federal Council?
a: No, everyone must vote yes or no
43269.e: The Government and Administration Organisation Act expressly allows abstentions. That is why an additional minimum number of yes votes is needed.
43269.m: In the Federal Council you may abstain.

43270.q: What usually happens before the Federal Council decides on an item from a department?
a: The other departments concerned give their opinion
The Federal Supreme Court examines it
43270.e: Before an item comes to the Federal Council, the offices and departments also affected can give their opinion. In this way conflicts are, as far as possible, settled before the meeting.
43270.m: Before a Federal Council decision, the departments concerned give their opinion.

43271.q: Which principle states that each Federal Councillor, as head, runs the administrative business of their department?
43271.e: The departmental principle complements the principle of collegiality. The departments prepare the Federal Council's business and deal with matters within their own responsibility.
43271.m: Under the departmental principle each Federal Councillor runs their own department.

43272.q: What is a decision called that the President of the Confederation takes in urgent cases instead of the whole Federal Council?
43272.e: If the Federal Council cannot meet in time, the President decides alone for the time being. The Federal Council must approve the decision afterwards.
43272.m: In urgent cases the President can take a presidential decision.

43273.q: In what written form does the Federal Council publish its decisions in addition to the press conference?
43273.e: For important decisions, press releases appear on admin.ch on the day of the meeting. This way everyone can get the information directly.
43273.m: The Federal Council also publishes its decisions as press releases.

43274.q: Who must be called together immediately if the Federal Council calls up a very large number of armed forces members for active service?
43274.e: If the Federal Council calls up more than 4000 members of the armed forces for active service, or the deployment is expected to last longer than three weeks, the Federal Assembly must be convened without delay. This keeps a large army deployment under parliamentary control.
43274.m: A large active service deployment requires Parliament to be convened at once.

43276.q: In which year did the Federal Criminal Court start work?
43276.e: The Federal Criminal Court began work on 1 April 2004. It was created so that federal criminal cases no longer had to be judged directly by the Federal Supreme Court.
43276.m: The Federal Criminal Court has been working since 2004.

43277.q: Since which year has the Federal Criminal Court had an Appeals Chamber as a second instance?
43277.e: The Appeals Chamber started work in 2019. Since then, judgments of the Criminal Chamber can be challenged within the Federal Criminal Court with a full review.
43277.m: The Federal Criminal Court's Appeals Chamber has existed since 2019.

43278.q: Which chamber of the Federal Criminal Court mainly hears complaints in international mutual legal assistance cases such as extraditions?
43278.e: The Objections Chamber deals with complaints against procedural acts of the Office of the Attorney General and the police. A large part of its work involves mutual assistance and extradition cases.
43278.m: The Objections Chamber decides on extraditions and international mutual assistance.

43279.q: Which chamber of the Federal Criminal Court rules at first instance on charges in federal criminal cases?
43279.e: The Criminal Chamber judges criminal cases under federal jurisdiction at first instance. Its judgments can be taken to the Appeals Chamber.
43279.m: The Criminal Chamber is the first instance at the Federal Criminal Court.

43280.q: Who elects the judges of the Federal Criminal Court?
43280.e: Like the members of the Federal Supreme Court, the judges of the Federal Criminal Court are elected by Parliament. The Judicial Committee prepares the election.
43280.m: Federal judges are elected by Parliament.

43281.q: Why was the Federal Criminal Court created in 2004?
a: To relieve the Federal Supreme Court
43281.e: Before then, the Federal Supreme Court partly judged federal criminal cases itself. The Federal Criminal Court created a separate first instance and relieved the Federal Supreme Court.
43281.m: The Federal Criminal Court relieves the Federal Supreme Court.

43282.q: To which court can judgments of the Federal Criminal Court's Appeals Chamber be taken?
a: The High Court of the canton of Ticino
43282.e: Decisions of the Appeals Chamber can be challenged with an appeal in criminal matters to the Federal Supreme Court. The Federal Supreme Court is the Confederation's highest judicial authority.
43282.m: Above the Federal Criminal Court stands the Federal Supreme Court.

43283.q: Which offence typically goes before the Federal Criminal Court rather than a cantonal court?
43283.e: Under the Criminal Procedure Code, counterfeiting money falls under federal jurisdiction. That is why such cases are judged not by a cantonal court but by the Federal Criminal Court.
43283.m: Counterfeit money is a case for federal justice.

43284.q: In which city is the Federal Administrative Court based?
43284.e: Since 2012 the Federal Administrative Court has worked in a new building in St Gallen. Before that it was temporarily in Bern.
43284.m: The Federal Administrative Court is in St Gallen.

43285.q: When did the Federal Administrative Court start work?
43285.e: The Federal Administrative Court began work on 1 January 2007, at first in temporary premises. At the same time the new Federal Supreme Court Act came into force.
43285.m: The Federal Administrative Court has existed since 2007.

43286.q: From which city did the Federal Administrative Court move to its present seat in summer 2012?
43286.e: Until 2012 the court worked temporarily in Bern. In summer 2012 it moved into the new building in St Gallen.
43286.m: The Federal Administrative Court moved from Bern to eastern Switzerland in 2012.

43287.q: Whose tasks did the Federal Administrative Court take over when it was founded?
a: About 36 federal appeals commissions and complaints services
The social law divisions of the Federal Supreme Court
The Objections Chamber of the Federal Criminal Court
43287.e: Before 2007 many separate appeals commissions and complaints services of the departments made decisions. The Federal Administrative Court brought these tasks together in one court.
43287.m: The Federal Administrative Court replaced many federal appeals commissions.

43288.q: Measured by the number of judges, which federal court is the largest?
43288.e: The Federal Administrative Court has (as of 2025) 78 judges and about 380 staff. This makes it larger than the Federal Supreme Court.
43288.m: The largest federal court is the Federal Administrative Court.

43289.q: Against whose decisions can you lodge an appeal with the Federal Administrative Court?
a: Against decisions of the federal administration
Against judgments of the Federal Supreme Court
43289.e: The Federal Administrative Court reviews rulings by federal authorities, for example in asylum, tax or environmental matters. Many cases concern asylum decisions.
43289.m: The Federal Administrative Court reviews decisions of the federal authorities.

43290.q: Which court usually decides finally on appeals against asylum decisions of the State Secretariat for Migration?
43290.e: Under the Federal Supreme Court Act, an appeal to the Federal Supreme Court in asylum matters is generally ruled out. So the Federal Administrative Court is usually the last instance here.
43290.m: In asylum matters the Federal Administrative Court usually has the last word.

43291.q: In which year did the people approve the judicial reform that led, among other things, to the creation of the Federal Administrative Court?
43291.e: The people and the cantons accepted the judicial reform on 12 March 2000. It was put into practice with new federal courts in the years that followed.
43291.m: The judicial reform was accepted in 2000.

43292.q: Who elects the judges of the Federal Administrative Court?
43292.e: The Federal Assembly elects the judges on the proposal of the Judicial Committee. Parties and language regions are also taken into account.
43292.m: The judges of the Federal Administrative Court are elected by Parliament.

43293.q: Who decided patent disputes before the Federal Patent Court was founded?
43293.e: Cantonal courts used to be responsible for patent disputes. Since 2012 a specialised federal court in St Gallen has ruled on them.
43293.m: Cantonal courts used to rule on patents.

43294.q: In which city did the Federal Patent Court start work?
43294.e: The Federal Patent Court is based in eastern Switzerland. It is responsible for patent disputes from all over Switzerland.
43294.m: The Federal Patent Court is at home in St Gallen.

43295.e: A patent gives the inventor the sole right to use a technical invention for a certain time. Names are protected as trademarks, and music and photos by copyright.

43296.q: What training do most of the part-time judges at the Federal Patent Court have?
43296.e: In 2025, about 30 of the part-time judges had a technical background and 12 a legal one. Technical expertise is central to patent questions.
43296.m: Many experts from technology and science judge at the Federal Patent Court.

43297.q: Apart from the official languages, which language is allowed at the Federal Patent Court with the parties' consent?
43297.e: Proceedings take place in German, French or Italian, and with the parties' consent also in English. This makes all three languages of the European Patent Office possible.
43297.m: At the Federal Patent Court you may also litigate in English with consent.

43298.q: For which patent disputes is the Federal Patent Court responsible?
a: For those from all over Switzerland
43298.e: The Federal Patent Court in St Gallen is responsible throughout Switzerland as the first instance for patent disputes. After that, you can go to the Federal Supreme Court.
43298.m: The Federal Patent Court is responsible for the whole of Switzerland.

43299.q: How many instances does a patent case that begins at the Federal Patent Court have?
43299.e: Against judgments of the Federal Patent Court there is only one appeal, to the Federal Supreme Court. So the procedure consists of two instances.
43299.m: In a patent case there is only the Federal Patent Court and the Federal Supreme Court.

43300.q: Which act created the Federal Patent Court?
43300.e: The Patent Court Act of 20 March 2009 created the Federal Patent Court. It regulates the organisation and jurisdiction of the court.
43300.m: The Federal Patent Court is based on the Patent Court Act of 2009.

43301.q: What kind of court is the Federal Patent Court?
a: A civil court of first instance
A criminal court of second instance
An administrative court for patent fees
43301.e: The Federal Patent Court decides civil disputes about patents, such as infringement claims or licensing questions. It has exclusive jurisdiction for this throughout Switzerland.
43301.m: Patent disputes are civil matters and go before the Federal Patent Court.

43302.q: Since 2011, who has elected the Attorney General of Switzerland?
43302.e: Since 1 January 2011 the Office of the Attorney General has been independent of the government. The United Federal Assembly elects its leadership on the proposal of the Judicial Committee.
43302.m: Today the Attorney General is elected by Parliament.

43303.q: Who elected the Attorney General until the end of 2010?
43303.e: Until 2010 the Federal Council elected the Attorney General, and the office was under the Department of Justice and Police. The reform was meant to strengthen the independence of criminal prosecution.
43303.m: The Office of the Attorney General used to be under the Federal Council.

43304.q: How long is the Attorney General's term of office?
43304.e: The Attorney General and the two deputies are elected for four years. Re-election is then possible.
43304.m: The Attorney General is elected for four years.

43305.q: Who has been Attorney General of Switzerland since 1 January 2022 (as of 2025)?
43305.e: Stefan Blättler was elected in September 2021 and took office at the start of 2022. Before that he was commander of the Bern cantonal police.
43305.m: Stefan Blättler has led the Office of the Attorney General since 2022.

43306.q: Because of unrecorded meetings with whom did Attorney General Michael Lauber come under criticism and resign in 2020?
a: President of the Confederation Simonetta Sommaruga
43306.e: Lauber met FIFA President Infantino several times while his office was investigating FIFA officials. He resigned at the end of August 2020.
43306.m: The FIFA affair cost Attorney General Lauber his job.

43307.q: Which woman from Ticino was Attorney General from 1994 to 1999?
43307.e: Carla Del Ponte was Attorney General from 1994 to 1999. She then became chief prosecutor of the international criminal tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda.
43307.m: Carla Del Ponte led the Office of the Attorney General in the 1990s.

43308.q: Why is the Office of the Attorney General supervised by its own supervisory authority and not by the Federal Council?
a: So that criminal prosecution remains independent of the government
Because the Federal Council has too little time
Because it belongs to the Federal Supreme Court
43308.e: Since 2011 the Office of the Attorney General has no longer been under the Federal Council. A supervisory authority elected by Parliament oversees it, so that the government cannot influence criminal proceedings.
43308.m: The Office of the Attorney General is meant to be independent of the government.

43309.q: For which offence is the Office of the Attorney General, and not a cantonal public prosecutor, responsible?
43309.e: Like explosives offences or prohibited intelligence activities, genocide falls under federal jurisdiction. Such cases are prosecuted by the Office of the Attorney General.
43309.m: Serious crimes against the state and international law are prosecuted by the Office of the Attorney General.

43310.q: Which scandal led to the resignation of Attorney General Rudolf Gerber in 1989?
43310.e: In the secret files scandal it became known that the federal police had kept watch on hundreds of thousands of people. Together with the Kopp affair, it led to Gerber's resignation and the reorganisation of the office.
43310.m: The secret files scandal shook the Office of the Attorney General in 1989.

43311.q: Who elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court?
43311.e: The National Council and the Council of States elect the federal judges together as the United Federal Assembly. It also elects the President and Vice-President of the court.
43311.m: Federal judges are elected by Parliament in a joint sitting.

43312.q: How often has the Federal Assembly refused to re-elect a federal judge so far?
a: Never, it is forbidden by law
43312.e: Non-re-elections at the Federal Supreme Court are very rare; only a few cases are known. But judges sometimes received clearly fewer votes after controversial rulings.
43312.m: Parliament only very rarely refuses to re-elect a federal judge.

43313.q: When do federal judges leave office by law?
a: At the end of the year in which they turn 68
43313.e: There is an age limit for federal judges. They leave office at the end of the year in which they turn 68.
43313.m: Federal judges step down at the latest in the year of their 68th birthday.

43314.q: Which body of Parliament advertises vacant judge posts and proposes candidates?
43314.e: The Judicial Committee of the Federal Assembly advertises posts, holds interviews with applicants and makes nominations. It also prepares the election of the Office of the Attorney General.
43314.m: The Judicial Committee prepares the election of judges in the federal parliament.

43315.q: For how long does the Federal Assembly elect the President of the Federal Supreme Court?
43315.e: The President and Vice-President of the Federal Supreme Court are elected for two years. They can be re-elected once.
43315.m: The presidency of the Federal Supreme Court usually changes after two or four years.

43316.q: How many full-time judges does the Federal Supreme Court have (as of 2025)?
43316.e: The Federal Supreme Court has 40 full-time and 19 part-time judges. The law allows 35 to 45 full-time judge posts.
43316.m: About forty full-time judges work at the Federal Supreme Court.

43317.q: Which party provides the most federal judges (as of 2025)?
43317.e: With 11 seats the SVP provides the most federal judges, followed by the Centre and the SP with 7 each. This reflects their share of the vote.
43317.m: The party with the most voters also provides the most federal judges.

43318.q: What happened in 2020 at the re-election of federal judge Yves Donzallaz?
a: He was re-elected despite opposition from his own party
He was replaced by drawing lots
43318.e: The SVP group wanted to prevent the re-election of its own judge because of his rulings. The Federal Assembly nevertheless confirmed Donzallaz in office.
43318.m: Donzallaz's re-election in 2020 sparked a debate about judicial independence.

43319.q: In Switzerland, what is meant by the “mandate tax” paid by judges?
a: Handing over part of their income to their own party
A fee for standing as a candidate in Parliament
A payment by the parties to the courts
43319.e: Elected judges regularly pay part of their income to their party. For many parties this is an important source of income.
43319.m: With the mandate tax, judges give part of their salary to their party.

43320.q: Which anti-corruption body of the Council of Europe called for federal judges to stop paying a mandate tax to parties?
43320.e: GRECO (the Group of States against Corruption) criticised the close ties between judges and parties. After the election such links should be cut.
43320.m: The Council of Europe's GRECO criticises the mandate tax of Swiss judges.

43321.q: Roughly how much is a federal judge's annual mandate payment to their party?
43321.e: According to SRF, in 2020 federal judges paid several thousand francs a year depending on their party: about 15,000 for the Greens and about 13,000 francs for the SP.
43321.m: Judges' mandate payments are often several thousand francs a year.

43322.q: Which federal body published the federal judges' mandate contributions to their parties for the first time for the year 2023?
43322.e: Under the new transparency rules on political funding, parties must report contributions from office holders every year. The Swiss Federal Audit Office published the federal judges' contributions for 2023 for the first time.
43322.m: Thanks to new transparency rules, mandate contributions can now be seen publicly.

43323.q: Which principle do critics see as most at risk from the mandate tax?
a: The separation of powers between the Confederation and the cantons
43323.e: Critics fear that judges remain financially and politically dependent on their party. But judges should be bound only by the law.
43323.m: The mandate tax is criticised because it could weaken judicial independence.

43324.q: How do the parties usually describe the mandate contributions of their judges?
43324.e: There is no legal duty to pay a mandate tax. The parties therefore stress that the contributions are voluntary, though in practice they are expected.
43324.m: The mandate payment is not required by law but is widespread.

43325.q: What advantage does a candidate for judge have in the system linked to the mandate tax?
a: She does not have to run her own election campaign
She is automatically elected for life
She may choose her own cases
43325.e: The party nominates its candidates and secures them the votes they need in Parliament. In return the party regularly receives money from the elected judges.
43325.m: In the election of judges, party and candidate benefit from each other.

43326.q: How is the Swiss practice of judges' mandate payments often described in international comparison?
a: As a model for the EU
As a duty under international law
43326.e: Judges handing over part of their salary to parties is hardly known internationally. That is why Switzerland is criticised for it, for example by GRECO.
43326.m: The mandate tax for judges is a Swiss peculiarity.

43327.q: Under the Justice Initiative, how were federal judges supposed to be chosen?
43327.e: The initiative was called “Selection of federal judges by drawing lots”. Suitable people were to be chosen by lot instead of being elected by Parliament.
43327.m: The Justice Initiative wanted to choose federal judges by lot.

43328.q: How many cantons voted in favour of the Justice Initiative?
43328.e: The initiative was rejected in all cantons. So it lacked not only a popular majority but any support from the cantons.
43328.m: The Justice Initiative did not win a majority in any canton.

43329.q: With what share of no votes was the Justice Initiative rejected?
43329.e: The initiative was clearly rejected with 68.07 per cent no. That is just over two thirds of voters.
43329.m: The Justice Initiative failed at the ballot box with just over two thirds voting no.

43330.q: Who was the main person behind the Justice Initiative?
43330.e: The businessman Adrian Gasser launched the initiative with a committee. For the referendum campaign he founded the “Bund für Gerechtigkeit” (League for Justice).
43330.m: Adrian Gasser was behind the Justice Initiative.

43331.q: Under the Justice Initiative, who was to decide on admission to the drawing of lots?
43331.e: An expert commission elected by the Federal Council was to check professional and personal suitability. Only suitable people would have gone into the draw.
43331.m: Under the Justice Initiative, an expert commission would have checked the candidates.

43332.q: Under the Justice Initiative, until when would the term of office of federal judges chosen by lot have lasted?
a: Until five years after the normal retirement age
43332.e: The term of office was to end five years after reaching retirement age. There would no longer have been re-elections, but removal from office would have been possible.
43332.m: The Justice Initiative wanted to abolish the re-election of federal judges.

43333.q: With how many valid signatures was the Justice Initiative submitted in 2019?
43333.e: The initiative was submitted on 26 August 2019 with 130,100 valid signatures. 100,000 were needed.
43333.m: The Justice Initiative succeeded in 2019 with well over the signatures needed.

43334.q: How did Parliament respond to the Justice Initiative with regard to a counter-proposal?
a: It did not adopt a counter-proposal
43334.e: Several counter-proposals failed in the National Council and the Council of States. The initiative therefore came to the vote without a counter-proposal.
43334.m: The Justice Initiative went to the people without a counter-proposal.

43335.q: Because of the rule that federal acts are binding, what does Switzerland not have, unlike Germany, for example?
a: A court that can strike down federal acts as unconstitutional
43335.e: Under Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, courts must apply federal acts even if they contradict the constitution. In Germany the Federal Constitutional Court can declare laws void.
43335.m: Switzerland has no constitutional review of federal acts.

43336.q: According to Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, what is binding on the Federal Supreme Court and the other authorities applying the law?
43336.e: Article 190 of the Federal Constitution says, in essence: federal acts and international law are binding on the Federal Supreme Court and the other authorities applying the law. They must apply them.
43336.m: Federal acts and international law are binding on Swiss courts.

43337.q: What does the rule that federal acts are binding mean for unconstitutional federal acts?
a: The courts must still apply them
The courts must strike them down
The Federal Council must delete them at once
43337.e: In Switzerland there is no constitutional review of federal acts. Even an unconstitutional federal act remains applicable.
43337.m: A federal act applies even if it contradicts the constitution.

43338.q: Which legal provision may the Federal Supreme Court strike down or not apply because it is unconstitutional?
43338.e: Article 190 of the Federal Constitution only protects federal acts and international law. The Federal Supreme Court can review cantonal acts for compatibility with the Federal Constitution.
43338.m: Cantonal laws are subject to review by the Federal Supreme Court.

43339.q: May the Federal Supreme Court state that a federal act is unconstitutional?
a: Yes, but it must still apply the act
No, it may not even examine it
Yes, and it may strike the act down
Only with the Federal Council's approval
43339.e: Article 190 of the Federal Constitution is a duty to apply, not a ban on review. The court can note a breach of the constitution and so encourage the legislator to correct it.
43339.m: The rule does not forbid review, but it requires the act to be applied.

43340.q: What is the heading of Article 190 of the Federal Constitution?
43340.e: The heading of Article 190 of the Federal Constitution is “Applicable law” (Massgebendes Recht). This is where the German term Massgeblichkeitsgebot comes from.
43340.m: Article 190 of the constitution deals with applicable law.

43341.q: Which international court can rule against Switzerland for violating the European Convention on Human Rights?
a: The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
The Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg
The International Criminal Court in The Hague
The Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen
43341.e: Switzerland ratified the ECHR in 1974. According to the practice of the Federal Supreme Court, the ECHR even takes precedence over more recent federal acts.
43341.m: The court in Strasbourg also watches over human rights in Switzerland.

43342.q: According to the wording of Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, to whom does the rule that federal acts are binding apply?
a: To the Federal Supreme Court and all authorities applying the law
Only to the Federal Supreme Court
43342.e: Article 190 of the Federal Constitution expressly names the Federal Supreme Court and the other authorities applying the law. Administrative authorities and cantonal courts must also apply federal acts.
43342.m: All authorities that apply the law are bound by federal acts.

43343.q: In Switzerland, who basically regulates the organisation of the courts of first and second instance?
43343.e: Procedural law has been unified at federal level since 2011, but the organisation of the courts remains a matter for the cantons. That is why the courts have different names depending on the canton.
43343.m: The cantons organise their own courts.

43344.q: What role does the High Court (Obergericht) of the canton of Zurich have in civil and criminal proceedings?
a: Appeal court as the highest cantonal court
Supervisor of the Office of the Attorney General
43344.e: The High Court hears appeals and complaints against decisions of the district courts. It is the canton's highest civil and criminal court.
43344.m: In many cantons the High Court is the second instance.

43345.q: What is the higher cantonal court in the canton of Ticino called?
43345.e: In Ticino the Tribunale d'appello (court of appeal) is the higher cantonal instance. Civil courts of first instance there are called Pretura.
43345.m: In Ticino the higher instance is called the Tribunale d'appello.

43346.q: What is the higher cantonal court in the canton of Geneva called?
43346.e: In Geneva the Cour de justice is the highest cantonal court. The Tribunal fédéral, on the other hand, is the Federal Supreme Court.
43346.m: Geneva's highest court is called the Cour de justice.

43347.q: Which canton has its own commercial court for disputes between companies?
43347.e: Commercial courts exist only in the cantons of Zurich, Bern, Aargau and St Gallen. They rule on disputes between companies listed in the commercial register.
43347.m: Only four cantons have a commercial court.

43348.q: What happened to the Court of Cassation of the canton of Zurich in 2011?
a: It became the Federal Supreme Court
43348.e: With the federal Civil Procedure Code and Criminal Procedure Code of 2011, the third cantonal level disappeared. Courts of cassation such as those in Zurich and St Gallen were abolished.
43348.m: Since 2011 there have been no cantonal courts of cassation.

43349.q: What are the courts of first instance for civil and criminal cases called in the canton of Bern?
43349.e: The canton of Bern is divided into court regions, whose courts are called regional courts. Other cantons call the first instance a district, circuit or Amt court, for example.
43349.m: In the canton of Bern, the regional courts rule at first instance.

43350.q: Which court in the canton of Zurich hears appeals against decisions of the cantonal administration as the highest cantonal authority?
43350.e: Besides the High Court, Zurich has its own Administrative Court and a Social Insurance Court. The Administrative Court deals with public law disputes.
43350.m: The canton of Zurich has a separate higher court for administrative matters.

43351.q: In civil proceedings, what must normally happen before a claim is filed with the court?
a: Mediation at the Federal Supreme Court
43351.e: Under Art. 197 of the Civil Procedure Code, court proceedings are normally preceded by an attempt at conciliation. Articles 198 and 199 set out the exceptions.
43351.m: Civil proceedings usually begin with conciliation.

43352.q: What has the conciliation officer traditionally been called in many cantons?
43352.e: The office of justice of the peace was introduced during the Helvetic Republic. In German-speaking Switzerland it is often a part-time role.
43352.m: Justices of the peace try to reconcile the parties in a dispute.

43353.q: For which disputes are there joint conciliation authorities made up of both sides?
a: Rent and lease, and gender equality
43353.e: Joint conciliation authorities include representatives of both sides, such as landlords and tenants. They deal with rent, lease and cases under the Gender Equality Act.
43353.m: Rental disputes go first to a joint conciliation authority.

43354.q: What can the conciliation authority do in cases with smaller amounts at stake if the parties cannot agree?
a: Send the case straight to the Federal Supreme Court
43354.e: In financial disputes of up to 10,000 francs, the conciliation authority can make a proposed judgment. It aims to avoid a court case.
43354.m: For smaller amounts, the conciliation authority can make a proposed judgment.

43355.q: What may the conciliation authority even do for very small amounts if the claimant requests it?
a: Pay the claim out of its own funds
Hand the dispute over to the police
43355.e: In financial disputes of up to 2000 francs, the conciliation authority can decide itself if asked to. This saves court proceedings for very small amounts.
43355.m: For very small amounts, the conciliation authority itself can decide.

43356.q: What does the claimant receive if no agreement is reached in conciliation proceedings?
a: An extract from the debt enforcement register
43356.e: If conciliation fails, the authority issues an authorisation to proceed. With it, the party can file a claim with the court within three months.
43356.m: After failed conciliation, the claimant gets authorisation to proceed.

43357.q: What happens if neither party rejects a proposed judgment of the conciliation authority in time?
a: It has the effect of a final decision
The Federal Supreme Court must review it
43357.e: If neither party rejects the proposal within 20 days, it is deemed accepted. It then has the effect of a final, binding decision.
43357.m: A proposed judgment that is not rejected becomes binding.

43358.q: What legal effect does filing a request for conciliation have on the limitation period?
a: It extends it to ten years
43358.e: Under Art. 135 of the Code of Obligations, a request for conciliation interrupts the limitation period. Anyone wanting to secure a claim can stop the clock this way.
43358.m: A request for conciliation interrupts the limitation period.

43359.q: Which order matches a typical path through the courts in a Zurich civil case?
a: District court, High Court, Federal Supreme Court
High Court, district court, Federal Supreme Court
Federal Supreme Court, High Court, district court
District court, Federal Criminal Court, Federal Supreme Court
43359.e: After conciliation, the district court rules at first instance. Then come the High Court as appeal court and the Federal Supreme Court.
43359.m: The path through the courts runs from district court via High Court to Federal Supreme Court.

43360.q: Why do many small civil disputes never reach the Federal Supreme Court?
a: There is a minimum value in dispute
The Federal Supreme Court only rules on criminal cases
43360.e: Appeals in civil matters usually require a value in dispute of at least 30,000 francs. This eases the workload of the Federal Supreme Court.
43360.m: Small civil disputes usually do not reach the Federal Supreme Court.

43361.q: Why is access to the Federal Supreme Court easier in rental and employment disputes?
a: Because these cases are especially important socially
Because tenants pay no court costs
Because no cantonal courts are responsible for them
Because the Federal Supreme Court has its own rental court
43361.e: In rental and employment matters the threshold is 15,000 instead of 30,000 francs. This gives tenants and employees with smaller amounts at stake access to the Federal Supreme Court too.
43361.m: Access to the Federal Supreme Court is easier in rental and employment cases.

43362.q: For which three areas of law has there been a separate appeal to the Federal Supreme Court since 2007?
a: Civil matters, criminal matters, public law
43362.e: The Federal Supreme Court Act of 2007 provides for appeals in civil matters, in criminal matters and in public law matters. Older types of appeal were abolished.
43362.m: Since 2007 there have been three standard appeals to the Federal Supreme Court.

43363.q: Which court can you turn to after the Federal Supreme Court over a breach of the Convention on Human Rights?
a: Court of Justice of the EU
