43363.e: Once all national courts have been used, an application to the ECtHR in Strasbourg is possible. It only checks whether the ECHR has been violated.
43363.m: On human rights questions, the court in Strasbourg stands above the Federal Supreme Court.

43364.q: Which court has usually ruled before a civil case reaches the Federal Supreme Court?
a: Only a justice of the peace
43364.e: The cantons appoint higher courts, such as the High Court, as the last instance. Only after that is the way to the Federal Supreme Court open.
43364.m: Before the Federal Supreme Court, a higher cantonal court should normally have ruled.

43365.q: What is the legal remedy for challenging a first-instance civil judgment at the higher cantonal court called?
43365.e: In an appeal, the higher court re-examines the facts and the law. For small amounts under 10,000 francs, only a limited objection (Beschwerde) is possible.
43365.m: First-instance civil judgments are usually challenged by appeal.

43366.q: What can you claim with a constitutional complaint to the Federal Supreme Court?
a: Only errors in calculating the value in dispute
That a Federal Council election was invalid
43366.e: With the subsidiary constitutional complaint, you can claim that fundamental rights such as equality before the law were violated. It is also available for small amounts.
43366.m: The subsidiary constitutional complaint protects constitutional rights even for small amounts.

a: A judge at the Federal Supreme Court
43367.e: Lay judges have not completed a law degree. They bring life experience and expert knowledge from other professions to the court.
43367.m: Lay judges decide cases without having studied law.

43368.q: Which type of court disappeared in Switzerland with the federal Criminal Procedure Code of 2011?
43368.e: Until 2011, some cantons had jury courts with professional judges and jurors. They were seen as slow and expensive and were abolished with the new code.
43368.m: Jury courts have not existed in Switzerland since 2011.

43369.q: At which courts do lay judges take part in most cantons?
a: At lower courts such as the district courts
43369.e: In most cantons, lay judges serve at first-instance criminal and civil courts. The rules are cantonal and therefore differ.
43369.m: Lay judges are found mainly at cantonal courts of first instance.

43370.q: Who rules together with the High Court judges at the Zurich Commercial Court?
43370.e: Commercial judges are experts from companies and industries who contribute their knowledge. They sit alongside legally trained High Court judges.
43370.m: Expert judges from business sit on the Commercial Court.

43371.q: Besides the presiding judge, who typically sits on an employment court in cantons such as Zurich?
a: Only professional judges from the High Court
43371.e: The employment court includes expert judges from both employer and employee circles. That way, practical knowledge from both sides goes into the judgment.
43371.m: The employment court has equal representation of both sides of industry.

43372.q: How are district judges elected in the canton of Zurich?
a: By the people of the district
43372.e: In the canton of Zurich, the voters of each district elect their district judges. Popular election of judges is a Swiss peculiarity.
43372.m: In many cantons, the people elect the first-instance judges.

43373.q: What requirement does the canton of Aargau set for being elected district judge or justice of the peace?
43373.e: In Aargau, anyone entitled to vote can be elected justice of the peace, district judge or substitute judge. Legal training is not required.
43373.m: In Aargau, anyone entitled to vote can become a district judge.

43374.q: What is the main aim of having lay judges in courts?
a: Faster proceedings at the Federal Supreme Court
43374.e: Lay judges are meant to bring an everyday view into court and strengthen trust in the justice system. Critics doubt that this is still necessary today.
43374.m: Lay judges are meant to bring the courts closer to the people.

43375.q: How did the people and the cantons vote in 2004 on the New Fiscal Equalisation scheme (NFA)?
a: The people said yes, the cantons no
43375.e: The NFA was accepted on 28 November 2004 with almost two thirds voting yes. Only Schwyz, Nidwalden and Zug rejected it, and it came into force in 2008.
43375.m: The NFA was clearly accepted at the ballot box in 2004.

43376.q: What is the main aim of fiscal equalisation between the Confederation and the cantons?
a: To reduce differences in the cantons' financial strength
To impose the same tax rates on all cantons
43376.e: Fiscal equalisation ensures that financially weak cantons can also fulfil their tasks. It is governed by the Federal Act on Financial and Cost Equalisation (FiLaG).
43376.m: Fiscal equalisation reduces the differences between poor and rich cantons.

43377.q: Which instrument of fiscal equalisation balances differences in the cantons' financial means (tax-raising capacity)?
43377.e: Resource equalisation distributes funds according to resource potential, that is the tax sources that can be tapped. Cantons with low tax-raising capacity receive money.
43377.m: Resource equalisation balances the cantons' different tax-raising capacity.

43378.q: Which part of fiscal equalisation compensates cantons for special burdens due to mountain areas or core city tasks?
43378.e: Cost equalisation has a geographical and topographical part and a socio-demographic part. It offsets costs that a canton cannot influence itself.
43378.m: Cost equalisation covers the cantons' special burdens.

43379.q: What has resource equalisation guaranteed every canton since the 2020 reform?
a: A minimum level of own funds per person
The Confederation taking over all its debts
43379.e: After equalisation, every canton should have at least 86.5 per cent of the Swiss average in own funds per person. Previously, a figure of 85 per cent was only a target.
43379.m: Resource equalisation guarantees every canton a minimum level of funds.

43380.q: What is the purpose of hardship compensation in the New Fiscal Equalisation scheme?
a: It protects financially weak cantons from losses due to the change of system
It funds mountain railways in remote regions
It compensates for damage after natural disasters
It pays the costs of cantonal hospitals
43380.e: Hardship compensation was meant to stop a financially weak canton being worse off because of the switch to the NFA. It is temporary and is being phased out step by step.
43380.m: Hardship compensation cushions the transition to the NFA.

43381.q: How does the NFA's hardship compensation develop over time?
a: It is reduced step by step
It stays the same for ever
It is only paid after natural disasters
43381.e: Hardship compensation stayed constant for eight years and then falls each year by 5 per cent of the original amount. It is a temporary transitional solution.
43381.m: Hardship compensation is a temporary transitional solution.

43382.q: According to the Confederation, how is resource equalisation for 2027 funded (as of June 2026)?
a: 60 per cent Confederation, 40 per cent financially strong cantons
50 per cent Confederation, 50 per cent all municipalities
Entirely by the financially strong cantons
43382.e: The vertical part comes from the Confederation, the horizontal part from the financially strong cantons. For 2027 the shares are about 60 and 40 per cent.
43382.m: The Confederation and the financially strong cantons fund resource equalisation together.

43383.q: What is the part of resource equalisation that financially strong cantons pay directly to financially weak cantons called?
43383.e: Payments between equal levels (canton to canton) are called horizontal. Payments from the Confederation to the cantons are called vertical.
43383.m: Horizontal equalisation flows from canton to canton.

43384.q: Which canton has for years had by far the highest resource index in Swiss fiscal equalisation?
43384.e: Thanks to many companies and high incomes, Zug has the greatest resource potential per person. It is therefore the largest contributor per person.
43384.m: Per person, Zug is the financially strongest canton in fiscal equalisation.

43385.q: Why have the cantons agreed to concentrate rare top-level treatments such as transplants in a few hospitals?
a: For better quality and lower costs
Because small hospitals may not employ surgeons
Because the Confederation owns all hospitals
Because health insurers require it by law
43385.e: For this the cantons concluded the Intercantonal Agreement on Highly Specialised Medicine (IVHSM). Those who perform many of the same operations have more experience and work more efficiently.
43385.m: The cantons concentrate top-level medicine in a few hospitals by agreement.

43386.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what may the cantons conclude with each other?
43386.e: Article 48 of the Constitution allows the cantons to conclude treaties and set up joint institutions. These treaties must not run counter to the law or interests of the Confederation.
43386.m: Cantons may conclude treaties with each other.

43387.q: What distinguishes a law-making concordat from a simple administrative agreement between cantons?
a: It applies directly to the population
It needs the Federal Council's approval
It applies for one year at most
43387.e: Law-making concordats contain rules like a law that apply directly to private individuals. Administrative agreements, by contrast, only govern cooperation between authorities.
43387.m: Law-making concordats work like laws for the population.

43388.q: What is meant to be prevented when the Confederation declares a concordat binding on all cantons?
a: Cantons benefiting without paying their share
The Confederation gaining too much power
43388.e: Under Article 48a of the Constitution, the Confederation can, at the request of cantons, declare certain treaties generally binding. This is meant to prevent free-riding, for example in the prison system or at universities.
43388.m: The Confederation can make certain concordats binding on all cantons.

43389.q: Which intercantonal concordat governs large-scale games such as lotteries and sports betting?
43389.e: Large-scale games are a matter for the cantons, which concluded the Gambling Concordat for this. Most of the proceeds go to charitable causes such as culture and sport.
43389.m: The Gambling Concordat governs lotteries and sports betting.

43390.q: Among other things, what did the 1970 Concordat on School Coordination regulate?
a: The start of the school year in late summer
English as the first foreign language
The founding of universities of applied sciences
43390.e: The 1970 School Concordat set, among other things, the start of the school year between mid-August and mid-October. Some cantons did not join it for a long time.
43390.m: The 1970 School Concordat standardised the start of the school year.

43391.q: In which year did Switzerland vote to move the start of the school year to late summer nationwide, after the concordat alone had not been enough?
43391.e: Because some cantons kept starting in spring, the start of the school year was written into the Federal Constitution in 1985. Since then the school year has begun in late summer everywhere.
43391.m: Since the 1985 vote, the school year has started in late summer everywhere.

43392.q: In which area can the Confederation declare intercantonal treaties binding on all cantons?
43392.e: Article 48a of the Constitution lists nine areas, such as education, the prison system and waste management. Defence, foreign and monetary policy are federal matters anyway.
43392.m: Article 48a lists nine areas for binding cooperation.

43393.q: To which cantons did the Federal Assembly refuse the guarantee in 1948 for constitutional articles on reunification?
43393.e: According to the Federal Assembly, the articles breached the guarantee of cantonal territory. In 1960 it reversed this decision and guaranteed them after all.
43393.m: The reunification articles of the two Basels were only guaranteed in 1960.

43394.q: Under what condition must the Confederation guarantee a cantonal constitution?
a: If it does not contradict federal law
If the Federal Council likes it politically
If it has at least 100 articles
43394.e: Article 51 of the Constitution: the Confederation guarantees a cantonal constitution if it does not contradict federal law. There is no political assessment.
43394.m: A cantonal constitution is guaranteed if it complies with federal law.

43395.q: Can a Federal Assembly decision on the guarantee be challenged at the Federal Supreme Court?
a: Yes, but only by the canton concerned
Only if the people demand it with signatures
43395.e: Under federal law, decisions on the guarantee cannot be challenged. However, the Federal Supreme Court can later review individual cases where cantonal law is applied.
43395.m: The Federal Assembly's decisions on the guarantee are final.

43396.q: May an amendment to a cantonal constitution come into force before the Confederation has guaranteed it?
a: Yes, the guarantee only confirms it afterwards
No, it only applies once guaranteed
Only with the Federal Supreme Court's permission
Only in cantons with a Landsgemeinde
43396.e: The guarantee confirms that the provision is compatible with federal law, but it does not create the law. So an amendment can already apply beforehand.
43396.m: Cantonal constitutional amendments can come into force before the guarantee.

43397.q: Which canton was refused the guarantee in 1977 for an article of its new constitution because it contained territorial claims against another canton?
43397.e: The first Jura constitution provided for taking in further areas of the Jura region. The Federal Assembly saw this as a breach of the territorial guarantee and of federal loyalty.
43397.m: The Jura article on further territory was not guaranteed in 1977.

43398.q: Which canton was refused the guarantee in 2013 for its then electoral system for the cantonal parliament?
43398.e: The National Council twice refused the guarantee because the Schwyz electoral system violated equal voting rights. Schwyz then introduced the double proportional (Pukelsheim) method.
43398.m: Schwyz had to change its electoral system after 2013.

43399.q: What is the effect when the Federal Assembly refuses to guarantee a cantonal constitutional provision?
a: The provision only applies for five more years
The canton loses its seat in the Council of States
The Federal Council must rewrite the provision
43399.e: If the guarantee is refused, the provision lapses retroactively to the date it came into force. The canton must amend it.
43399.m: A provision that is not guaranteed loses its validity retroactively.

43400.q: How often does the Federal Assembly refuse to guarantee a cantonal constitutional provision?
43400.e: The cantons usually check their constitutional amendments carefully in advance. That is why the guarantee has only been refused in very few cases, such as the Schwyz electoral system in 2013.
43400.m: The guarantee is refused only very rarely.

43401.q: What is the purpose of the Conference of Cantonal Governments (KdK)?
a: It represents the cantons' common interests towards the Confederation
It elects the members of the Council of States
It acts as a court in disputes between cantons
43401.e: The KdK coordinates the cantons and presents their positions to the Confederation, for example in European policy. Its secretariat is run by the ch Foundation for Federal Cooperation.
43401.m: The KdK brings together the cantons' voices towards the Confederation.

43402.q: Which policy area gave the main impetus for founding the Conference of Cantonal Governments?
a: The building of the national motorways
43402.e: The cantons wanted a greater say in the Confederation's foreign and integration policy. The KdK is still an important partner of the Confederation in European policy today.
43402.m: The KdK was set up so that the cantons could have a say in European policy.

43403.q: What does the KdK need in order to issue a joint statement of the cantons?
a: A qualified majority of the cantonal governments
The approval of the Federal Council
A popular vote in all cantons
A decision of the Council of States
43403.e: At least 18 of the 26 cantonal governments must agree. Cantons with a different view can submit a dissenting position.
43403.m: For a joint statement, the KdK needs a qualified majority.

43404.q: Who are the members of the Conference of Cantonal Governments?
a: The 46 members of the Council of States
The presidents of the cantonal parliaments
The mayors of the large cities
43404.e: Each of the 26 cantonal governments has a seat in the KdK. It is therefore a body of executives, not parliaments.
43404.m: The cantonal governments sit in the KdK.

43405.q: What is the building in Bern called where the KdK and many intercantonal conferences have had their secretariats since 2008?
a: Town Hall of the Äusserer Stand
43405.e: The KdK and numerous conferences of cantonal ministers are housed in the House of the Cantons on Speichergasse in Bern. This keeps the distance to the federal administration short.
43405.m: The intercantonal conferences work in the House of the Cantons in Bern.

43406.q: What are the intercantonal bodies of cantonal ministers, for example for education or health, called?
43406.e: Besides the KdK, there are conferences of cantonal directors such as the EDK for education or the GDK for health. They coordinate their specialist areas.
43406.m: The cantonal ministers meet in conferences of cantonal directors.

43407.q: Which conference of cantonal directors is responsible for education, culture and sport?
43407.e: The Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (EDK) coordinates the education system. It has existed since 1897.
43407.m: The EDK coordinates the cantons' education policy.

43408.q: In which body does the KdK adopt the cantons' joint positions?
43408.e: All cantonal governments are represented in the plenary assembly. It meets at least four times a year.
43408.m: The KdK decides its positions in the plenary assembly.

43409.q: What is the EDK's Swiss-wide survey that checks whether pupils reach the national basic skills called?
43409.e: The survey on reaching basic skills (ÜGK) tests samples of pupils in all cantons. PISA, by contrast, is an international OECD study.
43409.m: The ÜGK measures whether the national basic skills are reached.

43410.q: Why does the HarmoS concordat not apply in all cantons?
a: A concordat only applies to cantons that join it
The Confederation only enacted it for French-speaking Switzerland
The Federal Supreme Court partly overturned it
It only applies to bilingual cantons
43410.e: HarmoS is a treaty between cantons. It only binds the cantons that have joined; in several cantons the people rejected joining at the ballot box.
43410.m: A concordat only applies to the cantons that join it.

43411.q: At what age do children start school under HarmoS?
43411.e: The cut-off date is 31 July: anyone who is four by then starts kindergarten. Kindergarten thus became compulsory.
43411.m: Under HarmoS, compulsory schooling starts at four.

43412.q: What is the former 1st year of primary school called in the HarmoS numbering?
43412.e: HarmoS counts the two kindergarten years, which are called 1H and 2H. The former 1st class is therefore the third HarmoS year.
43412.m: In HarmoS numbering, the first primary class is year 3H.

43413.q: What are the nationally set targets that HarmoS provides for, for example in the language of schooling and maths, called?
43413.e: In 2011 the EDK adopted national education goals in the form of basic skills. They describe what almost all pupils should be able to do.
43413.m: HarmoS sets basic skills as national education goals.

43414.q: Which 2006 vote obliges the cantons to harmonise key parameters of schooling?
a: The vote on the education articles of the Federal Constitution
The vote on the School Concordat
The vote on universities of applied sciences
43414.e: On 21 May 2006, the people and the cantons accepted the new education articles with over 85 per cent voting yes. If harmonisation fails, the Confederation can issue rules.
43414.m: The 2006 education articles require harmonised schooling.

43415.q: What does HarmoS lay down for foreign language teaching?
a: The first foreign language from the 3rd, the second from the 5th primary year at the latest
Only one foreign language until lower secondary school
English as the compulsory first foreign language in all cantons
Foreign languages only from lower secondary level
43415.e: HarmoS adopts the EDK's 2004 language strategy. The cantons or regions decide which language comes first.
43415.m: Under HarmoS, children learn two foreign languages in primary school.

43416.q: Which body drew up the HarmoS concordat?
a: The Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (EDK)
43416.e: The EDK, made up of the cantonal education ministers, adopted HarmoS in 2007. The concordat came into force in 2009, after ten cantons had joined.
43416.m: HarmoS was drawn up by the EDK.

43417.q: How did Swiss voters decide in 2014 on abolishing lump-sum taxation nationwide?
a: They rejected abolition with about 59 per cent voting no
They accepted abolition with about 59 per cent voting yes
They narrowly accepted abolition, but it failed the majority of cantons
43417.e: The popular initiative was rejected by the people and the cantons on 30 November 2014. The cantons may therefore decide themselves whether to keep taxation based on expenditure.
43417.m: The cantons still decide on lump-sum taxation.

43418.q: What is the profit tax rate of the direct federal tax for legal entities?
43418.e: The Confederation levies a uniform 8.5 per cent on companies' net profit. On top of this come cantonal and municipal profit taxes, which vary greatly by canton.
43418.m: The Confederation taxes company profits at 8.5 per cent.

43419.q: What does the Federal Constitution expressly forbid in tax competition between the cantons?
a: Lower profit taxes than the neighbouring canton
43419.e: Under Article 127 paragraph 3 of the Constitution, the same income or wealth may not be taxed by two cantons. The Confederation takes the necessary measures.

43420.q: In 2007 the Federal Supreme Court declared degressive tax scales for very high incomes unconstitutional. Which canton had introduced them?
43420.e: Obwalden wanted to attract the rich with falling tax rates for very high incomes. The Federal Supreme Court saw this as a breach of taxation according to economic capacity.
43420.m: According to the Federal Supreme Court, degressive tax scales are unconstitutional.

43421.q: What share of the direct federal tax has gone to the cantons since 2020?
43421.e: With the TRAF tax reform, the cantons' share rose from 17 to 21.2 per cent. This gave the cantons room to lower their profit taxes.
43421.m: Since 2020 the cantons have received 21.2 per cent of the direct federal tax.

43422.q: Which tax reform, accepted by the people in 2019, abolished the tax privileges for status companies?
43422.e: TRAF was accepted on 19 May 2019 with about 66 per cent voting yes. Many cantons then lowered their profit tax rates.
43422.m: In 2019 TRAF ended the cantonal tax privileges for status companies.

43423.q: Which popular initiative wanted to introduce minimum tax rates for high incomes and wealth in all cantons in 2010?
43423.e: The Tax Fairness Initiative wanted to limit tax competition for high incomes. The people and the cantons rejected it on 28 November 2010.
43423.m: The Tax Fairness Initiative failed at the ballot box in 2010.

43424.q: Which canton was the first to abolish lump-sum taxation of rich foreigners by popular vote in 2009?
43424.e: Voters in the canton of Zurich abolished taxation based on expenditure in February 2009. Some other cantons followed later.

43425.q: Which minimum tax rate for large international companies did Swiss voters accept in 2023?
43425.e: On 18 June 2023, the OECD minimum tax for groups with a turnover of over 750 million euros was accepted. This limits tax competition for these companies.
43425.m: Since the OECD reform, large groups must pay at least 15 per cent tax.

43426.q: Roughly how many political municipalities did Switzerland have at the start of 2024?
43426.e: According to municipal monitoring, there were still 2131 municipalities at the start of 2024. In 2010 there were 2596; mergers in particular have reduced the number.
43426.m: Mergers have greatly reduced the number of municipalities.

43427.q: What is a common reason for a municipal merger?
a: Small municipalities can hardly find people for their offices
The Confederation requires every municipality to be the same size
Merged municipalities no longer have to levy taxes
43427.e: Many small municipalities lack people for the council and administration, and tasks are becoming ever more demanding. A merger creates larger, more professional structures.
43427.m: Mergers are meant to make municipalities more effective.

43428.q: Which large Grisons municipality was created in 2015 by a merger in the Lower Engadine?
43428.e: Scuol merged with several neighbouring municipalities in 2015. With about 438 square kilometres, it has since been the largest municipality in Switzerland by area.
43428.m: Since the 2015 merger, Scuol has been Switzerland's largest municipality by area.

43429.q: Which town on Lake Zurich in the canton of St Gallen was created in 2007 by joining two municipalities?
43429.e: Rapperswil and Jona merged on 1 January 2007. Rapperswil-Jona is now the second largest town in the canton of St Gallen.
43429.m: Rapperswil-Jona was created by a merger in 2007.

43430.q: Which Ticino cantonal capital grew greatly in 2017 by merging with twelve neighbouring municipalities?
43430.e: On 2 April 2017, 13 municipalities joined to form the new town of Bellinzona. Ticino is one of the cantons with a particularly large number of mergers.
43430.m: Bellinzona grew in 2017 through a large merger.

43431.q: Which canton has the most political municipalities (as of 2024)?
43431.e: Despite mergers, the canton of Bern has over 300 municipalities. Many of them are small rural municipalities.
43431.m: Bern is the canton with the most municipalities.

43432.q: According to a 2024 study, which alternative to merging do many Swiss municipalities often choose?
a: Inter-municipal cooperation, for example for home care or the fire brigade
Handing all tasks to the Confederation
43432.e: Many municipalities expand cooperation with neighbouring municipalities, for example for home care (Spitex) or the fire brigade. This makes them more professional and saves costs while keeping them independent.
43432.m: Many municipalities cooperate instead of merging.

43433.q: In Switzerland, who usually has the final say on a municipal merger?
a: The voters of the municipalities involved, often with the canton's approval
43433.e: Mergers are usually decided at municipal assemblies or ballot votes. The canton approves them and sometimes supports them with grants.
43433.m: Municipal mergers are usually decided by local voters.

43434.q: Why was the Moutier vote of 18 June 2017 on changing canton annulled?
a: Because of irregularities surrounding the vote
Because the Confederation forbade the change
Because turnout was under 50 per cent
Because the canton of Jura rejected the change
43434.e: The prefect's office declared the vote invalid in 2018 after complaints. The Bern Administrative Court confirmed this in 2019.
43434.m: The 2017 Moutier vote had to be repeated because of irregularities.

43435.q: How large was the yes vote for moving to the canton of Jura when the Moutier vote was repeated on 28 March 2021?
43435.e: 2114 voters (54.9 per cent) wanted to join Jura, 1740 were against. Moutier thus confirmed its wish to change canton.
43435.m: In 2021 Moutier voted for Jura with about 55 per cent.

43436.q: What was special about the Moutier vote of 28 March 2021?
a: It took place under federal supervision
It was decided by show of hands at a Landsgemeinde
Only young people were allowed to vote
43436.e: Because the first vote had been annulled, the repeat vote was accompanied by federal observers. This was a unique event in Switzerland.
43436.m: The 2021 Moutier vote was held under federal supervision.

43437.q: What was the treaty between the cantons of Bern and Jura that regulates the details of Moutier's move called?
43437.e: The Moutier Concordat regulates staff, assets and transitional questions. The voters of both cantons accepted it on 22 September 2024.
43437.m: The Moutier Concordat regulates the change of canton in detail.

43438.q: Which canton has the town of Moutier belonged to since 1 January 2026?
43438.e: After the 2021 votes and the 2024 Moutier Concordat, Moutier moved from the canton of Bern to the canton of Jura. Both cantons and the Federal Assembly agreed.
43438.m: Moutier has belonged to the canton of Jura since 2026.

43439.q: After the cantonal votes, which federal authority still had to approve Moutier's territorial change?
a: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs
43439.e: Under Article 53 paragraph 3 of the Constitution, a territorial change between cantons needs the approval of the Federal Assembly. The Federal Council presented a dispatch on it in 2024.
43439.m: Territorial changes between cantons need the Federal Assembly's approval.

43440.q: Which region did Moutier belong to until it changed canton?
43440.e: With about 7200 inhabitants, Moutier was the largest municipality of the French-speaking Bernese Jura. The region covers the south of the historical Jura, which stayed with Bern.
43440.m: Moutier was the largest municipality of the Bernese Jura.

43441.q: What distinguished the Laufental from the rest of the area of today's canton of Jura?
a: It is Protestant, the Jura Catholic
It lay south of Lake Biel
43441.e: The Laufental is German-speaking, while the canton of Jura is French-speaking. That is why in 1974 it did not stay with the new Jura but looked for a German-speaking partner canton.
43441.m: Unlike the Jura, the Laufental is German-speaking.

43442.q: Which event made the Laufental a Bernese exclave and so made a change of canton possible?
a: The founding of the canton of Jura
The building of the Jura railway tunnel
43442.e: With the founding of the canton of Jura in 1979, the Laufental was cut off from the rest of Bern's territory. The plebiscites of the 1970s gave it the right to decide on a change.
43442.m: Only the Jura question made the Laufental's change possible.

43443.q: How did the Laufental decide in the vote of 11 September 1983?
a: To stay with the canton of Bern
43443.e: Just under 57 per cent voted in 1983 to stay with Bern. However, this result did not last.
43443.m: In 1983 the Laufental first voted for Bern.

43444.q: Why did the 1983 Laufental vote have to be repeated?
a: Because the canton of Bern had unlawfully helped fund the campaign
Because too few ballot papers had been printed
Because the canton of Solothurn lodged a complaint
Because women were not allowed to vote
43444.e: The Bern finance affair showed in 1984 that the canton had supported the pro-Bern campaign from secret funds. The Federal Supreme Court ordered a repeat.
43444.m: The Bern finance affair led to the Laufental vote being repeated.

43445.q: How did the Laufental decide in 1989 in the vote on moving to Basel-Landschaft?
43445.e: The result was close: 51.7 per cent voted to join Basel-Landschaft. After that, the whole of Switzerland still had to agree.
43445.m: In 1989 the Laufental narrowly chose Basel-Landschaft.

43446.q: Who finally had to approve the Laufental's change of canton in 1993?
a: The people and the cantons of all Switzerland
Only the Grand Council of the canton of Bern
43446.e: At that time, territorial changes of cantons needed the approval of the people and the cantons as well as of those affected. On 26 September 1993 about 75 per cent voted yes.
43446.m: In 1993 all of Switzerland approved the Laufental's move.

43447.q: Which canton does the district of Laufen belong to today?
43447.e: Since 1994 the Laufental with its 13 municipalities has belonged to the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Before that it was a district of the canton of Bern.
43447.m: The Laufental has belonged to Basel-Landschaft since 1994.

43448.q: Which three cantons were on offer in the Laufental's first vote on a new canton in 1980?
43448.e: In January 1980 Basel-Landschaft got 52, Solothurn 32 and Basel-Stadt 16 per cent. In March 1980 Basel-Landschaft beat Solothurn in a run-off.
43448.m: In 1980 the Laufental chose Basel-Landschaft as its partner canton.

43449.q: How did the canton of Basel come to be divided in 1833?
a: After armed fighting between city and countryside
Through an inheritance dispute between two princes
Through a popular vote across Switzerland
43449.e: The countryside demanded more political rights. After the battle at the Hülftenschanz in August 1833, the Diet divided the canton.
43449.m: The Hülftenschanz stands for the division of the two Basels.

43450.q: In which year did the two Basels last vote on starting a cantonal merger?
43450.e: On 28 September 2014, both cantons voted on the merger initiative at the same time. A merger would have needed a yes in both cantons.
43450.m: In 2014 the two Basels voted on a cantonal merger.

43451.q: Which joint project of the two Basels failed in 2019 because voters in Basel-Stadt said no?
a: Merging the hospitals into one hospital group
43451.e: On 10 February 2019, Basel-Stadt rejected the treaty on the hospital group, while Basel-Landschaft approved it. This meant the hospital merger had failed.
43451.m: The hospital merger of the two Basels failed in the city in 2019.

43452.q: How did Basel-Stadt vote in 2014 on the initiative to merge the two Basels?
43452.e: In Basel-Stadt a majority of about 55 per cent said yes. The yes had no effect because Basel-Landschaft rejected it.

43453.q: If both had said yes in 2014, what would have been the next step towards merging the two Basels?
a: A joint constitutional council would have drafted a constitution for the new canton
The Federal Council would have united the cantons immediately
Basel-Stadt would have become a municipality of Basel-Landschaft
The Federal Supreme Court would have decided on the border
43453.e: The initiatives called for a constitutional council from both cantons. Voters would later have had to vote again on its draft constitution.
43453.m: A merger of the two Basels would first have needed a constitutional council.

43454.q: How did the 1969 vote on a reunification constitution for the two Basels turn out?
43454.e: On 7 December 1969 the city said yes, but Basel-Landschaft clearly said no. Since then, partnership instead of merger has been the guiding idea in Basel-Landschaft.
43454.m: Reunification already failed in Basel-Landschaft in 1969.

43455.q: Which hurdle has always made a merger of the two Basels particularly difficult?
a: It needs the approval of voters in both cantons
It needs the approval of all neighbouring countries
It needs the approval of the Council of Europe
It needs the approval of all 2000 Swiss municipalities
43455.e: A merger changes the existence of two cantons, so both cantons must agree. Under Article 53 of the Constitution it would also need the approval of the people and the cantons.
43455.m: A cantonal merger needs the approval of the cantons concerned and of the Confederation.

43456.q: Which partnership have the two Basels emphasised instead since the merger was rejected in 2014?
a: Close cooperation in areas such as the university and hospitals
A joint tax administration with a single tax
43456.e: The two cantons jointly run the University of Basel, for example, and cooperate in many areas through treaties.
43456.m: The two Basels cooperate as partners instead of merging.

43457.q: What is the executive of the city of Geneva called?
43457.e: The Conseil administratif with five members runs the city of Geneva. The city parliament is called the Conseil municipal.
43457.m: The city of Geneva is governed by the Conseil administratif.

43458.q: What is the municipal executive called in the municipalities of the canton of Ticino?
43458.e: In Ticino the Municipio runs the municipality, led by the Sindaco. The municipal parliament is called the Consiglio comunale.
43458.m: In Ticino the municipal government is called the Municipio.

43459.q: What is the city parliament of Winterthur called?
43459.e: The Winterthur parliament is called the Grosser Gemeinderat and has 60 members. The city government is called the Stadtrat.
43459.m: In Winterthur the city parliament is called the Grosser Gemeinderat.

43460.q: How many members does the parliament of the city of Bern have?
43460.e: The Bern city parliament has 80 members. It is elected every four years.
43460.m: The Bern city parliament has 80 members.

43461.q: What is the executive of the city of Lausanne called?
43461.e: In Lausanne the Municipalité with seven members forms the government. The parliament is called the Conseil communal.
43461.m: Lausanne is governed by the Municipalité.

43462.q: What is the city parliament of Lucerne called?
43462.e: In Lucerne the parliament is called the Grosser Stadtrat. The five-member executive is called the Stadtrat.
43462.m: The Lucerne city parliament is called the Grosser Stadtrat.

43463.q: Which electoral system is usually used to elect the large city parliaments in Switzerland?
a: Show of hands at the municipal assembly
43463.e: In larger towns, parliaments are almost everywhere elected by proportional representation. This gives the parties seats in proportion to their votes.
43463.m: City parliaments are usually elected by proportional representation.

43464.q: Who decides how far the autonomy of a Swiss municipality extends?
43464.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees municipal autonomy in accordance with cantonal law. That is why municipalities have different degrees of independence depending on the canton.
43464.m: The canton sets the extent of municipal autonomy.

43465.q: Which canton introduced voting rights for foreigners at municipal level as early as 1849?
43465.e: Neuchâtel has had municipal voting rights for foreigners since 1849. Today several cantons in French-speaking Switzerland have similar rules.
43465.m: Neuchâtel has had municipal voting rights for foreigners since 1849.

43466.q: Roughly how much more weight does a vote from Uri have in a Council of States election than one from Zurich (as of 2024)?
43466.e: Zurich has about 1.6 million inhabitants and Uri about 38,000, but both elect two members of the Council of States. Per person, the weight in Uri is therefore about 40 times greater.
43466.m: Per person, small cantons are strongly over-represented in the Council of States.

43467.q: How does the German Bundesrat, as the chamber of the states, differ from the Swiss Council of States?
a: It consists of members of the state governments who vote as instructed
It is directly elected by the people by proportional representation
It has exactly two members per state
It has no say at all in laws
43467.e: The German Bundesrat is made up of representatives of the state governments, who cast their votes as a block on instruction. The Council of States, by contrast, is elected by the people.
43467.m: The Council of States is elected by the people; the German Bundesrat is made up of delegates of the state governments.

43468.q: Who decides in the Council of States if the votes are tied?
a: The president of the council with the casting vote
The oldest member of the council
43468.e: The president of the Council of States does not normally vote. In the event of a tie, however, he or she has the casting vote.
43468.m: In a tie in the Council of States, the president decides.

43469.q: What does the ban on instructions mean for members of the Council of States?
a: They vote without instructions from their cantonal government
They may not ask the Federal Council questions
They must always vote like the National Council
43469.e: Under Article 161 of the Constitution, all members of parliament vote without instructions. Members of the Council of States represent their canton but are not bound by orders from the cantonal government.
43469.m: Members of the Council of States are not bound by instructions from their canton.

43470.q: Which assembly of cantonal envoys before 1848 is considered the forerunner of the Council of States?
43470.e: At the Diet, the envoys voted according to instructions from their cantons. The Council of States took over the idea of equal representation of the cantons.
43470.m: The Diet is the forerunner of the Council of States.

43471.q: Which two cantons elect their members of the Council of States by proportional representation?
43471.e: Almost all cantons elect the Council of States by majority vote. Jura and Neuchâtel use proportional representation instead.
43471.m: Only Jura and Neuchâtel elect the Council of States by proportional representation.

43472.q: Which French expression is often used for the Council of States because, as the smaller chamber, it is seen as particularly objective and thorough?
43472.e: With 46 members, the Council of States is seen as the calmer, more deliberative chamber. Hence the expression “chambre de réflexion”.
43472.m: The Council of States is seen as a “chambre de réflexion”.

43473.q: In a canton with majority voting, what happens if a member of the Council of States resigns during their term?
a: The first substitute on the list moves up
The seat stays empty until the next elections
The National Council chooses the successor
43473.e: In majority voting there are no substitutes on a list. The canton therefore organises a by-election.
43473.m: A vacant Council of States seat is filled by a by-election.

43474.q: In which month is the National Council re-elected every four years?
43474.e: The Federal Act on Political Rights sets the general election of the National Council on the second-to-last Sunday in October. In 2023 that was 22 October.
43474.m: The National Council is elected in October.

43475.q: What did the Federal Statistical Office have to correct three days after the 2023 elections?
a: The distribution of seats among the parties
The number of people entitled to vote
The date of the second rounds
43475.e: Because of an error in data transmission, the parties' vote shares had been calculated wrongly. The distribution of seats was not affected.
43475.m: In 2023 a data error affected only the party strengths, not the seats.

43476.q: In 2023 almost 6000 people stood for a seat in the National Council. How many seats does the National Council have?
43476.e: The National Council has 200 seats. In 2023, 5909 people stood on 618 lists, more than ever before.
43476.m: In 2023 almost 6000 people stood for the 200 National Council seats.

43477.q: What was the share of women among all candidates for the National Council in 2023?
43477.e: The Federal Statistical Office reported a 41 per cent share of women among candidates in 2023. Among those elected it was somewhat lower.
43477.m: About four in ten candidates for the National Council in 2023 were women.

43478.q: In 2023 the SVP, FDP, EDU, Lega and MCG together won 95 National Council seats. How many seats were they short of an absolute majority?
43478.e: The absolute majority in the 200-member National Council is 101 seats. 101 minus 95 leaves 6 seats missing.
43478.m: The absolute majority in the National Council is 101 seats.

43479.q: Which party has had the most seats in the Council of States since the 2023 elections?
43479.e: The Centre has 15 seats in the Council of States, followed by the FDP with 11. In the National Council, by contrast, the SVP is the strongest.
43479.m: The Centre is the strongest party in the Council of States.

43480.q: How many members does the Council of States have, which was also re-elected in 2023?
43480.e: Each canton has two seats, while the six cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden have one each. That makes 46 members.
43480.m: The Council of States has 46 members.

43481.q: Which party lost its only seat in the National Council in 2023?
43481.e: The PdA lost its seat in the canton of Neuchâtel to the SVP. Lega, EVP and EDU remained in the National Council.
43481.m: The Party of Labour has not been represented in the National Council since 2023.

43482.q: In which canton with only one National Council seat did the seat pass from the SVP to the Centre in 2023?
43482.e: In Nidwalden, Regina Durrer-Knobel of the Centre won the former SVP seat. In cantons with one seat, majority voting decides.
43482.m: In 2023 the Centre took the Nidwalden National Council seat from the SVP.

43483.q: What used to happen to the number of National Council seats before it was fixed at 200?
a: It was drawn by lot every year
It was always the same as today
It was set by the Federal Council
43483.e: There used to be one seat for a fixed number of inhabitants, so the National Council grew with the population. Since 1962, 200 seats have always been distributed.
43483.m: Today the National Council has a fixed 200 seats.

43484.q: Which two cantons each had exactly two National Council seats in the 2023 election?
43484.e: Schaffhausen and Jura each got two seats. Zug had three, Schwyz and Neuchâtel four each, Uri and Glarus only one seat.
43484.m: Schaffhausen and Jura each elect two members of the National Council.

43486.q: What share of the 200 National Council seats did the canton of Zurich hold in 2023 with 36 seats?
43486.e: 36 divided by 200 is 0.18. Zurich therefore holds 18 per cent of the seats.
43486.m: Almost one in five members of the National Council comes from the canton of Zurich.

43487.q: Why does a National Council seat in Appenzell Ausserrhoden need far more inhabitants than one in Appenzell Innerrhoden?
a: Both have one seat, but Ausserrhoden has more inhabitants
Innerrhoden gets a bonus as a Landsgemeinde canton
In Innerrhoden, Swiss abroad are also counted
43487.e: Every canton has at least one seat, and both Appenzells have exactly one. As Ausserrhoden has about three times as many inhabitants, its seat represents many more people.
43487.m: The guarantee of at least one seat leads to constituencies of unequal size.

43489.q: Three cantons with 52,000, 31,000 and 17,000 inhabitants share 10 seats using the Hare/Niemeyer method. How many seats does the smallest canton get?
43489.e: The quotas are 5.2, 3.1 and 1.7, so first 5, 3 and 1 seats. The tenth seat goes to the largest remainder, 0.7, which is the smallest canton.
43489.m: With Hare/Niemeyer, the largest remainders decide the last seats.

43490.q: How many National Council seats did the canton of Ticino have in the 2023 election?
43490.e: In 2023 Ticino had eight seats, the same as Valais. The number depends on the canton's resident population.
43490.m: In 2023 Ticino elected eight members of the National Council.

43491.q: Who sets the binding distribution of National Council seats among the cantons before each election?
43491.e: The Federal Council decides the distribution of seats in an ordinance, based on the official population figures. In 2021, for example, it was decided that Zurich would get a seat from Basel-Stadt.
43491.m: The Federal Council sets the National Council seat distribution by ordinance.

43492.q: Using Hagenbach-Bischoff, what is the distribution number for 24,000 party votes and 7 seats?
43492.e: 24,000 divided by 8 is exactly 3000. The law requires the next higher whole number, so the distribution number is 3001.
43492.m: Even when the result is a whole number, the distribution number is increased by one.

43493.q: 4 seats; A has 5200, B 3100 and C 1700 votes. How many seats does A get in total using Hagenbach-Bischoff?
43493.e: The distribution number is 2001, so A first gets 2 seats and B 1. For the remaining seat, A with 5200 divided by 3, that is 1733, is ahead of C with 1700 and B with 1550.
43493.m: Remaining seats go to the list with the highest quotient of votes divided by seats plus one.

43494.q: 3 seats; A has 4500, B 3000 and C 2500 votes. Who gets the remaining seat using Hagenbach-Bischoff?
43494.e: The distribution number is 10,000 divided by 4, that is 2501, so at first only A and B get one seat each. For the remaining seat, C with 2500 divided by 1 has the highest quotient, ahead of A with 2250.
43494.m: A list with no seat at first can still win one when the remaining seats are distributed.

43495.q: In a canton with 9 seats, what minimum share of the vote guarantees a seat to a list without a list alliance?
43495.e: The distribution number is just above the total votes divided by 10. Anyone with more than a tenth of the votes reaches it and gets a seat in the first distribution. More than 11.1 per cent would also be enough, but it is not the minimum.
43495.m: The fewer seats a canton has, the higher the natural threshold.

43496.q: A party has 9000 votes and already 2 seats. What is its quotient in the next distribution of remaining seats?
43496.e: You divide the votes by the seats already won plus one. 9000 divided by 3 is 3000.
43496.m: With every seat won, a party's quotient falls.

43497.q: In which law is the Hagenbach-Bischoff method for National Council elections laid down?
a: Federal Act on the Consultation Procedure
43497.e: Articles 40 and 41 of the Federal Act on Political Rights describe the distribution of seats. The method itself is not named there.
43497.m: The distribution of National Council seats is set out in the Federal Act on Political Rights.

43498.q: Why is the Hagenbach-Bischoff method also called a quasi-quota method?
a: It first distributes seats using a distribution number like a quota
It allocates seats according to fixed quotas per party
It reserves seats for women and young people
It requires a five per cent threshold
43498.e: In the first step, each party gets as many seats as the distribution number fits into its votes. Only then comes the highest-quotient calculation, so the result matches the D'Hondt method.
43498.m: Hagenbach-Bischoff starts like a quota method and ends like a divisor method.

43499.q: 6 seats; A has 4800, B 3300 and C 1900 votes. How many seats does B get using Hagenbach-Bischoff?
43499.e: 10,000 divided by 7 is 1428.6, so the distribution number is 1429. B gets 3300 divided by 1429, so 2 seats; together with A (3) and C (1), all 6 seats are already allocated.
43499.m: Sometimes all the seats are allocated in the first distribution.

43500.q: Which subject did Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff teach as a professor at the University of Basel?
43500.e: Hagenbach-Bischoff (1833 to 1910) held the chair of physics in Basel from 1863 to 1906. As a member of the Basel Grand Council, he campaigned for proportional representation.
43500.m: The man the Hagenbach-Bischoff method is named after was a physicist.

43501.q: Who is the double Pukelsheim method named after?
a: The Zurich cantonal minister Markus Pukelsheim
The Bern political scientist Hans Pukelsheim
43501.e: Friedrich Pukelsheim, a mathematician at the University of Augsburg, developed the method on behalf of the canton of Zurich. It is based on work by Michel Balinski and Peyton Young.
43501.m: The double Pukelsheim method comes from the mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim.

43502.q: What triggered the introduction of the double Pukelsheim method in Zurich in 2002?
a: A Federal Supreme Court ruling on unequal constituencies
An instruction from the Federal Council
A ruling of the European Court of Justice
43502.e: After the 2002 Zurich city council election, the Federal Supreme Court declared the previous system with very small constituencies unconstitutional. Small parties had hardly any chance of a seat there.
43502.m: A 2002 Federal Supreme Court ruling set the double Pukelsheim method in motion.

43503.q: In which election was the double Pukelsheim method first used in 2006?
a: The city council election in the city of Zurich
The Grand Council election in the canton of Aargau
The National Council election in the canton of Bern
The cantonal parliament election in Schwyz
43503.e: In 2006 the city of Zurich was the first to elect its parliament with the new method. The canton of Zurich followed for its cantonal parliament election.
43503.m: In 2006 the city of Zurich was the first to vote with the double Pukelsheim method.

43504.q: In the double Pukelsheim method, what is distributed in the upper apportionment?
a: The seats among the parties across the whole electoral area
The seats among the individual constituencies
The votes among the list alliances
43504.e: In the upper apportionment, each party gets its number of seats for the whole electoral area. So all votes count, regardless of constituency.
43504.m: The upper apportionment decides how many seats each party gets in total.

43505.q: In the double Pukelsheim method, what is decided in the lower apportionment?
a: In which constituencies the parties get their seats
How many seats each party gets in total
Which parties form a list alliance
How many seats each constituency has
43505.e: The lower apportionment distributes the party seats from the upper apportionment among the constituencies. Constituency and party divisors are adjusted in turn until all totals match.
43505.m: The lower apportionment distributes the party seats among the individual constituencies.

43506.q: Which rounding rule is used in the double Pukelsheim method?
43506.e: The method rounds as at school: from 0.5 up, otherwise down. This divisor method is called Sainte-Laguë or Schepers.
43506.m: The double Pukelsheim method rounds using the Sainte-Laguë method.

43507.q: With a divisor of 1000, parties A, B and C have voter numbers of 4300, 3600 and 2100. How many seats does B get with standard rounding?
43507.e: 3600 divided by 1000 is 3.6, which is rounded to 4. A gets 4 and C 2 seats, making 10 seats in total.
43507.m: In divisor methods, you divide the votes by a divisor and round.

43508.q: Which canton introduced the double Pukelsheim method by popular vote in 2021, giving up majority voting for its parliament?
43508.e: On 13 June 2021, voters in the Grisons approved proportional representation using the double Pukelsheim method. Before that, the Grand Council was largely elected by majority vote.
43508.m: In 2021 the Grisons switched from majority voting to the double Pukelsheim method.

43509.q: Which canton approved the double Pukelsheim method at the ballot box in February 2025?
43509.e: Basel-Landschaft approved it on 9 February 2025. Before that, Aargau, Schaffhausen, Zug, Nidwalden, Schwyz, Valais, Uri and the Grisons, among others, had introduced the method.
43509.m: In 2025 Basel-Landschaft decided to switch to the double Pukelsheim method.

43510.q: Whom did the Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Innerrhoden confirm as member of the Council of States in April 2023?
43510.e: Innerrhoden elects its member of the Council of States at the Landsgemeinde, months before the other cantons. In 2023 Daniel Fässler of the Centre was confirmed.
43510.m: In Appenzell Innerrhoden, the member of the Council of States is elected at the Landsgemeinde.

43511.q: In most cantons, which majority is enough in the second round of a Council of States election?
43511.e: In the second round, whoever gets the most votes is elected. An absolute majority is only required in the first round.
43511.m: In the second round, getting the most votes is usually enough to win.

43512.q: In Switzerland, who decides which method is used to elect members of the Council of States?
43512.e: The Federal Constitution leaves the rules for Council of States elections to the cantons. That is why there are differences, for example in the electoral method or the voting age.
43512.m: The cantons regulate the election of their members of the Council of States themselves.

43513.q: For how many years are members of the Council of States elected today?
43513.e: Today the term of office is four years in all cantons. In most cantons the election takes place at the same time as the National Council election.
43513.m: Members of the Council of States are elected for four years.

43514.q: Why did the number of Council of States seats rise from 44 to 46 in 1979?
a: The canton of Jura was founded
The Council of States was enlarged for the Swiss abroad
43514.e: With the founding of the canton of Jura in 1979, a new full canton with two seats was added. Since then the Council of States has had 46 members.
43514.m: With the canton of Jura, the Council of States grew to 46 seats in 1979.

43515.q: Who won the second Zurich seat in the Council of States in the second round in November 2023?
43515.e: Green Liberal Tiana Moser beat Gregor Rutz of the SVP in the second round. Daniel Jositsch had already been elected in the first round.
43515.m: In 2023 Tiana Moser won a Zurich Council of States seat for the GLP.

43516.q: Who won the first Council of States seat for the Mouvement Citoyens Genevois in the canton of Geneva in 2023?
43516.e: Former Geneva cantonal minister Mauro Poggia was elected in the second round. The sitting Green member, Lisa Mazzone, lost her seat.
43516.m: Mauro Poggia has been a member of the Council of States for the MCG since 2023.

43517.q: Which principle is shown by the fact that Zurich, with about 1.6 million inhabitants, and Uri, with about 38,000, have the same number of Council of States seats?
a: The equal status of the cantons
43517.e: In the Council of States every canton counts equally, regardless of its size. In this way the smaller chamber balances the population-based representation in the National Council.
43517.m: In the Council of States, large and small cantons have the same weight.

43518.q: How long was the term of office of members of the Council of States in many cantons in the past?
43518.e: In the past, many cantons elected their members of the Council of States for just one year at a time. Today the term is four years in all cantons.
43518.m: Today members of the Council of States are elected for four years everywhere.

a: An election without a ballot, because there are no more candidates than seats
A secret election in the polling booth
An election the media do not report on
43519.e: If only as many candidates come forward as there are seats, they are deemed elected. In 2023, for example, a member of the Council of States for Obwalden was elected tacitly.
43519.m: In a tacit election, there is no ballot.

43520.q: Which criticism is often made of tacit elections?
a: They take a very long time
They are banned at federal level
43520.e: In a tacit election, voters cannot have a say. Critics see this as a lack of democratic competition.

43521.q: Why are there no tacit elections for the Council of States in the canton of Uri?
a: There is no deadline for registering candidates
Uri elects the Council of States at the Landsgemeinde
Uri elects the Council of States by proportional representation
Uri always requires at least three candidates
43521.e: Without a registration procedure, it is never certain that there is only one candidate. So there must always be a vote, and even people who have not registered can receive votes.
43521.m: In Uri there must always be a ballot in Council of States elections.

43522.q: Which argument is put forward in favour of tacit elections?
a: A lack of opposing candidates can express approval
Tacit elections are required at federal level
Tacit elections prevent deals between parties
43522.e: If nobody stands against a sitting office holder, this can show satisfaction with their work. Also, small parties can put up their own candidates at any time.
43522.m: A tacit election can also be a sign of broad support.

43523.q: In a National Council election in a canton with proportional representation, what happens if no more candidates are registered in total than there are seats?
a: The cantonal government declares them all elected
The election is postponed by a year
The Federal Council appoints more candidates
The seats stay empty until the next election
43523.e: Article 45 of the Federal Act on Political Rights provides for a tacit election in this case. No ballot then takes place.
43523.m: A tacit election is also possible in National Council elections.

43524.q: What is a tacit election called in French-speaking Switzerland?
43524.e: In French-speaking Switzerland people speak of an “élection tacite”. “Tacite” means silent or unspoken.
43524.m: In French, a tacit election is called an “élection tacite”.

43525.q: In a majority election without compulsory registration, whom may you write on the ballot paper?
a: Only people from your own municipality
43525.e: Without a registration procedure, votes are not limited to official candidates. Any name of a person eligible for the office is valid.
43525.m: Without compulsory registration, any eligible person can be elected, even without standing.

43526.q: Why do tacit elections happen mainly in small cantons?
a: Because there are often no opposing candidates there
Because voting rights are restricted there
Because the Confederation requires it there
Because no parties are allowed there
43526.e: In small cantons there are fewer possible candidates, and parties often decide not to stand against a popular office holder.
43526.m: A lack of opposing candidates leads to tacit elections.

43527.q: What rights does a council member elected in a tacit election have?
a: The same as a member elected at the ballot box
They may only take part in an advisory role
They must be confirmed after one year
43527.e: A tacit election is a fully valid election. The person elected has all the rights and duties of the office.
43527.m: Those elected tacitly are full members of their council.

43528.q: Between which lists is a sub-list alliance allowed in National Council elections?
a: Only between lists of the same party
Only between lists from different cantons
Only between lists of Federal Council parties
43528.e: Sub-list alliances are only allowed between lists of the same group, such as a youth, women's or regional list. In 2022 the Federal Council and Parliament made clear that different parties may not form a sub-list alliance.
43528.m: Sub-list alliances are only allowed within the same party.

43529.q: How did the EDU win a National Council seat in the canton of Zurich in 2023?
a: Through a list alliance with several small parties
Through a remaining seat without an alliance
Through a sub-list alliance with the SVP
43529.e: The EDU was allied with Mass-voll, Aufrecht and the Swiss Democrats. Their combined votes were enough for one seat, which went to the EDU as the strongest list in the group.
43529.m: List alliances can help small parties win a seat.

43530.q: 4 seats; C has 7100 votes, A 1500 and B 1400. A and B form a list alliance. How many seats does the alliance get using Hagenbach-Bischoff?
43530.e: The distribution number is 2001; C gets 3 seats and the alliance with 2900 votes 1 seat. Without the alliance, C, with 1775 votes per seat, would also have won the fourth seat.
43530.m: A list alliance pools votes that would otherwise be lost individually.

43531.q: A list alliance of A with 1500 and B with 1400 votes wins one seat. Who gets it?
a: The strongest list in the canton
43531.e: Within the alliance, the seats are again distributed using Hagenbach-Bischoff. A has more votes than B and therefore gets the seat.
43531.m: Within a list alliance, the stronger list wins.

43532.q: Which disadvantage of the Hagenbach-Bischoff method do list alliances reduce?
a: The number of invalid ballot papers
43532.e: The method slightly favours large parties, and the leftover votes of small lists often win no seat. Allied lists are first treated as one list, so fewer votes are lost.
43532.m: List alliances reduce the loss of leftover votes.

43533.q: In which order are National Council seats distributed when there are list alliances?
a: First to the list groups, then to the lists
First to the lists, then to the groups
First to candidates, then to lists
To all lists at once, without groups
43533.e: In the first distribution, allied lists count as a single list. Then the group's seats are distributed among its individual lists.
43533.m: First the list group gets its seats, then its individual lists.

43534.q: What happens to a vote for party A if A is allied with party B?
a: It can help B win a seat
It is automatically credited to B
43534.e: The votes of allied lists are added together for the first distribution. If the group wins a seat and B has more votes, the seat goes to B.
43534.m: Voting for an allied list also indirectly strengthens the partner list.

43535.q: According to the Federal Statistical Office, which type of sub-list made up almost half of all the parties' sub-lists in 2023?
43535.e: Many parties put up youth or senior lists. Many candidates under 30 stood on such age-group lists.
43535.m: Youth parties often stand with their own sub-lists.

43536.q: By which features do sub-lists of the same party typically differ?
43536.e: The Federal Act on Political Rights allows sub-list alliances between lists of the same party that differ, for example, by gender, wing, region or age. In this way a party appeals to different groups of voters.
43536.m: Sub-lists appeal to different groups of voters of the same party.

43537.q: Why do parties in a canton often put up several sub-lists?
a: To reach more voters without losing votes
To get more seats per canton than allocated
To get round the list alliance
To have to disclose campaign costs
43537.e: Several lists bring more candidates and appeal to different groups. Through the sub-list alliance, the votes still flow together to the party.
43537.m: Several sub-lists increase a party's reach.

43538.q: Why does the canton of Schaffhausen usually have the highest election turnout in Switzerland?
a: Postal voting is only possible there
The election takes place at the Landsgemeinde
43538.e: Schaffhausen is the only canton with compulsory voting, enforced by a small fine. In 2023 turnout in the National Council election was 61.6 per cent.
43538.m: With compulsory voting, turnout in Schaffhausen is well above average.

43539.q: Why did turnout in the 2023 National Council election in Appenzell Innerrhoden fall to about 25 per cent?
a: The election took place at the Landsgemeinde
The election date fell in the summer holidays
43539.e: In Innerrhoden only Thomas Rechsteiner of the Centre stood. Turnout fell from 48.7 to 24.5 per cent, more than in any other canton.
43539.m: Without a choice, fewer people vote.

43540.q: How did Swiss-wide turnout in the 2023 National Council election compare with 2019?
a: It rose slightly to almost 47 per cent
It fell to under 30 per cent
It rose to over 70 per cent
43540.e: Turnout rose from 45.1 to 46.6 per cent. The canton of Glarus saw the largest increase.

43541.q: How has turnout in National Council elections developed in the long term since the period between the wars?
a: It fell from about 80 to under 50 per cent
It rose from about 50 to 80 per cent
It always stayed at about 70 per cent
It was always under 20 per cent
43541.e: After figures of around 80 per cent between the wars, turnout fell in the long term. In 1979 it dropped below half for the first time.
43541.m: Since 1979, turnout in National Council elections has mostly been under 50 per cent.

43542.q: After which reform did turnout in National Council elections rise to about 80 per cent from 1919?
43542.e: In 1919 the National Council was elected by proportional representation for the first time. Turnout then rose to about 80 per cent; in 1848 it had been only about 45 per cent.
43542.m: With proportional representation, turnout rose sharply.

43543.q: With 5,500,000 people entitled to vote and a turnout of 46.6 per cent, how many people vote?
43543.e: 5,500,000 times 0.466 is 2,563,000. That is how many people would have voted.
43543.m: The number of voters is those entitled to vote times turnout.

43544.q: Turnout rose from 45.1 to 46.6 per cent. Roughly by how many per cent did it rise in relative terms?
43544.e: The increase is 1.5 percentage points. 1.5 divided by 45.1 gives a relative increase of about 3.3 per cent.
43544.m: Percentage points and per cent are not the same.

43545.q: According to election studies, which group in Switzerland takes part in elections particularly rarely?
43545.e: Turnout rises with age and education. Young adults under 25 vote much less often than older people.
43545.m: Young people vote less often than older people.

43546.q: Who could vote electronically in the 2023 National Council elections in the cantons of Basel-Stadt, St Gallen and Thurgau?
a: Some of the Swiss living abroad
All voters in the three cantons
Only members of the armed forces on duty
43546.e: After a break of several years, e-voting was allowed again in trials in 2023. Those eligible were mainly some of the Swiss voters abroad registered in these cantons.
43546.m: In 2023 e-voting was used again on a trial basis in three cantons.

43547.q: What was the outcome of the 2007 Glarus Landsgemeinde decision on a voting age of 16?
43547.e: The Landsgemeinde narrowly approved it in 2007. At the same time, there were even motions to raise the voting age to 20.
43547.m: Glarus introduced a voting age of 16 by a narrow majority.

43548.q: What percentage of voters in the canton of Zurich rejected a voting age of 16 in 2022?
43548.e: Zurich voters rejected the proposal in 2022 with 64 per cent voting no. In the same year Bern also rejected it, with 67 per cent.
43548.m: In 2022 Zurich and Bern clearly said no to a voting age of 16.

43549.q: Which of these cantons rejected a voting age of 16 at the ballot box with the highest share of no votes?
43549.e: Basel-Landschaft rejected the proposal in 2018 with 84.5 per cent voting no. Basel-Stadt rejected it in 2009 with 72, Zurich in 2022 with 64 and Neuchâtel in 2020 with 58.5 per cent.
43549.m: In Basel-Landschaft, a voting age of 16 failed particularly clearly.

43550.q: Which canton rejected a voting age of 16 at the ballot box twice, in 2009 and 2021?
43550.e: Uri said no with 79.9 per cent in 2009 and with 68.4 per cent in September 2021. The rejection was weaker the second time but still clear.
43550.m: Uri rejected a voting age of 16 in two votes.

43551.q: Which of these cantons rejected a voting age of 16 at the ballot box most narrowly?
43551.e: Neuchâtel rejected it in 2020 with 58.5 per cent voting no. In Basel-Landschaft, Uri and Aargau the share of no votes was much higher, in Aargau in 2024 almost 80 per cent.
43551.m: In 2020 Neuchâtel came closest to a voting age of 16.

43552.q: What happened in 2024 to the plan to introduce a voting age of 16 at federal level?
a: The people and the cantons accepted it
The Council of States put it into force
The Federal Council put it to the people
43552.e: The National Council had first supported the parliamentary initiative. At the start of 2024 it dropped the proposal, so the issue is off the table at federal level for now.
43552.m: At federal level, the voting age stays at 18 for now.

43553.q: Which explanation do political scientists give for why Glarus of all places accepted a voting age of 16?
a: The open vote at the Landsgemeinde
43553.e: Political scientist Daniel Kübler attributes the yes to the Landsgemeinde. At the ballot box, the proposal would probably have been rejected as it was elsewhere.
43553.m: The Landsgemeinde made a voting age of 16 possible in Glarus.

43554.q: Why may 16-year-olds in Glarus vote in Council of States elections but not in National Council elections?
a: The canton regulates the Council of States election
The Council of States is elected at the Landsgemeinde
The age for the National Council is 20
The Council of States is a youth chamber
43554.e: The Council of States election is a cantonal election, for which the cantonal voting age of 16 applies. For the National Council election, the federal voting age of 18 applies.
43554.m: In Glarus, 16-year-olds already help elect the Council of States.

43555.q: Which canton is the only one with a voting age of 16 at cantonal level (as of 2025)?
43555.e: Glarus introduced a voting age of 16 at the Landsgemeinde in 2007. In many other cantons it failed at the ballot box.
43555.m: Only Glarus has a cantonal voting age of 16.

43556.q: To whom are the adopted demands of the Federal Youth Session handed over?
a: The president of the National Council
43556.e: The Parliamentary Services then pass the demands on to the relevant committees of both chambers. These must take note of them and can take them up or decide not to.
43556.m: The demands of the Youth Session go to the president of the National Council.

43557.q: Who takes part in the Federal Youth Session?
a: Young people aged 14 to 21 from all over Switzerland
43557.e: Every year about 200 young people debate in the Federal Palace. You do not need to be a party member or have the right to vote.
43557.m: Young people aged 14 to 21 debate at the Youth Session.

43558.q: Which organisation has the main responsibility for the Federal Youth Session?
a: The Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs
The umbrella organisation of youth parties
43558.e: The Swiss National Youth Council (SAJV) runs the project. It is carried out by young volunteers on the organising committee and in the forum.
43558.m: The SAJV is responsible for the Federal Youth Session.

43559.q: What was held from 1997 to 2005 in addition to the Federal Youth Session?
a: Regional youth sessions in almost all cantons
A youth session in the European Parliament
A youth council in the Federal Council
43559.e: Regional sessions were meant to reach more young people. They took place in almost all cantons.
43559.m: Regional youth sessions were meant to broaden participation.

43560.q: Where is the Youth Session Forum present during the sessions of the Federal Parliament?
43560.e: The forum, with about ten members, represents the demands in the Federal Palace. It works with members of parliament across party lines.
43560.m: The Youth Session Forum follows up the demands directly in the Federal Palace.

43561.q: How binding are the demands of the Youth Session on Parliament?
a: They are examined but not binding
They go straight to the people
43561.e: The demands are submitted as petitions and dealt with by the relevant committees. These can take them up or decide not to.
43561.m: The demands of the Youth Session are suggestions, not laws.

43562.q: How old are the volunteers on the organising committee and in the forum of the Youth Session?
43562.e: The organising committee and the forum are made up of young volunteers aged between 16 and 25. They work unpaid and represent different political views.
43562.m: Young people organise the Youth Session for young people.

43563.q: Which fundamental right is the basis for handing the Youth Session's demands to Parliament?
43563.e: The demands are submitted as petitions. Everyone has the right of petition, including people without the right to vote.
43563.m: Even young people without the right to vote can approach the authorities with petitions.

43564.q: What is the task of the Youth Session Forum?
a: It follows up the demands of the Youth Session
It helps decide on laws in Parliament
It preselects the members of the Federal Council
It counts the votes in popular votes
43564.e: The forum is made up of about ten young people and young adults. It makes sure the demands are not forgotten after the session.
43564.m: The Youth Session Forum makes sure the demands are followed up.

43565.q: Which donations to a party must be disclosed under federal law?
a: Large donations over 15,000 francs per person per year
43565.e: Donations exceeding 15,000 francs per person per year must be disclosed. Smaller donations do not have to be reported individually.
43565.m: Only donations over 15,000 francs are disclosed.

43566.q: What is the penalty for deliberately breaking the transparency rules on political funding?
a: A prison sentence of up to ten years
Loss of the right to vote
43566.e: The Federal Act on Political Rights provides for fines of up to 40,000 francs. This also applies to unlawful anonymous or foreign donations.
43566.m: Breaches of the transparency rules are punished with a fine.

43567.q: What does the Swiss Federal Audit Office do if it suspects a breach of the transparency rules?
a: It reports it to the cantonal prosecuting authorities
It removes the party's parliamentary group
43567.e: The Audit Office cannot impose sanctions. It reports suspected cases to the relevant cantonal prosecuting authority.
43567.m: Only the prosecuting authorities may punish, not the Audit Office.

43568.q: What must a large National Council election campaign disclose before the election?
a: Nothing, it is reported only years later
43568.e: Campaigns spending more than 50,000 francs report their budget at least 45 days before the election. The final accounts follow after the election.
43568.m: Large election campaigns disclose their budget before the election.

43569.q: Under federal law, who must disclose campaign funding in Council of States elections?
a: Only those elected, after the election
Nobody, the Council of States is exempt
43569.e: For Council of States elections, the federal obligation only applies to elected people who spent more than 50,000 francs on their campaign. They submit their final accounts within 30 days of taking office; cantonal rules can require more.
43569.m: Under federal law, only those elected to the Council of States disclose their finances.

43570.q: How often must the parties in the Federal Assembly disclose their finances?
a: Only if there is a suspicion
43570.e: Parties report their income and large donations of the previous year annually. The first report, for 2023, was due by the end of June 2024.
43570.m: Parties disclose their finances every year.

43571.q: At which federal elections did the new transparency rules on political funding apply for the first time?
43571.e: The rules came into force on 23 October 2022. So they applied to the whole election year before the elections of 22 October 2023.
43571.m: The 2023 elections were the first with transparency rules.

43572.q: Besides the parties in the Federal Assembly, who else must disclose their funding?
a: Independent members of the Federal Assembly
The members of the Federal Council
43572.e: Besides the parties, members of parliament without a party must also disclose their donations every year. This leaves no loophole for independents.
43572.m: Independents in the Federal Parliament must also disclose their funding.

43573.q: Which federal body checks and publishes the information on political funding?
a: The Office of the Attorney General
43573.e: The Swiss Federal Audit Office collects the reports from parties and campaigns and makes them public. Since March 2024 this has also applied to referendum campaigns.
43573.m: The Audit Office publishes the information on political funding.

43574.q: In which year did the SVP first become the party with the largest share of the vote in National Council elections?
43574.e: In the 1999 elections the SVP reached 22.5 per cent, putting it ahead of the SP and FDP for the first time. It has been the strongest party ever since.
43574.m: Since 1999 the SVP has been Switzerland's strongest party.
